composer.name: François Couperin
composer.epithet: A Parisian organist whose harpsichord pieces turn ornament, delayed resolution and the timing of a released key into structural events.
facts: Nephew of Louis Couperin; succeeded his father Charles at Saint-Gervais
Organist of Saint-Gervais from 1685; royal chapel organist from 1693; royal chamber harpsichordist from 1717
Four books of harpsichord pieces, 27 ordres; organ masses, chamber music, motets and Leçons de Ténèbres
composer.background:
François Couperin belonged to a family whose connection with the organ of Saint-Gervais in Paris lasted for generations. His father Charles died in 1679, when François was ten; Michel-Richard de Lalande temporarily held the post intended for the boy. Couperin took it up in 1685. His uncle Louis, who had died before François was born, had already established a distinctive harpsichord language of broken chords, dance rhythms and unmeasured preludes. The younger Couperin inherited a profession and a repertory. His own published harpsichord music would increasingly substitute named character pieces for a predictable succession of dances.

In 1693 he won one of the four organist positions at Louis XIV’s royal chapel. Serving by quarter, he combined court employment with his Parisian responsibilities. He taught members of the royal family and took part in chamber performances; in 1717 he became a royal chamber harpsichordist. These overlapping appointments help explain his range: a musician who supplied an organ verset for a service might also teach the fingering of an ornament or play a concert with violin and viol.

era.heroCaption: Johannes Vermeer, The Music Lesson (Lady at the Virginals with a Gentleman)

forces: Two treble instruments and continuo; here violin, flute, viola da gamba and keyboard
performers: New Comma Baroque: Matthew C. Cataldi, Baroque violin; Leighann Daihl, Baroque flute; Phillip W. Serna, viola da gamba; Emily J. Morlan, historical keyboards
intro: Couperin puts an Italian-style trio sonata before the French dances of La Piémontaise. Two treble lines exchange phrases above a bass shared by viol and keyboard; the four players make three written parts.

cues.title: Three parts, four players
cues.text: Violin and flute carry the two upper lines; viol and keyboard share the bass. In this slow opening, listen for notes held across a change of harmony: one part waits to resolve while the others have already moved.

cues.title: A lower concert pitch
cues.text: The period instruments play at approximately A = 415 Hz, about a semitone below modern concert pitch. The score’s G minor consequently sounds lower than the same notes on a modern piano; the relationships between the parts remain unchanged.

cues.title: An inherited organ loft
cues.text: Couperin’s father Charles was organist of Saint-Gervais in Paris. When Charles died in 1679, the post was reserved for the ten-year-old François; Lalande held it until the boy could take over.

cues.title: The lines move faster
cues.text: The sustained opening gives way to quicker exchanges. Follow the little figures between violin and flute rather than treating one as melody and the other as accompaniment: their positions in the argument keep changing.

cues.title: The slow paragraph returns
cues.text: The quick passage closes and the notes lengthen again. Couperin’s sonade is built from these changes of pace, not from a single dance rhythm carried through from beginning to end.

cues.title: An Italian disguise
cues.text: In the preface to Les Nations, Couperin says he first presented one of his sonatas as the work of an Italian whose name was an anagram of his own. Its success encouraged him to write more. The account is Couperin’s own.

cues.title: Vivement et marqué
cues.text: The next quick section asks for marked articulation. The bass supplies a regular foundation while the upper parts exchange shorter figures; crisp beginnings make their imitation easier to follow.

cues.title: A royal chapel organist
cues.text: In 1693 Couperin became one of Louis XIV’s royal chapel organists. His work crossed church and chamber: organ masses, small sacred vocal works, keyboard lessons and music for an intimate instrumental company.

cues.title: An air, not an aria
cues.text: After the pause, the music becomes quieter and less busy. Couperin labels this part an air and asks for gracefulness: the melodic outline now matters more than the quick section’s running exchanges.

cues.title: Ornament and main note
cues.text: Throughout these airs, distinguish a line’s principal notes from the ornaments around them. A trill can delay the arrival on a stable note; it is part of the phrase’s timing, not an extra layer applied after the melody.

cues.title: Four names in print
cues.text: Les Nations appeared in 1726 as four ordres: La Françoise, L’Espagnole, L’Impériale and La Piémontaise. Each joins an Italian-style sonata to French dances. The national titles do not turn the pieces into collections of local folk tunes.

cues.title: Minor colour within the airs
cues.text: The airs do not remain in one mode. Listen for the darker third of the minor and for the bass moving underneath the treble lines: a change of harmony can alter the character without requiring a louder sound.

cues.title: Teaching the release
cues.text: Couperin published L’Art de toucher le clavecin in 1716. It treats fingering, ornaments and articulation as practical questions. On a plucked keyboard, the instant when a finger leaves a key can matter as much as the attack.

cues.title: Major without a crescendo
cues.text: The major mode has returned, but the ensemble does not need a large increase in volume to announce it. Listen to the altered third of the chord and to the way a phrase settles over the bass.

cues.title: Corelli beside Lully
cues.text: Couperin also wrote musical apotheoses of Corelli and Lully. These named tributes make his aim explicit: Italian sonata writing and French dance could belong to the same repertory, rather than demand opposing allegiances.

cues.title: A marked final paragraph
cues.text: A cadence separates the airs from the conclusion. The sound gains weight again, with a measured pace before the final quick section. The change comes from articulation and harmonic movement within the same small ensemble.

cues.title: The last quick exchange
cues.text: The final Légèrement sets the parts moving again. Keep the bass in view beneath the upper lines: its regular progress prevents the shorter figures from obscuring where each phrase is heading.

cues.title: A cadence, then release
cues.text: The quick movement reaches its final cadence and the instruments release together. This ends the sonade; in the complete La Piémontaise, an allemande begins the French dance sequence that follows.

composer.name: Antonio Vivaldi
composer.epithet: A violinist and theatre composer who made the returning orchestral refrain organise a soloist’s changing keys, textures and physical risks.
facts: Violin with his father Giovanni Battista, a violinist at St Mark’s, Venice
Violin teacher at the Ospedale della Pietà from 1703; maestro de’ concerti from 1716; theatre work in Venice and other cities
More than 500 concertos; operas, sacred vocal music, sonatas and chamber cantatas
composer.background:
Vivaldi was born in Venice, the son of a barber who became a professional violinist at St Mark’s. Giovanni Battista Vivaldi taught his son the violin and remained involved in his musical work. Antonio trained for the priesthood and was ordained in 1703, acquiring the nickname il prete rosso, the red priest, from his hair. He soon ceased regularly celebrating Mass, later explaining that a condition of tightness in the chest prevented him. He travelled extensively, taught and managed operatic productions.

In 1703 the Ospedale della Pietà appointed him violin teacher. The Pietà was a charitable institution that cared for abandoned children; its celebrated performing body consisted of girls and women whose training could continue into adult professional responsibility within the institution. Concerts and services attracted Venetian patrons and foreign visitors. Vivaldi’s employment was periodically renewed and sometimes interrupted, but the connection endured for decades. The players supplied a practical laboratory: a concerto could be written for a particular instrumental skill, tried in performance, and followed by another that changed the problem.

performers: John Harrison, violin; Wichita State University Chamber Players; Robert Turizziani, conductor
intro: The opening refrain gives the orchestra something to return to while the solo violin pursues the birds, streams and storm of the accompanying sonnet. Programme and concerto form occupy the same bars.

cues.title: A refrain to remember
cues.text: The strings establish E major with short phrases and their quieter echoes. This is the ritornello: orchestral material that will return between the solo episodes, sometimes shortened or moved into another key.

cues.title: The birds answer
cues.text: The violin writing breaks into trills, repeated notes and little answering calls. These are the sonnet’s birds greeting spring; the change from a shared orchestral phrase to separate calls also marks the first episode.

cues.title: The Pietà’s violin teacher
cues.text: Vivaldi became violin teacher at Venice’s Ospedale della Pietà in 1703. The institution cared for abandoned children and maintained an exceptionally trained ensemble of girls and women; teaching and composing belonged to the same employment.

cues.title: A poem beside the parts
cues.text: The Four Seasons appeared in Amsterdam in 1725, with sonnets linked to the instrumental parts. The poems’ author is uncertain. They describe musical events already specified in the score, rather than supplying a later listener’s invented story.

cues.title: Thunder breaks the pattern
cues.text: The storm episode interrupts the settled major-key exchanges. Repeated-note tremors and rushing violin figures represent thunder and lightning; the harmony moves away from the opening E major towards the minor.

cues.title: Priest and theatre musician
cues.text: Vivaldi was ordained in 1703, the year of his Pietà appointment. His first surviving opera, Ottone in villa, reached the stage in Vicenza in 1713; he subsequently combined composing with the financial and practical work of an opera impresario.

cues.title: The refrain comes home
cues.text: E major reappears after the minor-key stretch. Listen for the familiar orchestral gesture rather than a new theme: the ritornello makes the return of the home key recognisable even when the surrounding violin figures change.

cues.title: The orchestra has the ending
cues.text: The closing refrain gives the ensemble the last word. Its compact phrases and echo dynamics replace the soloist’s more mobile writing; the final E major chord is allowed to decay before the recording ends.

composer.name: Jean-Philippe Rameau
composer.epithet: A theorist of chord roots who began his operatic career at fifty and made harmonic surprise part of French theatrical action.
facts: Organist in French provincial cities, including Clermont-Ferrand; first harpsichord book published in 1706
Traité de l’harmonie, 1722; Nouveau système de musique théorique, 1726
First opera, Hippolyte et Aricie, 1733; tragédies en musique, opéras-ballets and court entertainments
composer.background:
Rameau was born in Dijon, where his father worked as an organist. The documentation of his first four decades is much thinner than that of his Parisian operatic career. He held church appointments in several French cities, published a first book of harpsichord pieces in Paris in 1706, and worked again at Clermont-Ferrand before settling permanently in the capital in the early 1720s. Keyboards, church duties and the analysis of musical practice formed his training. By the time he wrote his first surviving opera he had already published the theoretical book for which his name was known.

The Traité de l’harmonie réduite à ses principes naturels appeared in 1722. Rameau proposed that chords and their connections could be understood through a fundamental bass. Inversion became central: a chord could retain its identity while one of its upper notes moved into the bass. His explanations developed across later books, and his claims to a foundation in nature changed as he engaged with acoustics. The theory attempts to explain why harmonic progressions cohere.

work: Nouvelles Suites de pièces de clavecin · Suite in A minor
intro: A gavotte becomes six variations, each preserving its harmonic route while changing what the hands must do. Marcelle Meyer plays the harpsichord score on piano, making the difference between held notes and rapid attacks especially clear.

cues.title: The dance before the variations
cues.text: The gavotte lays out the melody and harmonic route that all six doubles will retain. Its two strains repeat: the first is eight bars, the second sixteen. Remember the cadence points as well as the tune; later, rapid notes will fill the spaces between them.

cues.title: Before the Paris operas
cues.text: Rameau’s father was an organist in Dijon. Jean-Philippe also earned his living at church keyboards, including Clermont-Ferrand’s cathedral, before settling in Paris in the early 1720s. His first harpsichord book had appeared in 1706.

cues.title: The first double
cues.text: The right hand spins a continuous line of semiquavers above the theme in the left. A double is a variation, not a repeat played louder: the dance’s harmonic outline survives under a new distribution of movement.

cues.title: A theory of chord roots
cues.text: Rameau published his Traité de l’harmonie in 1722. Its fundamental bass follows the roots of chords, not necessarily their lowest sounding notes. Different arrangements of the same chord can therefore belong to one harmonic identity.

cues.title: The hands exchange jobs
cues.text: The second double reverses the first: the right hand keeps the theme while the left supplies the running semiquavers. Listen below the tune. The harmonic route is familiar, but the part doing the most work has changed register.

cues.title: Keep the cadence in view
cues.text: The fast notes are not a second, unrelated composition. Follow the approach to each cadence: the moving part fills out harmonies that occupied fewer attacks in the gavotte. Repetition lets you compare the route even when the surface becomes busier.

cues.title: Movement between the outer voices
cues.text: In the third double, the outer voices frame the quicker inner writing. Try following a held upper note while the notes underneath continue: one pianist must keep several different lengths of note audible at once.

cues.title: An opera debut at fifty
cues.text: Hippolyte et Aricie, Rameau’s first opera, opened in Paris in October 1733, just after his fiftieth birthday. His reputation as a theorist and keyboard composer came before the theatre career that would occupy his next three decades.

cues.title: Repeated notes, renewed attacks
cues.text: The fourth double makes repeated notes a technical problem in their own right. Each attack must speak cleanly without turning the pulse into a series of jolts; the underlying dance still determines where the phrase comes to rest.

cues.title: The tune inside the figuration
cues.text: The fifth double combines arpeggios and repeated notes in the right hand. The theme is embedded in that activity rather than placed plainly above it. Listen for the longer contour through the shorter attacks.

cues.title: The lower hand takes over
cues.text: The sixth double transfers the rapid pattern to the left hand. Its leaps and repeated attacks must remain distinct while the right hand gives the theme and harmony their shape. The piece ends with a change of keyboard mechanics, not a new melody.

cues.title: Weight without rushing
cues.text: Meyer gives the closing phrases more weight without abandoning their pulse. Keep listening for separate attacks in the lower line: the piano’s resonance can join successive notes, but Rameau’s figures still depend on their individual beginnings.

cues.title: The last chord dies away
cues.text: The keyboard stops its rapid motion and the final chord decays. There is no return of the gavotte in its original plain form: the sixth double supplies the ending.

composer.name: Johann Sebastian Bach
composer.epithet: An organist, teacher and church musician who made a bass line, a dance rhythm and a fugue subject carry the same argument.
facts: Family musicians in Eisenach and Ohrdruf; school at Lüneburg; study of German, French and Italian scores
Arnstadt · Mühlhausen · Weimar · Köthen · Thomaskantor in Leipzig, 1723–50
Organ, harpsichord, clavichord and violin; an examiner of organs and a teacher of keyboard players
Cantatas, Passions, the B minor Mass, organ and keyboard cycles, concertos, unaccompanied string music
composer.background:
Bach was born into a family of professional musicians in Eisenach, where his father Johann Ambrosius served as a town musician. The surname already meant a trade: relatives supplied organists, cantors and instrumentalists across Thuringia. His mother died in 1694 and his father in 1695; at ten he went to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist in Ohrdruf who had studied with Pachelbel. Keyboard instruction belonged to that household, alongside school and choir. In 1700 Bach travelled to Lüneburg, where a place in the choir of St Michael’s school gave a boy without substantial means access to an education and a musical library.

The early career was practical and local. After a brief appointment at Weimar, he became organist of the New Church in Arnstadt in 1703, with a recently built instrument to test and play. His duties included working with students, and the town’s records preserve disputes over both his behaviour and his music. In 1705 he obtained leave to hear Dieterich Buxtehude in Lübeck and stayed away much longer than authorised. Buxtehude’s organ works offered a model in which free passagework, recurring basses and strict counterpoint could occupy the same piece. Bach’s own organ preludes would retain that alternation between improvisatory display and composed argument.

work: The Well-Tempered Clavier, Book I · BWV 869
intro: The final fugue of Book I has four voices and a subject that uses all twelve notes of the chromatic scale. Listen for the subject’s semitone pairs inside the longer line: dissonance is built into its identity, not added afterwards.

cues.title: One voice, twelve notes
cues.text: One voice gives the subject without accompaniment. Its line includes all twelve notes of the chromatic scale, but this is not twelve-tone music: the notes lean towards and away from a clear B minor centre.

cues.title: The answer makes two
cues.text: A second voice takes up the subject at the dominant, F♯. The first does not disappear: it continues with a slower counter-line. The same pianist must make a new beginning audible without cutting off the phrase already in progress.

cues.title: A family trade
cues.text: Bach’s father was a town musician in Eisenach. After both parents died, the ten-year-old Johann Sebastian went to live with his elder brother Johann Christoph, an organist in Ohrdruf. Keyboard playing was a household profession before it became his own employment.

cues.title: Follow a middle voice
cues.text: Throughout the fugue, resist listening only to the highest notes. A subject in an inner part can carry the argument while the upper voice continues its counterpoint. Four voices mean four continuing lines, not four hands or four instruments.

cues.title: Every major and minor key
cues.text: Book I of The Well-Tempered Clavier is dated 1722. Its twenty-four pairs proceed from C major and C minor up through the keyboard to this B minor pair. “Well-tempered” requires a tuning usable in every key; it does not prescribe modern equal temperament.

cues.title: A quieter continuation
cues.text: The sound retreats without breaking the contrapuntal thread. Listen for the subject’s small semitone movements inside this quieter writing: reducing the weight of the attack need not make the dissonances less distinct.

cues.title: The texture gains weight
cues.text: The middle stretch grows brighter and more forceful. The tension comes from lines continuing against one another: a note can be consonant when it begins, then clash when another voice moves beneath it.

cues.title: A singer in the household
cues.text: In December 1721 Bach married Anna Magdalena Wilcke, a professional court singer. The keyboard books associated with her preserve music by Bach and other composers. Musical instruction and domestic performance shared the same household.

cues.title: Major harmonies within the fugue
cues.text: Major-key harmonies now provide a contrast to the prevailing minor. The subject’s identity survives a change of tonal surroundings: its intervals and rhythm remain recognisable even when their harmonic meaning changes.

cues.title: Copied before it was printed
cues.text: The Well-Tempered Clavier circulated in manuscript during Bach’s lifetime. Its first printed editions appeared only in the early nineteenth century. For the intervening generations of players, studying the collection often meant obtaining or making a handwritten copy.

cues.title: Let a clash remain
cues.text: In these minor-key passages, listen to how long a dissonance lasts before it resolves. Smoothing every collision with a change of emphasis can hide the independent voice-leading; the held note needs to remain audible while the other parts move.

cues.title: Music for appointed services
cues.text: Bach became Thomaskantor in Leipzig in 1723. Alongside teaching, he had to provide music for Sundays and feast days. His 1730 memorandum to the town council sets out the singers and instrumentalists he considered necessary for properly equipped church music.

cues.title: The strongest late surge
cues.text: The last stretch gains weight again. Listen for the bass as well as the top line: the ending has to settle the harmonic argument beneath all four voices, not merely stop the melody.

cues.title: A major third at the end
cues.text: The final harmony turns B minor into B major: D♮ gives way to D♯. This raised third, often called a Picardy third, changes the colour of the last chord without changing its root. Ishizaka lets it decay into silence.

forces: Flute, solo violin, obbligato harpsichord, strings and continuo
performers: Advent Chamber Orchestra; Roxana Pavel Goldstein, violin; Constance Schoepflin, flute; Matthew Ganong, harpsichord
intro: Three soloists share the foreground until the harpsichord takes it over. Bach expands an accompanist’s instrument into a solo voice, then gives it a cadenza long enough to interrupt the concerto’s normal balance.

cues.title: The orchestra sets the terms
cues.text: After a short lead-in, the strings establish the D major ritornello. Its coordinated rhythm gives the movement a recurring point of reference; the solo passages will loosen that coordination and explore other keys.

cues.title: Three instruments in conversation
cues.text: Flute, violin and harpsichord form the solo group. Listen for the keyboard’s moving notes as well as the two more sustained lines: it already has a written-out part beyond the chords normally supplied by a continuo player.

cues.title: A month in confinement
cues.text: Bach accepted the Köthen court’s offer in 1717 before obtaining permission to leave Weimar. His employer had him confined for almost a month. Only after his dismissal could he take up the new post with Prince Leopold.

cues.title: A turn towards the minor
cues.text: The tonal ground has darkened towards B minor, D major’s relative minor. The change does not require a new speed: the continuing pulse carries the soloists into a different harmonic region.

cues.title: A dedication, not a premiere
cues.text: Bach dated the manuscript of the six concertos 24 March 1721 and dedicated it to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg. The date belongs to the presentation copy; the collection brings together music with different compositional histories.

cues.title: A figure at another pitch
cues.text: Listen for sequences: a short pattern repeats higher or lower while its harmony changes. The repeated shape makes the passage intelligible even when the notes move quickly; the bass tells you whether it is approaching a cadence or continuing elsewhere.

cues.title: A quieter, busier texture
cues.text: The sound becomes lighter without losing its rapid internal movement. This is an important concerto distinction: fewer or softer-sounding parts need not mean fewer notes. Listen to the keyboard activity underneath the longer instrumental lines.

cues.title: Weight returns to the ensemble
cues.text: The texture gains weight and the pulse becomes more emphatic. Compare the coordinated attacks with the thinner passage just before: the concerto’s contrasts depend on how parts move together, not only on which instrument carries the tune.

cues.title: D major comes into view
cues.text: The home key becomes stable again. The returning orchestral material is useful as a landmark, but it is not yet the ending: the harpsichord’s largest intervention still lies ahead.

cues.title: Prince Leopold’s court
cues.text: Bach worked at Köthen from 1717 to 1723. The court’s Calvinist worship did not demand the elaborate weekly cantatas later required in Leipzig. Its instrumental ensemble gave him a different centre of professional activity: chamber and orchestral music.

cues.title: The later coffeehouse concerts
cues.text: From 1729 Bach directed Leipzig’s Collegium Musicum, associated with Zimmermann’s coffeehouse. There he performed instrumental music outside the church service, including keyboard concertos. The public keyboard soloist was part of his working life, not merely an idea on paper.

cues.title: The harpsichord is left alone
cues.text: The other instruments fall away and the harpsichord begins its extended cadenza. Without sustained flute or bowed strings, the sound is made entirely of plucked attacks and their decay. The former accompanist now has to supply melody, bass and harmonic direction alone.

cues.title: Listen through the quick notes
cues.text: Throughout the cadenza, follow the bass beneath the running figures. A rapid arpeggio spreads one chord across time; a sequence moves the same pattern through different chords. The number of attacks alone does not tell you how quickly the harmony changes.

cues.title: A composed display
cues.text: Bach writes out this solo rather than leaving an empty space for improvisation. The changing figures belong to the movement’s construction. Listen for how the same two hands keep a bass line distinct while moving rapidly through the keyboard’s upper registers.

cues.title: The dominant keeps returning
cues.text: The cadenza repeatedly comes back to A, the dominant of D. That bass note points towards the home key without allowing the orchestra to re-enter yet; the upper notes keep changing its immediate harmonic colour.

cues.title: Preparing the ensemble’s return
cues.text: The keyboard still has the whole texture to itself. Listen for the contrast that is approaching: the last solo figures will give way to the opening ensemble rhythm, so the return is a change in the way sound is produced as well as a return of material.

cues.title: The ritornello ends the solo
cues.text: The orchestra returns in D major with the familiar ritornello. The harpsichord gives up its unaccompanied foreground, and the coordinated string rhythm restores the proportions heard at the beginning.

cues.title: A full ensemble cadence
cues.text: The movement closes with the orchestra, not with one more solo flourish. The final D major chord releases into the room; the concerto’s quieter Affettuoso follows in the complete work.

composer.name: George Frideric Handel
composer.epithet: A German-trained composer of Italian opera who made the English chorus an actor in public musical drama.
facts: With Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow in Halle; theatre work in Hamburg; study and commissions in Italy, 1706–10
Hanover briefly; settled in London in 1712; became a British subject in 1727
Italian operas, English oratorios, anthems, concertos, chamber cantatas and ceremonial orchestral music
composer.background:
Handel grew up in Halle, the son of a barber-surgeon, and studied with Friedrich Wilhelm Zachow, organist of the town’s principal church. Zachow’s teaching included counterpoint, keyboard playing and the copying of other composers’ music. Handel briefly enrolled at the university and held an organist’s post before moving to Hamburg in 1703. Its public opera house offered a different education: he played in the orchestra and encountered the practical demands of singers, stage machinery and mixed theatrical repertory. His first opera, Almira, was performed there in 1705, with a German text incorporating Italian arias.

From 1706 to 1710 Handel worked in Italy, writing cantatas, sacred music and opera for patrons in Florence, Rome, Naples and Venice. Rome gave him access to virtuoso singers and to instrumentalists associated with Corelli. The Latin Dixit Dominus of 1707 demands rapid, independent choral lines and sustained control of dissonance; the chamber cantatas make emotional turns within much smaller forces. Agrippina, performed in Venice at the end of 1709, assembles much previously written material into a calculated theatrical comedy. Reuse was already part of his method: a successful musical gesture could acquire a different function when assigned to a new character and situation.

forces: Chorus and orchestra with trumpets and timpani
performers: London Symphony Orchestra; London Philharmonic Choir; Hermann Scherchen, conductor; Frederick Jackson, chorus master
intro: The chorus that closes Part II alternates three kinds of speech: a tune sung together, a line passed between voices, and long notes held above moving counterpoint. Its force comes from those changes of texture, not from singing everything loudly.

composer.name: Domenico Scarlatti
composer.epithet: An Italian court musician in Lisbon and Madrid who made keyboard sonatas out of hand crossings, repeated notes and abrupt changes of harmonic ground.
facts: Son of the opera composer Alessandro Scarlatti; born in the same year as Bach and Handel
Naples and Rome; Portuguese royal service from 1719; followed Maria Bárbara to Spain in 1729
555 keyboard sonatas in Ralph Kirkpatrick’s catalogue; earlier operas, cantatas and sacred music
composer.background:
Domenico Scarlatti was born in Naples, the sixth child of Alessandro Scarlatti, an established composer of opera and sacred music. He entered professional musical life as a teenager, working as an organist and composing for the stage. Domenico eventually concentrated on keyboard music in courts far from Naples, taking a different path from his father’s large operatic career. His first decades included church appointments, singers, theatrical commissions and the practical education of a musician expected to supply whatever his employer required.

In Rome he worked for the exiled Polish queen Maria Casimira and at St Peter’s, writing both opera and sacred music. The ten-part Stabat Mater, usually associated with these Roman years, combines four soprano lines with pairs of altos, tenors and basses. Its voices enter in changing combinations, and the density of the counterpoint can contract around a particular text.

composer.name: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach
composer.epithet: A keyboard player who made hesitation, interruption and a change of mind into musical form.
facts: With his father, Johann Sebastian Bach; law studies at Leipzig and Frankfurt an der Oder
Keyboard player to Frederick II in Berlin and Potsdam, 1740–67 · Hamburg music director, 1768–88

composer.background:
Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach was the second surviving son of Johann Sebastian Bach and Maria Barbara Bach. He was born in Weimar in 1714; Georg Philipp Telemann was one of his godfathers. The family moved to Cöthen in 1717 and Leipzig in 1723, where his father became Thomaskantor. Emanuel learned the keyboard and composition at home, then studied law at Leipzig and Frankfurt an der Oder. He made music his profession: by 1738 he had entered the circle of the Prussian crown prince Frederick, who became king in 1740.

Frederick played the flute, composed and maintained an orchestra whose leading musicians included Johann Joachim Quantz and the brothers Graun. Bach’s employment was chiefly as a keyboard accompanist. In his own publications he pursued a style independent of the king’s Italianate melodic preferences. His six ‘Prussian’ keyboard sonatas of 1742 and six ‘Württemberg’ sonatas of 1744 put contrasting textures, unexpected rests and highly ornamented slow movements inside the three-movement sonata. The player had to manage changes of character as precisely as changes of fingering.

intro: A clavichord can alter a note after the finger has struck it. In this late fantasia, Bach makes an instrument quiet enough for a private room speak in interruptions, pauses and sudden changes of register.

cues.title: A very quiet instrument
cues.text: The clavichord’s metal tangents strike the strings and remain in contact while the keys are held. Unlike a harpsichord, it responds to changes of finger pressure after the attack; the player controls the note’s continuation as well as its beginning.

cues.title: Speech becomes a run
cues.text: The separated gestures gather into quicker notes, then pull back again. Listen to the gaps between them: a pause can end a sentence without supplying a comfortable final chord.

cues.title: A practical book
cues.text: Bach published the two parts of his Essay on the True Art of Playing Keyboard Instruments in 1753 and 1762. Fingering, ornaments, accompaniment and improvisation belong to the same practical education: expression is something a player learns to do.

cues.title: The king’s accompanist
cues.text: From 1740 Bach served Frederick II of Prussia, who played the flute. His employment required accompaniment at the royal keyboard; his own sonatas and fantasias allowed abrupt changes of character that went beyond the king’s preferred style.

cues.title: The pace changes
cues.text: The music begins another stretch of faster figuration. A free fantasia does not promise a single continuous tempo: a run can accelerate the argument without establishing a new movement.

cues.title: Room around each note
cues.text: The busy passage subsides into widely separated attacks. Benson lets the decay of the instrument occupy the spaces that a modern piano could fill with sustained resonance.

cues.title: Hamburg after Berlin
cues.text: In 1768 Bach succeeded Telemann as Hamburg’s music director. Responsibility for the city’s principal churches replaced service to one king; church music, teaching and public concerts occupied the last twenty years of his life.

cues.title: Punctuation without bar-lines
cues.text: Much of this fantasia dispenses with regular bar-lines. Follow the length of a gesture rather than trying to count a constant beat: an isolated chord, a melodic answer and a flourish need not occupy equal amounts of time.

cues.title: Pressure, then a break
cues.text: This is one of the recording’s strongest outbursts. The sound grows markedly louder, then drops almost out of hearing; the interruption matters as much as the run that precedes it.

cues.title: A sentence breaks off
cues.text: Another retreat leaves only a few attacks in the next phrase. The clavichord cannot sustain a long orchestral crescendo, so contrast comes from the weight and spacing of successive notes.

cues.title: Burney at the clavichord
cues.text: Charles Burney visited Bach in Hamburg in 1772 and described him playing the clavichord until nearly eleven at night. His account singles out expression and variety of modulation, rather than rapid execution alone.

cues.title: Connoisseurs and amateurs
cues.text: From 1779 Bach issued keyboard collections for “Kenner und Liebhaber” — connoisseurs and amateurs. Sonatas, rondos and fantasias shared those volumes; the distinction concerned different sorts of listener, not simply easy and difficult pieces.

cues.title: More notes, more force
cues.text: The small-scale gestures gather into another rapid passage. The increase in activity is also an increase in loudness, not merely an ornamental layer added to the same quiet line.

cues.title: An abrupt restart
cues.text: The rapid texture stops and the music resumes with fewer, more widely spaced notes. Bach changes the manner of speaking without inserting the formal silence that would separate two movements.

cues.title: His father’s pupil
cues.text: Emanuel was Johann Sebastian Bach’s second surviving son and learned music from him. The family connection does not make this a late Baroque suite: the free fantasia puts interruption and the performer’s handling of time at the centre of its design.

cues.title: A crest without a finish
cues.text: A louder phrase gives way to another quiet suspension. Listen for how little the volume tells you about finality: a strong arrival can be followed by a new question rather than an ending.

cues.title: The fingers accelerate
cues.text: Quick notes again crowd the line. The gestures remain short enough to change direction suddenly; the following retreat is built into the passage rather than added as a separate slow section.

cues.title: The last keyboard years
cues.text: The fantasia dates from 1787. That year also brought the sixth collection for connoisseurs and amateurs and new teaching pieces for the third edition of the Essay’s first part: Bach was still composing, publishing and revising his teaching material.

cues.title: Keep the pauses audible
cues.text: Throughout these quiet phrases, listen for the distinction between a held note and a gap after its release. On a clavichord, the end of the finger’s contact is an audible part of articulation.

cues.title: One last fast passage
cues.text: The texture becomes busy and forceful once more. This final burst soon gives way to the widely spaced notes of the closing Largo.

cues.title: The closing Largo
cues.text: The last slow passage restores measured time after the free figuration. The music withdraws instead of adding a final display of speed.

cues.title: The last resonance
cues.text: The final notes decay into silence. Leave the quiet intact: the recording preserves several seconds after the instrument has stopped.

composer.name: Joseph Haydn
composer.epithet: A court musician who taught the symphony and quartet to argue with the listener’s expectations.
facts: Choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral, Vienna; practical instruction from Nicola Porpora
Esterházy household, 1761–1809; active court duties reduced after 1790
Visits in 1791–92 and 1794–95; twelve symphonies for the English public
104 numbered symphonies · string quartets · keyboard sonatas and trios · masses · operas · oratorios
composer.background:
Haydn was born in Rohrau, near the border between Lower Austria and Hungary, in 1732. His father was a wheelwright who sang and played the harp by ear; his mother had worked as a cook. Music began at home. After early schooling in Hainburg, he became a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. The work gave him daily experience of church music and a singer’s understanding of phrases, but little systematic composition teaching. When his voice broke, he lost the position and had to earn his living outside the cathedral.

In the 1750s he taught, accompanied and played whatever engagements he could obtain. Working for the singing teacher and composer Nicola Porpora gave him practical instruction in Italian vocal style. He studied scores and keyboard music, including the sonatas of C. P. E. Bach, whose sudden contrasts offered another model besides the regular phrases of the fashionable galant style. Employment by Count Morzin in the late 1750s brought an orchestra and the first symphonies. In 1760 he married Maria Anna Keller; the marriage was unhappy and childless. His professional stability came from a different household.

intro: The loud chord is only the first interruption. Haydn takes a tune made from a few notes of C major through four variations, changing its scoring, mode and rhythmic density without losing its outline.

cues.title: Almost a nursery tune
cues.text: Quiet strings present a tune built largely from the notes of a C major chord. Its regular phrases and repeated notes make it easy to remember; the variations will need that memory.

cues.title: The famous interruption
cues.text: The repeated phrase has become quieter still. Its last chord is about to arrive with the full orchestra and timpani: the surprise is a change of volume, not a wrong note.

cues.title: Variation one: decoration
cues.text: The first variation keeps the theme’s harmonic route and adds a more active violin line. Listen beneath the decoration for the same regular arrivals: new notes do not yet mean a new shape.

cues.title: From court to London
cues.text: Haydn entered Esterházy service in 1761. After Prince Nikolaus died in 1790, the reduced court establishment left him free to accept Johann Peter Salomon’s invitation to London; the composer arrived there in January 1791.

cues.title: Variation two: minor
cues.text: C major turns to C minor, and the orchestra presses harder. The tune’s familiar outline survives, but E♭ replaces E: a small pitch change alters the character of the whole phrase.

cues.title: A paying public
cues.text: Salomon was a violinist as well as an impresario. His London concerts placed Haydn’s new symphonies before ticket-buying listeners rather than a single household; the twelve London symphonies were written for the visits of 1791–92 and 1794–95.

cues.title: Variation three: less weight
cues.text: The minor-key force gives way to a quieter C major variation. Haydn changes the scoring as well as the notes: wind colour and lighter accompaniment restore space around the melody.

cues.title: The orchestra he knew
cues.text: At Eszterháza Haydn composed, rehearsed, directed opera and dealt with the musicians’ practical needs. Decades of writing for a resident ensemble preceded these London works; his orchestral contrasts came from daily experience with players.

cues.title: Variation four: more force
cues.text: The last variation brings a stronger orchestral attack and quicker internal movement. The simple theme now supports much more activity than it did at the beginning.

cues.title: Not Haydn’s title
cues.text: “Surprise” is the English nickname. German audiences call the symphony “Mit dem Paukenschlag” — “with the drum stroke”. Both names single out one event in a four-movement work.

cues.title: The largest sound yet
cues.text: The variation reaches its broadest orchestral weight. Listen for how the tune’s short phrases keep the mass of sound organised before Haydn cuts the volume away.

cues.title: The coda looks back
cues.text: The quiet coda changes the harmony underneath the familiar tune. This is a different sort of surprise from the early drum stroke: the wind melody remains recognisable while the accompanying chords make it less settled.

cues.title: A quiet conclusion
cues.text: C major settles without another large orchestral blow. The movement ends at the opposite dynamic extreme from its last variation.

composer.name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
composer.epithet: An opera composer whose instrumental music gives different voices the freedom to disagree.
facts: By his father Leopold; extensive performing tours from childhood
Salzburg · Italy · Mannheim and Paris · Vienna from 1781
Italian opera seria and opera buffa; German Singspiel with spoken dialogue

composer.background:
Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756, the seventh child of Leopold Mozart and Anna Maria Pertl; only he and his sister Maria Anna survived infancy. Leopold was a violinist and composer in the archbishop’s service, and in the year of Wolfgang’s birth published an influential violin treatise. He taught both children. Maria Anna, called Nannerl within the family, became an accomplished keyboard player, and the first tours presented brother and sister together. The family’s travels were an educational system as well as a business: the children encountered instruments, performers, repertories and audiences that a Salzburg childhood alone could not have supplied.

The long tour of 1763–66 took them through German courts, Paris, London and the Netherlands. In London Mozart met Johann Christian Bach, whose clear phrases and Italianate melodic style offered a model different from the contrapuntal teaching associated with Bach’s father. Illness repeatedly interrupted the itinerary. Leopold managed engagements, publicity and money while supervising composition, and the surviving correspondence documents the costs and uncertainties behind the public demonstrations. Wolfgang learned to write for named performers and immediate occasions before he had an independent adult household.

intro: No ceremonial introduction: the accompaniment is already moving when the violin tune arrives. The same falling semitone supplies melody, transition and contrapuntal argument across this compact sonata movement.

cues.title: Exposition: already in motion
cues.text: The violas begin the accompaniment; the violins enter with repeated notes leaning down a semitone. That small interval is the first theme’s working material, not merely an expressive decoration.

cues.title: The transition interrupts
cues.text: The fuller orchestra drives away from the quiet opening. Faster movement and stronger attacks prepare a contrasting tonal area rather than simply repeating the violin tune more loudly.

cues.title: The second theme
cues.text: The second theme belongs to B♭ major, G minor’s relative major. Strings and winds share a chromatic line; the phrases move by semitone even though the larger harmonic setting has changed.

cues.title: Three symphonies in 1788
cues.text: Mozart entered his last three symphonies in his catalogue during the summer of 1788. Their keys are E♭ major, G minor and C major; the intended concerts remain uncertain, so the Forty’s agitation is not evidence of a documented private programme.

cues.title: Development, without the repeat
cues.text: This performance omits the exposition repeat. Instead of hearing the opening again in G minor, we meet its motif in the remote key of F♯ minor; Mozart now breaks it into fragments and moves those fragments between parts.

cues.title: A fragment in several voices
cues.text: Throughout this development, listen for the first theme’s small cell rather than a complete melody. Imitation lets different parts begin the same idea before the previous statement has finished.

cues.title: Vienna, not a court post
cues.text: Mozart settled in Vienna in 1781 after leaving the service of Salzburg’s archbishop. Teaching, concerts, publication and commissions supported his household; by 1788 his letters to Michael Puchberg were repeatedly asking for loans.

cues.title: Recapitulation: the opening returns
cues.text: The first theme returns in G minor. In sonata form, a recapitulation must do more than bring back a tune: it must redirect music that previously left home so that the later themes can remain in the tonic.

cues.title: A longer route home
cues.text: The transition is substantially expanded on its return. Mozart brings developmental counterpoint into the recapitulation; familiar material does not mean the argument has become predictable.

cues.title: The second theme, altered
cues.text: The second theme returns in the tonic region, now G minor rather than B♭ major. Its outline is familiar, but the harmonic change removes the contrast that the exposition established.

cues.title: Two orchestral versions
cues.text: Mozart later added clarinets to this symphony and rewrote the oboe parts around them. Both versions survive. The revision documents his return to the work; it does not tell us the exact circumstances of its first performance.

cues.title: Coda: one more insistence
cues.text: After the closing material appears to have made its point, Mozart adds a final extension. Quiet chords interrupt the pressure, then the opening motif helps force the last G minor cadence; there is no turn to a consoling major ending.

work: Clarinet Concerto in A major, K. 622
performers: William McColl, basset clarinet; University of Washington Symphony Orchestra, Abraham Kaplan
intro: Mozart wrote this concerto for a clarinet with extra low notes, not the standard orchestral instrument. William McColl plays a basset clarinet he built himself: listen to the distance between its low register and the singing upper line.

cues.title: The soloist begins
cues.text: The clarinet starts the slow movement without a long orchestral introduction. Its D major melody moves in phrases shaped for breath, with a spare accompaniment that leaves the solo line exposed.

cues.title: The orchestra answers
cues.text: The orchestra repeats the melody with greater weight. The exchange is not a contest of volume: Mozart lets a phrase first heard from one player become a statement for the ensemble.

cues.title: The crowded year 1791
cues.text: Mozart completed the concerto in 1791, the year of The Magic Flute and La clemenza di Tito. He died on 5 December, leaving the Requiem unfinished; the concerto belongs to that concentrated final year, not to a documented farewell programme.

cues.title: Keep hearing the breath
cues.text: Throughout the opening section, listen to how each melodic clause reaches a point where a singer could breathe. The orchestra can repeat the shape, but the clarinet makes the physical length of the phrase particularly apparent.

cues.title: The middle section
cues.text: The central episode keeps the clarinet in the foreground and gives it more mobile figuration. A major, the dominant of D, becomes an important point of reference as the soloist moves farther from the opening melody.

cues.title: Stadler’s extra low notes
cues.text: Anton Stadler’s basset clarinet extended below the ordinary instrument’s written low E to low C. Mozart wrote the concerto for that range. McColl uses a basset clarinet of his own construction in this recording.

cues.title: Ornament becomes the line
cues.text: Here the solo writing is more active than the opening song. Listen for movement between registers rather than treating every run as a detachable flourish: the changing register is part of the phrase.

cues.title: Preparing the return
cues.text: The middle section draws towards a cadence and relaxes. The opening melody will return after this preparation, rather than arriving through the abrupt cut that begins some of Mozart’s fast movements.

cues.title: The opening melody returns
cues.text: The clarinet restores the first melody in D major. This is a three-part design: opening song, contrasting middle and a shortened return, rather than a sonata development and recapitulation.

cues.title: A missing manuscript
cues.text: Mozart’s complete autograph of the concerto is lost. The early published version adapted the low passages for ordinary clarinet; modern basset-clarinet editions reconstruct the extended line from the surviving evidence rather than from a complete original score.

cues.title: The ensemble takes over
cues.text: The orchestra gives the returning material a fuller answer. Its stronger sound briefly replaces the exposed solo texture before the clarinet resumes the closing discussion.

cues.title: Coda, not another episode
cues.text: The closing passage prolongs D major instead of introducing another contrasting section. The clarinet can still decorate the line, but the harmonies increasingly confirm the home key.

cues.title: A university performance
cues.text: William McColl plays with the University of Washington Symphony Orchestra under Abraham Kaplan. The recording dates from December 1987; the instrument is McColl’s reconstruction, not an eighteenth-century clarinet preserved from Stadler’s lifetime.

cues.title: The final D major
cues.text: The last cadence confirms D major and the sound falls away. The soloist’s low register belongs to the same instrument as the opening singing line; no second clarinet has been added for the descent.

composer.name: Ludwig van Beethoven
composer.epithet: A pianist who turned small rhythmic cells into long arguments, then rebuilt the forms that contained them.
facts: Christian Gottlob Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792 · Vienna and its surrounding villages thereafter
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · one opera
Progressive hearing loss documented in letters from 1801; conversation books used from 1818
composer.background:
Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770, probably on 16 December, and baptised on 17 December. His father Johann sang in the electoral court chapel, and his grandfather Ludwig had been its Kapellmeister. The family name came from the Low Countries; the ‘van’ did not indicate nobility. Johann attempted to present his son as a child prodigy, but Beethoven’s more substantial training came from Christian Gottlob Neefe, who introduced him to Bach’s keyboard music and helped him obtain work as an organist. Playing viola in the court orchestra also gave him practical knowledge of instrumental and operatic repertory.

The Bonn years supplied more than a musical apprenticeship. The court of Elector Maximilian Franz, educated patrons and friends such as the Breuning family brought Beethoven into contact with Enlightenment literature and social ideas. After his mother’s death in 1787 and his father’s worsening incapacity, he assumed increasing responsibility for the household. In 1792 he left for Vienna to study with Haydn. The intended period of further training became permanent residence: the French occupation of Bonn in 1794 ended the old electoral establishment to which he might have returned.

intro: The four-note opening is not just a tune. Beethoven uses its rhythm as accompaniment, transition and punctuation, so that a whole sonata movement can grow from something the listener remembers after two seconds.

cues.title: A rest, then four notes
cues.text: Each opening gesture begins after a rest. Three short notes drive into a held note, but the second held note occupies more written time than the first; the two statements are not exact rhythmic copies.

cues.title: Rhythm underneath the tune
cues.text: Throughout the first-theme group, follow the short-short-short-long rhythm as it passes through the texture. Beethoven can make it an accompaniment or an answering figure without giving it a new melodic identity.

cues.title: A major-key second theme
cues.text: The second group turns towards E♭ major, the relative major of C minor. Its more sustained melody contrasts with the opening, but the short rhythmic cell persists underneath: contrast does not require wholly unrelated material.

cues.title: The long premiere concert
cues.text: The Fifth was first performed at Vienna’s Theater an der Wien on 22 December 1808. The same concert included the Sixth Symphony, the Choral Fantasy and the first public performance of the Fourth Piano Concerto, with Beethoven as soloist.

cues.title: The exposition is repeated
cues.text: The opening comes back because the players take Beethoven’s repeat. This is not the recapitulation: we hear the exposition’s departure from C minor to E♭ major a second time before the development begins.

cues.title: Recognise the same route
cues.text: On the repeat, listen beyond the famous opening. The rising pressure of the transition and the softer second group occur in the same order; remembering that route makes the later changes in the recapitulation audible.

cues.title: Several works at once
cues.text: Beethoven first sketched the Fifth in 1804, then returned to it in 1807. Between those stages came work on Leonore, the Fourth Symphony, the Violin Concerto and the “Razumovsky” quartets; the Fifth was not written in one uninterrupted burst.

cues.title: Development: the ground moves
cues.text: The development begins without another complete exposition. Beethoven takes the short cell through changing harmonies and separates its components, making a familiar rhythm work without the familiar sequence of themes.

cues.title: Less than a melody
cues.text: Listen for how short the working units become. A rhythm, a sustained note or an exchange between orchestral groups can carry the development after the complete opening tune has disappeared.

cues.title: The texture loses weight
cues.text: The sound thins during the later development. The return will be effective partly because Beethoven has reduced the orchestra’s weight before restoring the opening gesture.

cues.title: Recapitulation: the opening enlarged
cues.text: The opening rhythm returns with much greater orchestral weight. This is the recapitulation: the movement’s earlier materials now have to stay connected to C, rather than establish E♭ as a second tonal centre.

cues.title: The oboe interrupts
cues.text: The recapitulation pauses for an oboe’s short, unaccompanied Adagio. This interruption has no equivalent at the same point in the exposition: one player briefly suspends the orchestral pulse.

cues.title: The second theme comes home
cues.text: The second group returns in C major rather than E♭ major. Changing the tonic’s mode allows the lyrical material to remain major, but the movement has not yet secured a major-key ending.

cues.title: The unsent testament
cues.text: In 1802 Beethoven wrote to his brothers about his worsening hearing and isolation while staying at Heiligenstadt. The document remained unsent. The Fifth followed years later; its rhythmic argument is not a literal transcription of that letter.

cues.title: Coda: another development
cues.text: The coda is not a few closing chords. It renews the pressure, turns away from the recapitulation’s major mode and works the small rhythmic units again before the final C minor close.

cues.title: The rhythm keeps working
cues.text: Throughout this extended ending, hear the opening cell as a means of continuation, not just recognition. Repeated attacks and replies keep postponing a cadence that could otherwise have ended the movement much sooner.

cues.title: Only the first movement
cues.text: The movement closes in C minor. The symphony’s C major breakthrough belongs to the finale, two movements later, where Beethoven adds piccolo, contrabassoon and trombones; none of those instruments is part of this opening movement.

intro: A sixteen-bar theme supports six variations, then returns without its accumulated decoration. The central problem is how far Beethoven can change rhythm, texture and register while keeping the theme’s harmonic outline audible.

composer.name: Franz Schubert
composer.epithet: A Viennese songwriter who made the piano an equal narrator, and carried the harmonic dislocations of the Lied into symphonies and chamber music.
facts: Vienna Stadtkonvikt, 1808–13; composition with Antonio Salieri, 1812–16
Assistant in his father’s school; music tutor to the Esterházy family at Zseliz in 1818 and 1824; thereafter chiefly an independent composer
Johann Michael Vogl · Josef von Spaun · Franz von Schober · Johann Mayrhofer · Moritz von Schwind

composer.background:
Schubert grew up in a schoolmaster’s household in Himmelpfortgrund, then a suburb of Vienna. His father taught him violin, his brother Ignaz taught him piano, and the parish musician Michael Holzer supplied further instruction. Family quartet sessions put Franz on viola, between the melody and the bass: he knew chamber music from an inner part. In 1808 he entered the imperial chapel choir and the Stadtkonvikt boarding school. Its orchestra introduced him to Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven as a player, while Antonio Salieri began giving him composition lessons in 1812.

After leaving the school in 1813, he trained as a teacher and became an assistant in his father’s classroom. Composition continued around the timetable. Gretchen am Spinnrade, dated 19 October 1814, gives Goethe’s girl a right-hand spinning wheel, a left-hand treadle and a vocal line that repeatedly tries to escape them. Schubert was seventeen. In 1815 he wrote roughly 140 songs, including Erlkönig, as well as symphonies, church music and stage works. Voice and piano already carried distinct dramatic responsibilities in his songs.

work: Impromptu in G♭ major, D. 899 No. 3
intro: The right hand has two jobs: carrying the melody and keeping the broken chords in motion underneath it. Schubert makes a single pianist sustain a singer, an accompaniment and a bass line at three different levels of weight.

composer.name: Hector Berlioz
composer.epithet: He made orchestral colour, the position of a sound in space, and the return of a remembered melody into structural events.
facts: Flute and guitar as a boy; Paris Conservatoire with Jean-François Le Sueur and Anton Reicha
Critic for the Journal des débats; Conservatoire librarian; touring conductor
Shakespeare, Goethe and Virgil supplied the subjects of his largest works
Four symphonies; operas; dramatic and sacred choral works; songs; an orchestration treatise
composer.background:
Berlioz grew up in La Côte-Saint-André, between Lyon and Grenoble, in the household of a physician who taught him Latin and expected him to study medicine. He learned flute and guitar, but never acquired the pianist’s routine of composing at a keyboard. Virgil’s account of Dido’s death affected him as a schoolboy; forty years later he would set it in Les Troyens. Sent to Paris in 1821, he attended anatomy lectures while spending his evenings at the Opéra. The theatre’s performances of Gluck offered a different education: declamation, orchestral gesture and the pacing of a dramatic scene.

He abandoned medicine, studied with Jean-François Le Sueur and entered the Conservatoire in 1826. His first large works included a Messe solennelle and the unfinished opera Les Francs-juges, whose overture survived independently. The Prix de Rome required a prescribed cantata; Berlioz finally won it in 1830, on his fourth attempt. The prize sent him to the Villa Medici, but the decisive musical experiences had already happened in Paris. Conservatoire performances under François-Antoine Habeneck introduced him to Beethoven’s symphonies, while an English theatrical company introduced him to Shakespeare.

movement: IV. Marche au supplice — Allegretto non troppo
intro: Berlioz makes an execution march the fourth movement of a symphony. Low strings, brass and percussion turn a regular tread into public spectacle; one remembered melody interrupts the machinery.

cues.title: An execution in a dream
cues.text: This is the fourth of five movements. In Berlioz’s printed programme, an opium-dazed musician dreams that he has murdered his beloved and is being led to execution; the quiet opening prepares the procession rather than announcing a triumphant march.

cues.title: The melody walks down
cues.text: Cellos and double basses carry a descending march tune. Its weight comes from the low register and repeated steps; the answering orchestral accents interrupt rather than smooth out the line.

cues.title: An actress in Paris
cues.text: Berlioz saw Harriet Smithson as Ophelia and Juliet in Paris in 1827. She inspired the symphony’s beloved, but did not attend its premiere; hearing the revised work in December 1832 brought them together. They married in October 1833.

cues.title: The brass take command
cues.text: The march becomes louder and more openly ceremonial. The brass-led tune turns towards B♭ major, the relative major of G minor: the same two-flat key signature can support both the prisoner’s heavy steps and the procession’s public display.

cues.title: Paris hears the symphony
cues.text: François-Antoine Habeneck conducted the premiere at the Paris Conservatoire on 5 December 1830. Berlioz later recalled that the march took the audience by storm; his account also admits that two rehearsals had not been enough.

cues.title: Back to the low tread
cues.text: The volume drops and the darker march material returns. Listen to how quickly Berlioz rebuilds the sound: the withdrawal lasts only a few phrases before the full orchestral weight presses forward again.

cues.title: A march with a past
cues.text: In his memoirs Berlioz says he wrote this movement in one night. The manuscript supplies a qualification: he reworked a guards’ march from his abandoned opera Les Francs-juges. The remembered beloved was added for the symphony.

cues.title: A thought before the blow
cues.text: The march breaks off for a quiet recollection. A solo clarinet gives the opening of the idée fixe, the melody representing the beloved throughout the symphony; listen for how little of it the orchestra allows to survive.

cues.title: The sentence is carried out
cues.text: The orchestral blow cuts across the recollection. Brass and percussion turn the ending into a blunt G major proclamation: the bright final chord belongs to the crowd’s celebration, not to a reprieve for the condemned man.

cues.title: Four movements are not enough
cues.text: The final chords decay, but the symphony has one movement left. The witches’ sabbath will bring the beloved’s melody back on E♭ clarinet, stripped of its earlier singing character.

composer.name: Felix Mendelssohn
composer.epithet: A composer-conductor who turned quicksilver string writing, Bachian counterpoint and remembered landscapes into tightly organised concert music.
facts: Piano with Ludwig Berger; composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter in Berlin
Music director, Düsseldorf, 1833–35; Gewandhaus conductor, Leipzig, from 1835; founder of Leipzig Conservatoire, 1843
Brother of Fanny Hensel; married Cécile Jeanrenaud in 1837; five children
Symphonies, concert overtures, concertos, oratorios, chamber music and Songs without Words
composer.background:
Felix Mendelssohn was born in Hamburg in 1809 and grew up in Berlin, where his father Abraham’s banking wealth supported an unusually extensive education. His grandfather was the Jewish philosopher Moses Mendelssohn; Felix and his siblings were baptised as Christians in 1816, and the family used the additional surname Bartholdy. He studied piano with Ludwig Berger and composition with Carl Friedrich Zelter, alongside his elder sister Fanny. The family’s concerts extended their classroom education with repeated opportunities to hear their own music, revise it and discuss it with experienced performers.

Zelter’s teaching joined Bach’s counterpoint to classical forms. The boy wrote string symphonies, concertos and chamber works before the pieces usually treated as his starting point. At sixteen he composed the E♭ major Octet, Op. 20, for four violins, two violas and two cellos. Its eight independent parts create different densities inside one ensemble: the first violin’s long ascent, the other instruments’ pulsing accompaniments and the finale’s fugal entries continually reshape the texture. The scherzo’s soft, rapid articulation became a recurrent technical problem in his later orchestral writing.

era.name: Romanticism
era.heroCaption: Caspar David Friedrich, Two Men Contemplating the Moon

intro: A falling figure in the bassoons and lower strings generates an entire concert overture. Mendelssohn keeps its outline recognisable while changing the harmony, register and weight around it.

cues.title: Begin below the violins
cues.text: Bassoons, violas and cellos introduce the falling figure in B minor. It begins after a rest, so the pulse is already moving when the melody appears; listen for that small gap each time the figure returns.

cues.title: Before entering the cave
cues.text: On 7 August 1829 Mendelssohn sent his family a letter containing the overture’s opening twenty-one bars. He visited Fingal’s Cave the following day. The musical sketch therefore preceded the celebrated visit, rather than being composed inside the cave.

cues.title: A figure beneath the surface
cues.text: Throughout the opening, follow the short descending figure rather than only the highest melody. Its repetitions supply continuity while changing harmonies and orchestral layers prevent it from becoming a fixed accompaniment.

cues.title: A longer singing phrase
cues.text: The lyrical second subject expands the short opening gesture into a longer line. The harmony moves towards D major, B minor’s relative major, while the accompaniment retains the motion that made the opening restless.

cues.title: Two rates of movement
cues.text: Listen beneath the broad melody for the smaller moving notes. Mendelssohn separates melodic pace from accompanimental activity: a phrase can seem to float even while the instruments underneath it keep working.

cues.title: The first large crest
cues.text: The orchestral sound gathers weight. The following half-minute brings the loudest sustained passage of this recording; the compact opening material can now carry a whole ensemble rather than a low-register murmur.

cues.title: An overture without an opera
cues.text: The Hebrides was written for the concert hall, not to introduce a stage work. Its first performance took place in London on 14 May 1832; Mendelssohn continued revising the score after that performance.

cues.title: The development opens out
cues.text: The large orchestral crest subsides, and the harmony starts moving through less settled territory. This is development: familiar fragments are recombined and moved into new surroundings rather than replaced by a new main tune.

cues.title: The bass changes the view
cues.text: Listen to the low notes under the recurring material. Changes there alter the harmonic meaning of a familiar contour; the overture can move far from B minor without abandoning its opening vocabulary.

cues.title: Turner visits Staffa
cues.text: Turner visited Staffa in 1831, two years after Mendelssohn, and exhibited Staffa, Fingal’s Cave in 1832. His painting includes a steamship. The supposedly remote landscape was already a destination reached through modern transport.

cues.title: A sudden change of weight
cues.text: A brief swell gives way to a much darker-coloured orchestral sound. Listen for the difference between volume and colour: a passage can become less bright without disappearing or losing its forward motion.

cues.title: Repeated attacks gather force
cues.text: The texture becomes more insistently articulated. Repeated short attacks give the music a firmer tread, and the gradual increase in volume turns that articulation into another orchestral build-up.

cues.title: Keep the contour in mind
cues.text: Through this louder passage, keep the opening’s downward contour in memory. Sonata form makes recognition a practical listening task: the return matters because a short idea has remained traceable through the development.

cues.title: The opening ground returns
cues.text: The sound withdraws and the opening material returns around B minor. This recapitulation restores the overture’s starting ground, but it does not simply replay the earlier sequence unchanged.

cues.title: The orchestra draws back
cues.text: The volume falls further. In this exposed passage, small changes of attack and balance matter more than the size of the orchestra; listen for how a quiet line remains audible without being forced.

cues.title: Building a musical institution
cues.text: Mendelssohn became conductor of Leipzig’s Gewandhaus concerts in 1835. In 1843 he founded the Leipzig Conservatoire. Composing, rehearsing an orchestra and organising musical education belonged to the same working life.

cues.title: The closing drive begins
cues.text: The quiet span gives way to sharper attacks and a growing orchestral sound. B minor reasserts itself as the overture approaches its close; the familiar material now has less space between its surges.

cues.title: Follow the separate attacks
cues.text: Listen for the separation between notes inside the fuller sound. Mendelssohn’s fast orchestral writing needs coordinated articulation as well as volume; blurring the attacks would hide the smaller figures that carry the movement.

cues.title: One more gathering of force
cues.text: The sound swells once more before the final withdrawal. The overture does not maintain its orchestral weight to the last instant: its ending makes room for the low, falling material to be heard without that mass.

cues.title: The figure outlasts the surge
cues.text: The closing sound contracts into B minor. After the full-orchestra passages, the reduced ending makes the opening figure’s small scale audible again.

composer.name: Frédéric Chopin
composer.born: 1 March 1810, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: He made the piano sing through ornament, contrapuntal voice-leading and the unstable accents of Polish dance.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; Józef Elsner at Warsaw’s Main School of Music, 1826–29
Warsaw until 1830; Paris from 1831; summers at George Sand’s house in Nohant
Teaching, publication and selected performances, more often in salons than large public halls
Almost entirely centred on the piano: études, mazurkas, polonaises, nocturnes, preludes, ballades, scherzos, sonatas and concertos
composer.background:
Chopin was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810, to a French-born father, Nicolas, and a Polish mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska. The family soon moved to Warsaw, where Nicolas taught French. The name Fryderyk belongs to his Polish life; Frédéric became usual in France. His family observed his birthday on 1 March, although the baptismal record gives 22 February. Piano lessons with Wojciech Żywny introduced Bach and Mozart alongside the fashionable repertory of the day. As a child he composed polonaises and played in aristocratic houses, but his later musical education extended beyond the cultivation of a prodigy.

Józef Elsner taught him harmony and composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music from 1826 to 1829. Chopin heard Italian opera, encountered Polish vernacular music during visits outside the capital and learned the working forms of the virtuoso concerto. The F minor Concerto was composed before the E minor, despite their eventual numbering as Nos. 2 and 1. Both preserve an extended orchestral opening, but once the piano enters, its vocal line and ornament determine the movement’s scale. The slow movements belong as much to operatic singing as to the display repertory of a concert pianist.
