era.heroCaption: Caspar David Friedrich, Two Men Contemplating the Moon

intro: Chopin gives the piano the title of a narrative poem without supplying a plot. Two themes return in altered proportions, and a fast coda overturns the measured pace of the opening.

cues.title: Octaves before a home key
cues.text: The two hands rise together in octaves rather than dividing into melody and accompaniment. A pause and a suspended dissonance delay the arrival of G minor; the introduction announces a speaker before establishing a regular pace.

cues.title: The first theme settles
cues.text: A quiet G minor melody begins over a swaying accompaniment. The metre is 6/4: six quarter-note beats grouped into two broad halves. That generous span lets the melody lean across the beat without losing its underlying movement.

cues.title: Leaving Warsaw behind
cues.text: Chopin left Poland in November 1830, shortly before the uprising against Russian rule. After months in Vienna he settled in Paris in 1831. He never returned to Poland; Polish émigrés remained an important part of his Parisian circle.

cues.title: Keep hearing the singing line
cues.text: Listen for the melody through the increasing keyboard activity. The pianist has to distinguish its longer notes from the faster material around them; equal weight on every note would change the phrase into a succession of attacks.

cues.title: The opening restraint breaks
cues.text: The sound becomes much louder and the keyboard writing more active. Chopin expands the first theme’s surroundings before introducing the contrasting tune; this surge is still part of the opening argument, not the final coda.

cues.title: Make room for another tune
cues.text: The rush subsides and the attacks become widely spaced. Listen for the longer, more sustained second theme that follows this release; its first appearance is quiet enough to make its later transformation conspicuous.

cues.title: A room above Paris
cues.text: In October 1831 Chopin described his new Paris room at 27 Boulevard Poissonière, with its view from Montmartre to the Panthéon. His letters from those first months mix excitement about the opera and musicians with loneliness and news of the defeated Polish uprising.

cues.title: A ballade without words
cues.text: The First Ballade appeared in print in 1836. Its title borrows a literary genre for solo piano, but Chopin supplied no narrative programme: thematic returns can suggest recollection and reversal without identifying characters or events.

cues.title: Familiar material gathers weight
cues.text: The middle of the piece begins quietly, then grows in force. Listen for earlier material gaining a denser accompaniment and a broader register: development here changes the scale of an idea as well as its harmony.

cues.title: The lyrical theme enlarged
cues.text: The singing material now occupies a much louder, fuller texture. Its broad phrasing has survived the change: the challenge is to hear a sustained line inside chords and passagework that could otherwise dominate it.

cues.title: Schumann recognises a favourite
cues.text: When Chopin visited Leipzig in 1836, Schumann told him how highly he valued the new G minor Ballade. In Schumann’s account of their conversation, Chopin replied that it was his own favourite too. The exchange is evidence of their shared judgement, not of a hidden literary plot.

cues.title: Another crest, another release
cues.text: A forceful passage gives way to lighter, faster-moving detail. Notice that speed of attack and loudness separate here: the piano can become busier while the sound itself grows less heavy.

cues.title: The broad theme comes back
cues.text: The lyrical theme returns with greater weight than at its first appearance. E♭ major is restored, but the quiet song has become a large statement; the order of return puts this theme before the G minor melody.

cues.title: The first melody recalled
cues.text: The first theme has returned in G minor, quieter and compressed after the broad lyrical statement. Its recollection does not restore the opening’s equilibrium: the harmony is already preparing the final fast section.

cues.title: Presto con fuoco
cues.text: The coda changes the gait as well as the speed. Chopin replaces the six-beat span with a driving two-beat metre; leaps, chords and running figures now carry the music towards its ending instead of reopening the themes.

cues.title: Do not flatten the accents
cues.text: Throughout the coda, follow the accented notes rather than counting every fast note equally. The pianist’s leaps and displaced emphases disturb the surface while the larger two-beat measure keeps the passage from becoming rhythmically shapeless.

cues.title: The rush is interrupted
cues.text: The continuous drive breaks into forceful gestures and quiet gaps. Chopin makes the pauses part of the ending: the next attack has to restart the momentum rather than simply continue it.

cues.title: The last descent
cues.text: The final keyboard rush collapses into the closing chords. G minor is the destination, not a major-key consolation; after the last attack, the resonance is allowed to decay.

work: Nocturne in D♭ major, Op. 27 No. 2
intro: A rocking left hand supports a melody that repeatedly grows a second voice. Listen for the difference between the notes that carry the phrase and the ornaments that delay their arrival.

cues.title: A singer above broken chords
cues.text: The left hand establishes a rocking accompaniment in D♭ major, and the right hand carries a slower singing line. The marking is Lento sostenuto: slow and sustained, although the piano’s sound begins to decay as soon as each note is struck.

cues.title: One voice becomes two
cues.text: The contrasting phrase lets the melody move in thirds and sixths, as if a second singer had joined it. Listen for both notes of the duet, not just the top one; their spacing is part of the change in expression.

cues.title: The phrase grows more insistent
cues.text: The sound grows stronger and the surface becomes busier. The left hand’s continuity makes the intensification measurable: the accompaniment keeps moving while the upper voices acquire more notes and harmonic pressure.

cues.title: A Parisian dedication
cues.text: The two Op. 27 Nocturnes were published in 1836 and dedicated to Countess Thérèse d’Apponyi, whose Paris salon Chopin frequented. The dedication places the music in a network of patrons and performers, rather than identifying a secret subject for the piece.

cues.title: Learning from the opera
cues.text: After reaching Paris in 1831, Chopin became a regular opera-goer. His letters name singers including Giuditta Pasta, Maria Malibran and Giovanni Battista Rubini. The sustained phrase and decorated return in his piano writing belong to the same practical world of singing.

cues.title: A darker second expansion
cues.text: The returning music has become more forceful and moves away from the opening major-key calm. The pianist must still keep the two melodic voices distinct; increasing the volume does not turn their duet into a single line.

cues.title: The melody returns again
cues.text: D♭ major and the opening melody come back. This nocturne is built from repeated returns and expansions, not a simple quiet–stormy–quiet design; ornament changes what a familiar phrase contains each time.

cues.title: The final crest approaches
cues.text: Another rise in the paired melodic writing leads to the recording’s largest swell. Listen for the longer phrase through the ornamental movement: its destination matters more than the number of notes needed to reach it.

cues.title: The coda stays close
cues.text: The final expansion gives way to a quieter closing span. D♭ remains the harmonic centre, but small chromatic changes continue inside the texture; staying in one place does not require every accompanying note to stay still.

cues.title: Chopin plays in Leipzig
cues.text: Chopin played this nocturne during his September 1835 visit to Leipzig, where he met Schumann and Mendelssohn at Friedrich Wieck’s house. Mendelssohn later told his sister Fanny that he had learnt a substantial part of the new piece by ear.

cues.title: Listen past the attack
cues.text: The closing notes are increasingly separated by their own resonance. Listen to the sound after the key is struck: pedalling and release determine how one harmony remains audible while the next is prepared.

cues.title: D♭ fades into silence
cues.text: The final major harmony is left to decay. No new phrase follows it: the remaining sound is the piano’s resonance, gradually disappearing.

composer.name: Robert Schumann
composer.epithet: His music lets remembered fragments, concealed names and competing inner voices interrupt the forms that contain them.
facts: Piano with Friedrich Wieck; composition with Heinrich Dorn; extensive private study of Bach and Beethoven
Co-founder of the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, 1834; editor until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
Leipzig Conservatoire teacher; municipal music director, Düsseldorf, 1850–53
composer.background:
Schumann grew up in Zwickau, where his father August was a bookseller and publisher. Reading and music developed together: Jean Paul’s novels, with their interruptions, doubles and changes of narrative voice, mattered alongside piano lessons. Sent to Leipzig to study law in 1828, he spent more time on music and literature; a period in Heidelberg did not reconcile him to a legal career. He returned to Leipzig to study piano seriously with Friedrich Wieck. Wieck’s daughter Clara, already performing publicly as a child, gave him an immediate example of the professional discipline he hoped to acquire.

A persistent problem with his right hand ended the prospect of a virtuoso career. The familiar account of a finger-strengthening device leaves the injury’s medical cause uncertain. Composition and criticism became his principal occupations. The early published piano works already had distinct literary and formal premises: the Abegg Variations derive a theme from letters, while Papillons relates its dances to the masked-ball ending of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The miniatures’ sudden juxtapositions recreate the experience of a narrative changing speakers and levels.

era.name: Romanticism
era.heroCaption: Caspar David Friedrich, Two Men Contemplating the Moon

work: Piano Concerto in A minor, Op. 54
performers: Sviatoslav Richter, Witold Rowicki, Warsaw National Philharmonic Orchestra
intro: The piano interrupts the orchestra almost before it has begun; then soloist and woodwind share a melody. Schumann builds his concerto around exchanges of material rather than a succession of solo displays.

cues.title: No orchestral waiting room
cues.text: A single orchestral attack launches a descending cascade of piano chords. Schumann dispenses with the long orchestral introduction familiar from Mozart’s concertos: the soloist is involved in the argument almost from the first sound.

cues.title: The oboe offers a melody
cues.text: An oboe-led wind phrase answers the piano’s forceful opening. Its descending C–B–A and repeated A will supply much of the movement’s material; the piano takes it over rather than introducing an unrelated solo tune.

cues.title: The strings start moving
cues.text: The strings introduce a more continuously moving figure. Its displaced accents make the accompaniment active enough to become thematic material; later, this connecting passage will return with the force of a fanfare.

cues.title: A possible name in notes
cues.text: The main theme’s C–B–A–A has been read as “CHiArA”, an Italian form of Clara’s name: German notation calls B natural H. Schumann used musical name-ciphers elsewhere, but this particular reading is an interpretation, not an explanation he left with the concerto.

cues.title: The same theme in major
cues.text: Instead of supplying an entirely new second subject, Schumann brings back the principal melody in C major. The change of mode and the exchanges between piano and woodwinds make familiar material serve a new formal purpose.

cues.title: A concerto began as fantasy
cues.text: Schumann wrote a one-movement Fantasy for piano and orchestra in May 1841. Only in 1845 did he revise it and add the Intermezzo and finale. The first movement therefore carries a self-contained dramatic shape inherited from an independent work.

cues.title: The soloist can accompany
cues.text: Throughout these exchanges, listen for moments when the piano’s activity supports a wind melody rather than competing with it. Technical difficulty and melodic prominence are separate things: the busiest part need not be the foreground.

cues.title: A difficult work to sell
cues.text: Schumann could not find a publisher for the independent Fantasy. Expanding it into a three-movement concerto gave the music a more conventional concert format, though the first movement retained its close interweaving of soloist and orchestra.

cues.title: A slow movement inside
cues.text: The sound withdraws into A♭ major and the pace broadens. Piano and clarinet exchange a slower version of the principal melody; a section of development briefly behaves like a chamber-music slow movement.

cues.title: Clara tries the first version
cues.text: In August 1841 Clara played the Fantasy at a closed rehearsal with the Leipzig Gewandhaus Orchestra and Mendelssohn conducting. The work was tested by the pianist for whom it had been written, several years before the complete concerto reached a public audience.

cues.title: Listen for the opening gesture
cues.text: The quiet dialogue is giving way to more forceful music. Keep the opening’s descending chordal gesture in mind: Schumann uses that interruption again during the development, so the gentle melody does not control the movement uninterrupted.

cues.title: The development reaches its peak
cues.text: The sound reaches its strongest burst, then gives ground. The piano and orchestra are working with material already introduced; the intensity comes from compression, register and harmonic movement rather than a new main melody.

cues.title: The composer as editor
cues.text: Schumann helped found the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik in 1834 and edited it until 1844. He contributed more than three hundred articles. Composition and criticism overlapped for a decade; the concerto’s completion came after he had relinquished the journal.

cues.title: The principal theme comes home
cues.text: A minor returns and the principal melody is heard again in its quieter opening character. This is the recapitulation: after the development’s interruptions, the first part of the movement can be recognised in a sustained sequence.

cues.title: The moving bridge returns
cues.text: The active string material returns after the quiet melody. The change is abrupt enough to register as a new layer of motion, although it is a familiar part of the opening now doing its work again.

cues.title: Bright attacks, quick replies
cues.text: A sharper orchestral outburst gives way to more active piano writing. Listen for the handover between sustained ensemble weight and separately articulated notes, rather than treating both as one continuous increase in volume.

cues.title: Dresden, December 1845
cues.text: Clara gave the complete concerto’s premiere in Dresden on 4 December 1845. Ferdinand Hiller, the work’s dedicatee, conducted. The solo part was not an abstract display written for an interchangeable virtuoso; its first advocate was a musician Schumann knew at close quarters.

cues.title: Major does not mean new
cues.text: The major-key restatement remains closely connected to the first melody. Listen for its descending shape through the change of harmony: a recognisable contour can survive even when the surrounding chords make it sound less troubled.

cues.title: A household of working musicians
cues.text: Clara combined touring and teaching with family responsibilities; she and Robert had eight children between 1841 and 1854. Their diaries record mutual musical study as well as conflicts over the time and quiet each needed to work.

cues.title: The ensemble presses towards a stop
cues.text: The orchestra gathers force before the solo cadenza. Listen for the difference between an intensification that continues the argument and a cadence that clears a space for the pianist alone.

cues.title: The pianist is left alone
cues.text: The orchestra stops for the cadenza. Schumann writes the passage into the score rather than leaving the soloist to invent it; the principal themes remain the material, now redistributed between the pianist’s two hands.

cues.title: Hear more than one voice
cues.text: In the cadenza, listen for a moving line against held or repeated notes in another register. The pianist has to reproduce something of the earlier ensemble conversation without the help of a second instrument.

cues.title: The solo crest recedes
cues.text: The cadenza’s strong, active passage begins to subside. The sound becomes less crowded, giving the coming orchestral return a different scale from the pianist’s own accumulation of notes.

cues.title: A new gait for the close
cues.text: For the closing span, Schumann recasts the principal material in 2/4 rather than the movement’s opening 4/4. Listen for the tighter two-beat gait as piano and orchestra resume their partnership; this is another transformation of the theme, not an unrelated finale.

cues.title: The last build-up
cues.text: The final drive produces another strong swell before the closing gestures. A minor remains the destination of this movement; the concerto’s eventual A major ending belongs to its finale, two movements away.

cues.title: A definite first-movement ending
cues.text: The closing chords cut off the movement’s motion, and their resonance fades. Unlike the link between the concerto’s second and third movements, this first ending allows a real pause.

composer.name: Franz Liszt
composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: The touring pianist who made a single theme change character, and eventually stripped virtuosity down to a few unresolved notes.
facts: Piano with Carl Czerny and composition with Antonio Salieri in Vienna; later composition with Anton Reicha in Paris
Weimar masterclasses; first president of the Hungarian Royal Academy of Music, founded in 1875
Piano music and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; two programme symphonies; concertos, songs and sacred music
composer.background:
Liszt was born in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Hungarian kingdom, where his father Adam worked on an Esterházy estate. Hungary remained his declared homeland, although German and French were his principal languages. Adam taught him piano before taking him to Vienna in 1822 for lessons with Carl Czerny, who had studied with Beethoven, and Antonio Salieri. The family moved to Paris the following year. The Conservatoire refused him admission as a foreigner; private teaching and public concerts supplied his education instead. His early career therefore joined two institutions that would remain distinct in his adult life: the disciplined lesson and the commercial concert platform.

Adam died in 1827, leaving the sixteen-year-old Liszt to support himself and his mother by teaching. Paris offered an education beyond the keyboard: Victor Hugo, the religious social thinker Félicité de Lamennais, Chopin and Berlioz belonged to his intellectual or musical circle. Hearing Paganini in 1832 suggested that a pianist might make technical difficulty carry the same theatrical force as the violinist’s leaps and harmonics. Liszt responded with prolonged practice and transcription: his piano version of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, published in 1834, aimed to preserve orchestral detail.

intro: Four sharply separated sections turn a piano into a band: march, quick dance, slow declamation and a finale driven by repeated octaves. Argerich makes the changes of pace as conspicuous as the changes of register.

cues.title: Four sections, one pianist
cues.text: The opening is a measured march in D♭ major, with the melody above a regular chordal bass. Liszt will replace this tread with a quick dance, then a slow song, before the extended fast finale.

cues.title: After the touring years
cues.text: Liszt ended his regular career as a travelling virtuoso in 1847. When this rhapsody appeared in 1853, he was based in Weimar, conducting and composing rather than moving from one paid recital to the next.

cues.title: The march breaks apart
cues.text: The volume drops and a light run loosens the march’s regular pulse. A cadenza is a passage where the soloist can suspend the beat; here it separates two kinds of dance rather than ending a concerto.

cues.title: Whose Hungarian music?
cues.text: The rhapsodies draw on songs, published dances and the improvisatory playing of Romani bands. These are not the same sources as the rural songs Bartók later collected. Liszt reshapes an existing performing culture for the concert piano.

cues.title: The slow song
cues.text: The quick dance stops and the Andante enters B♭ minor. The melody has room for pauses and ornaments; the bass no longer needs to mark every step of a dance.

cues.title: A song before Liszt
cues.text: The slow section’s melody is by Ádám Pálóczi Horváth and was published in 1813. Liszt had already used it in his earlier “Rumanian Rhapsody”. This apparently spontaneous piano song has a written history stretching back forty years before publication.

cues.title: Conducting another exile’s opera
cues.text: In Weimar, Liszt conducted the first performance of Wagner’s Lohengrin on 28 August 1850. Wagner, wanted after the Dresden uprising, could not attend. Liszt’s work for other composers continued after he had stopped touring for his own income.

cues.title: A second cadenza
cues.text: A rapid flourish breaks out of the slow section. The notes spread across the keyboard, then leave a quiet gap before the fast finale: register and silence make the join audible.

cues.title: The friss begins
cues.text: The final fast dance starts quietly in B♭ major. Listen to the repeated bass rhythm: it gives the pianist a fixed support while the melody is enlarged into increasingly demanding versions.

cues.title: The octave machinery
cues.text: The dance gains weight and speed. Liszt doubles the tune in octaves, requiring the hand to repeat and move as a unit; the technical problem is to keep a melody audible inside that repeated attack.

cues.title: More than fast notes
cues.text: The playing is now much louder, but the tune still has to be phrased. Follow the longer melodic notes through the repeated octaves, rather than treating each attack as a separate musical event.

cues.title: A different home key
cues.text: The rhapsody finishes in B♭ major, not the D♭ major in which it began. The final drive includes some of the performance’s heaviest attacks, followed by a short resonance rather than a gradual fade.

composer.name: Giuseppe Verdi
composer.born: 10 October 1813, Le Roncole, near Busseto (then in the French Empire)
composer.epithet: An opera composer who made a change of vocal phrase, bass note or ensemble balance alter the relations between people on stage.
facts: Ferdinando Provesi in Busseto; private study with Vincenzo Lavigna in Milan after rejection by the Conservatoire
La Scala, Milan · La Fenice, Venice · Paris Opéra · theatres in Naples, Rome, St Petersburg and Cairo
Francesco Maria Piave, Salvadore Cammarano and Arrigo Boito among his principal librettists
Operas from Oberto (1839) to Falstaff (1893); the Requiem, sacred pieces, songs and a string quartet
composer.background:
Verdi was born in Le Roncole, near Busseto, where his parents kept an inn and shop. He learnt the organ locally and studied with Ferdinando Provesi in Busseto. The merchant and amateur musician Antonio Barezzi helped finance further training in Milan, but the Conservatoire rejected him in 1832. Private study with Vincenzo Lavigna, who had worked at La Scala, gave him access to counterpoint and practical theatrical knowledge instead. In 1836 he married Barezzi’s daughter Margherita and took up municipal musical duties in Busseto. His route to opera passed through a provincial network of patronage, church work and teaching.

The first opera, Oberto, reached La Scala in 1839 and secured further commissions. By then Verdi had lost his daughter Virginia; his son Icilio died that year, and Margherita died in 1840. The comedy Un giorno di regno failed at La Scala in September 1840. Nabucco brought success in March 1842. Temistocle Solera’s libretto offered large public scenes, sharply opposed groups and an exiled people whose collective song could carry a dramatic burden usually assigned to a principal singer.

intro: Before the party starts, Verdi gives Violetta an orchestral portrait: exposed high strings, then the melody she will sing when she leaves Alfredo. Toscanini recorded this complete prelude in Carnegie Hall in 1929.

cues.title: Before the public face
cues.text: High, divided violins begin quietly, without the weight of the full orchestra. This is Violetta’s opera before it is her party: the exposed string writing anticipates the frailty that the stage’s social bustle will conceal.

cues.title: Venice, March 1853
cues.text: La traviata was first performed at La Fenice on 6 March 1853, with a libretto by Francesco Maria Piave. Its central figure is a Parisian courtesan, not a queen or a mythological heroine; illness, money and respectability determine her fate.

cues.title: A first expansion
cues.text: The introduction grows much stronger, then withdraws again before the broader melody. Verdi separates the two ideas with a change in weight: the quiet opening is not simply an accompaniment waiting for a singer.

cues.title: A contemporary French source
cues.text: Piave adapted Alexandre Dumas fils’s La Dame aux camélias, whose heroine Marguerite Gautier became Violetta. Dumas had first published the story as a novel in 1848, then made it a play staged in Paris in 1852: Verdi was adapting very recent theatre.

cues.title: Melody beneath the decoration
cues.text: Listen through the light upper-string decoration to the longer melody underneath. It anticipates Violetta’s “Amami, Alfredo” — “Love me, Alfredo” — in Act II, when she leaves him. The same line can carry either an orchestral portrait or a direct plea.

cues.title: A household outside marriage
cues.text: When Verdi composed La traviata, he was living at Sant’Agata with the retired soprano Giuseppina Strepponi. They had moved there in 1851 and married in 1859. A household outside marriage was part of the composer’s own circumstances, not just his opera’s plot.

cues.title: The prelude withdraws
cues.text: The decorated phrase thins into a quiet ending. Verdi leaves space before the party begins: the prelude closes without the brilliant orchestral punctuation that would turn it into a conventional overture.

composer.name: Richard Wagner
composer.epithet: An opera composer who made the orchestra remember what the characters conceal, and built a theatre for the result.
facts: Composition with Theodor Weinlig in Leipzig; practical theatre work in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga
Royal Saxon Kapellmeister, Dresden, 1843–49; founder of the Bayreuth Festival, first held in 1876
Wrote his own librettos, alongside extensive and often polemical prose
Thirteen completed operas; the four-part Ring; songs, orchestral works and piano music
composer.background:
Wagner grew up among actors, singers and theatrical households in Leipzig and Dresden. His father died in 1813; his mother subsequently married the actor and painter Ludwig Geyer. Literature preceded serious musical training: as a schoolboy Wagner attempted a tragedy before he had mastered composition. Beethoven’s symphonies and Weber’s operas supplied different models, one for the weight of an orchestral argument, the other for a German theatre of supernatural events and sharply characterised instruments. Lessons with Theodor Weinlig in 1831 gave him a grounding in counterpoint. The later claim to have rebuilt opera came from someone who first learned its routines as a working theatre musician.

He held posts in Würzburg, Magdeburg, Königsberg and Riga, married the actress Minna Planer in 1836, and repeatedly found himself in debt. His early operas tried incompatible languages: Die Feen follows German Romantic opera, while Das Liebesverbot, after Shakespeare’s Measure for Measure, adopts a more Italianate manner. In 1839 the Wagners fled Riga and travelled by sea to London, then to Paris. There he copied, arranged and wrote journalism while trying to enter the operatic establishment. Meyerbeer, whom Wagner would later attack, helped him obtain a hearing for Rienzi. Wagner knew the grand-opera machinery of public ceremony, political catastrophe and large chorus from practical experience.

intro: A pilgrims’ hymn frames the restless music of Venus’s mountain. This concert-band arrangement transfers Wagner’s opposition between sustained chorale and rushing figuration to wind, brass and percussion.

cues.title: The pilgrims before Venus
cues.text: A slow hymn opens the overture. In the opera it belongs to pilgrims travelling to Rome; here its sustained notes establish the first of two competing kinds of music, before the restless writing associated with Venus’s mountain.

cues.title: Breath inside a long line
cues.text: Listen to the continuity of the hymn across the players’ breathing. In a wind band, sustained phrases have to be handed between breaths and balanced between instrumental groups; no section of bowed strings can carry the line underneath them.

cues.title: The hymn becomes chromatic
cues.text: The opening’s relatively plain harmony begins to move through more chromatic chords. Notes shift by semitone while the slow phrase continues: the hymn contains harmonic tension before the fast music has even begun.

cues.title: A court post in Dresden
cues.text: Wagner became Royal Saxon Kapellmeister in Dresden in 1843, following the success of Rienzi. He composed Tannhäuser while holding that post and conducted its first performance there on 19 October 1845. Practical theatre work preceded his later theories of music drama.

cues.title: The hymn in full voice
cues.text: The chorale reaches its first broad, loud statement. The brass gives the sustained melody weight while faster accompanying motion fills the spaces between its notes. Two different speeds now occupy the same texture.

cues.title: Long notes, moving accompaniment
cues.text: Follow the slow melody without losing the faster notes around it. The accompaniment prevents a sustained chord from becoming motionless; Wagner can extend the hymn without requiring its tune to become more elaborate.

cues.title: Receding from the first climax
cues.text: The sound contracts after the broad statement. The hymn’s chromatic continuation remains, but the volume and brilliance fall; the slow opening must retreat before the fast centre can begin.

cues.title: A pilgrimage with consequences
cues.text: Tannhäuser has left Venus’s subterranean realm but cannot reconcile that experience with the court’s ideal of love. After praising Venus during a song contest, he travels to Rome to seek absolution. The pilgrims’ music therefore belongs to an action, not merely a religious atmosphere.

cues.title: The Dresden post ends
cues.text: Wagner’s involvement in the Dresden uprising of May 1849 forced him into exile. Liszt helped him escape and later conducted Lohengrin’s premiere in Weimar. The composer who had supervised Tannhäuser in his own theatre could no longer attend his next opera’s first performance.

cues.title: Inside the Venusberg
cues.text: The fast music begins to replace the slow hymn. Shorter figures, more frequent attacks and brighter writing establish the contrasting centre of the overture: the music associated with Venus’s realm.

cues.title: Figuration rather than a hymn
cues.text: The quick figures matter as much as any single tune here. Listen for how the upper parts keep the texture in motion while the harmony changes underneath; the opening chorale’s long, shared breaths have been replaced by smaller units.

cues.title: A broader song emerges
cues.text: A more sustained tune pushes through the fast material. In the opera this music belongs to Tannhäuser’s praise of Venus: the same character who seeks salvation also gives the opposing world a full lyrical voice.

cues.title: The central span presses harder
cues.text: The broad tune drives towards a louder peak, with the accompanying motion still active. Wagner lets the central music acquire almost the same public weight as the pilgrims’ hymn rather than confining it to light decoration.

cues.title: A quieter inner episode
cues.text: The forceful passage gives way to a quieter, more exposed episode. The larger melody no longer dominates the whole band; small figures and changes of register can be heard separately again.

cues.title: Two claims on one singer
cues.text: The opera opposes Venus to Elisabeth, the woman waiting for Tannhäuser at the Wartburg. His predicament is staged through competing voices and recurring music. The overture compresses that conflict into instrumental themes before either woman appears.

cues.title: The line broadens again
cues.text: Longer notes reassert themselves after the lighter episode. Listen to the change in articulation before the volume rises: a more sustained phrase begins gathering the ensemble towards another full statement.

cues.title: The Paris revision
cues.text: For the Paris production of 1861, Wagner expanded the Venusberg scene and added the ballet expected at the Opéra. Its placement in Act I helped provoke the Jockey Club’s disruption. The production was withdrawn after three performances; this recording presents the self-contained overture, not the extended ballet.

cues.title: The upper texture brightens
cues.text: The sound becomes brighter as the fast material presses on. The changing register matters independently of volume: some of the most penetrating writing comes as the loudness is already beginning to recede.

cues.title: Making room for the hymn
cues.text: Listen for the fast span to release its pressure. The volume falls sharply before the pilgrims’ material returns, allowing the opening’s slower phrase lengths to become audible again rather than arriving as a sudden final fanfare.

cues.title: The opening music returns
cues.text: The pilgrims’ hymn is back, still well below the final volume. Recognise its long phrases before the full-band conclusion: the ending is built by enlarging music already heard, not by introducing a new victorious theme.

cues.title: A work never settled
cues.text: Wagner kept revising Tannhäuser across his career. In her diary on 23 January 1883, Cosima recorded his remark that he still owed the world Tannhäuser. He died in Venice three weeks later, nearly thirty-eight years after the first performance.

cues.title: The hymn gains its full weight
cues.text: The returning hymn grows into the final broad statement. The bass and brass sustain the slower phrase while quicker motion continues around it; the two kinds of writing can now be heard together.

cues.title: Keep hearing the inner motion
cues.text: Do not follow only the loudest melody. The hymn moves in long values while decorative notes continue underneath and around it. The conclusion does not merely stop the fast music; it fits that motion around the slow tune.

cues.title: The last sustained ascent
cues.text: The ensemble keeps its full weight into the closing bars. The final rise is stronger than the first presentation of the hymn, so repetition changes the overture’s proportions as well as its volume.

cues.title: A complete concert ending
cues.text: The last chord releases into a short decay. This version ends with the pilgrims’ music; it does not continue into the Venusberg ballet, as the later combined Overture and Bacchanale does.

composer.name: Anton Bruckner
composer.epithet: A church organist who built symphonic movements from long harmonic spans, separate instrumental blocks and the silences between them.
facts: St Florian; harmony and counterpoint with Simon Sechter, 1855–61; form and orchestration with Otto Kitzler, 1861–63
Organist at St Florian and Linz Cathedral; Vienna Conservatory teacher from 1868; University of Vienna lecturer from 1875
Nine numbered symphonies, two earlier symphonies outside that sequence, masses, motets and other choral works
Several symphonies survive in distinct authorial versions, which later editors have treated differently
composer.background:
Bruckner was born in Ansfelden, near Linz, where his father was a schoolmaster and church musician. Teaching, organ playing and the parish liturgy belonged to the same local profession. After his father’s death in 1837, he became a choirboy at the Augustinian abbey of St Florian. The abbey gave him daily contact with sacred music and a large organ, but his first adult qualification was as a schoolteacher. He worked in small Upper Austrian communities before returning to St Florian in 1845. The later symphonist emerged from this practical church-and-school environment.

He became the abbey’s organist and moved to Linz Cathedral in 1855. By then he was thirty-one, yet he submitted himself to six further years of harmony and counterpoint study with Simon Sechter in Vienna, much of it conducted through written exercises and correspondence. Sechter’s discipline discouraged free composition while the technical work continued. Bruckner sought formal certification even after he had become an accomplished organ improviser. This extended apprenticeship matters when hearing a symphonic climax: its apparent mass rests on carefully managed lines, prepared dissonances and a bass that controls the rate of harmonic change.

work: Symphony No. 7 in E major, WAB 107
movement: III. Scherzo — Sehr schnell; Trio — Etwas langsamer
performers: University of Music and Theatre Munich
intro: The Seventh’s scherzo compresses Bruckner’s block-like construction into nine minutes. A repeated string figure and a trumpet call drive the outer sections; the slower trio changes both their pace and their weight.

cues.title: A fast third movement
cues.text: After the long Adagio, Bruckner gives the orchestra a fast scherzo in A minor. A repeated string figure supplies the motion; a trumpet call gives it a sharply profiled theme. The marking “Sehr schnell” means “very fast”.

cues.title: The first full block
cues.text: The orchestra reaches its first sustained loud passage. Listen to how the repeated rhythm remains distinct beneath the larger sound: adding instruments does not require Bruckner to replace the small figure driving the movement.

cues.title: An organist still studying
cues.text: Bruckner became organist at Linz Cathedral in 1855. Already in his thirties, he continued studying harmony and counterpoint with Simon Sechter, then form and orchestration with Otto Kitzler. The symphonies followed an unusually long period of formal training.

cues.title: Motion without volume
cues.text: The texture is quieter, but its repeated attacks keep the scherzo moving. Distinguish the speed of those small notes from the slower changes in harmony: two different rates of motion occupy the same passage.

cues.title: Gathering the outer section
cues.text: The volume begins another sustained climb. The short rhythmic material survives the expansion, then the whole block stops before a different tempo begins.

cues.title: The slower trio
cues.text: The trio replaces A minor with F major and relaxes the pace. Its phrases are longer and less insistently repeated. “Trio” here means the contrasting middle section of a scherzo, not an ensemble of three players.

cues.title: St Florian’s daily work
cues.text: After his father’s death in 1837, Bruckner became a choirboy at St Florian. He later returned there as a teacher and organist. Church music and classroom work preceded the career that eventually brought him to Vienna’s conservatory.

cues.title: The trio grows stronger
cues.text: The softer middle section has its own rise in intensity. A quieter texture need not mean a static one: the phrases gather weight before the trio’s last withdrawal.

cues.title: The pause has weight
cues.text: The trio recedes and leaves a marked separation before the fast music returns. Keep the original repeated figure in mind: its reappearance will identify the larger form more decisively than a new tune would.

cues.title: The scherzo returns
cues.text: The original fast figure returns after the pause, with the A minor setting restored. This is the scherzo’s da capo: the opening section comes back as a whole, not merely as a remembered phrase.

cues.title: Recognising the first crescendo
cues.text: The return reaches the same kind of sustained loud block heard near the beginning. Its position is now easier to follow: the repeated figure has already shown how it can expand into this much larger sound.

cues.title: Recognition at sixty
cues.text: Arthur Nikisch conducted the Seventh’s orchestral premiere in Leipzig in December 1884. Bruckner was sixty. The symphony brought the public success that had eluded several earlier works, without requiring him to abandon their long spans or separated instrumental groups.

cues.title: Wagner without the theatre
cues.text: Kitzler introduced Bruckner to Wagner’s scores in Linz. The Seventh’s preceding Adagio uses four Wagner tubas, but this scherzo is built from symphonic repetition and contrast rather than characters or a stage narrative.

cues.title: The final accumulation
cues.text: The last stretch rebuilds the louder texture. Bruckner repeats and enlarges a limited stock of rhythmic material instead of supplying a fresh closing melody; the length of the crescendo becomes part of the form.

cues.title: A sharply cut ending
cues.text: The scherzo ends with a forceful stop rather than a long taper. After the last attacks, the remaining sound is the room’s decay: the contrast between block and silence is audible at its smallest scale.

composer.name: Johannes Brahms
composer.epithet: A composer who made a small interval generate a large form, and let conflicting rhythms keep a familiar melody unsettled.
facts: Piano with Otto Friedrich Willibald Cossel; piano and composition with Eduard Marxsen in Hamburg
Seasonal work in Detmold, 1857–59; Vienna Singakademie, 1863–64; Gesellschaft der Musikfreunde concerts, 1872–75
Based in Vienna; summer composition in Baden-Baden, Pörtschach, Mürzzuschlag and Bad Ischl
Four symphonies, four concertos, chamber music, piano music, songs and choral works; no opera
composer.background:
Brahms was born in Hamburg, the son of a professional musician, Johann Jakob Brahms, who played several instruments, and Christiane Nissen, a seamstress. His father supplied an introduction to practical music-making; Otto Friedrich Willibald Cossel and Eduard Marxsen gave him systematic piano and composition lessons. The young Brahms played for income and learned the trade from inside, accompanying, arranging and performing. Marxsen’s teaching connected keyboard technique with the study of Bach, Mozart and Beethoven. Those composers supplied working materials: Brahms’s later scores are full of old procedures subjected to new rhythmic pressure.

In 1853 he toured with the Hungarian violinist Ede Reményi and met Joseph Joachim, who became a lifelong collaborator. Joachim sent him to Robert and Clara Schumann in Düsseldorf. Robert’s article “Neue Bahnen”, published that October, announced the twenty-year-old as a major new figure before his music was widely available. The endorsement opened publishers’ doors and imposed an awkward expectation of scale. His early piano sonatas, already orchestral in weight and contrast, could be treated as promises of symphonies he had not yet written. Brahms responded by publishing selectively and destroying much of the work he did not wish to preserve.

work: Symphony No. 3 in F major, Op. 90
intro: Instead of a scherzo, Brahms writes a C minor song in three beats. Trumpets and timpani remain silent while the melody passes between the strings and solo winds.

cues.title: A melody for cellos
cues.text: The cellos begin the main tune over a gently moving accompaniment. Its phrases lean across the three-beat bars; the melody’s breathing and the accompaniment’s pulse do not always coincide.

cues.title: Follow the smaller swell
cues.text: The phrase grows towards a local high point, then relaxes without a full orchestral outburst. Listen beneath the tune: the accompanying parts keep moving even when the melody holds a note.

cues.title: A summer in Wiesbaden
cues.text: Brahms wrote the Third Symphony in Wiesbaden during the summer of 1883. He was fifty. His First had appeared only seven years earlier, after a long gestation; the Third belongs to a period when a new symphony no longer required decades of preparation.

cues.title: The middle section
cues.text: The opening song gives way to shorter, more insistently repeated gestures. The accompaniment becomes more active while the volume falls; a change of section does not need a louder entrance.

cues.title: A brief expansion
cues.text: The middle section opens into a brighter, fuller phrase, then contracts again. This is a local expansion within the interlude, not yet the return of the first melody.

cues.title: Schumann’s public prediction
cues.text: In 1853, Robert Schumann’s article “Neue Bahnen” announced the twenty-year-old Brahms before his music was widely published. The praise helped launch his career, but also made each large work answer a public prediction made thirty years before this symphony.

cues.title: The horn takes over
cues.text: The opening melody returns in C minor, now led by the horn rather than the cellos. The tune is recognisable, but its sustained notes have a different attack and a different way of tapering away.

cues.title: No trumpets or drums
cues.text: Throughout this movement, Brahms keeps the trumpets and timpani silent. Notice how much variety he obtains from changes within the middle register: a familiar line can alter character without acquiring either percussion or a brass fanfare.

cues.title: Vienna, December 1883
cues.text: Hans Richter conducted the Vienna Philharmonic in the premiere on 2 December 1883. All four movements end quietly. The Third therefore withholds the emphatic ending an audience might expect not only here, but at every major stopping point.

cues.title: The strings fill out
cues.text: The returning song now has a fuller string sound. Brahms brings violins and cellos together for its late statement, increasing the weight of the melody without changing its basic contour.

cues.title: One swell, then quiet
cues.text: The coda makes one last swell, the largest in this performance, before the volume drops sharply. The closing C minor harmony is quiet; the movement does not turn its final cadence into a change of mood.

work: Symphony No. 4 in E minor, Op. 98
intro: Brahms ends his last symphony with thirty variations on an eight-bar pattern derived from Bach. The repeating foundation survives changes of rhythm, register and orchestration, but the final cadence refuses the customary escape into the major.

cues.title: Eight bars, thirty variations
cues.text: Winds and brass state an eight-bar theme in forceful chords. It will underpin thirty variations. This is a passacaglia: a repeating pattern controls the harmony while the music above and around it changes.

cues.title: Follow the harmonic skeleton
cues.text: The opening chords have already given way to much quieter writing. Do not expect the eight notes always to remain at the top: the pattern can move into the bass or an inner voice while its harmonic outline stays recognisable.

cues.title: Brass held in reserve
cues.text: This is the first movement of the symphony to use trombones. Brahms has withheld that weight through three movements, so the finale’s chordal statements have an instrumental resource the earlier music never possessed.

cues.title: Bach’s pattern, altered
cues.text: The theme comes from the closing chorus of Bach’s cantata Nach dir, Herr, verlanget mich, BWV 150. Brahms adds a chromatic note. A procedure associated with Baroque variation becomes the organising principle of a nineteenth-century symphonic finale.

cues.title: Variation without stopping
cues.text: The variations run into one another rather than pausing like separate miniatures. Listen for the repeated harmonic cycle beneath the changing surface: a phrase can grow busier without making the underlying pattern any longer.

cues.title: Two summers in the mountains
cues.text: Brahms composed the Fourth during the summers of 1884 and 1885 at Mürzzuschlag in Austria. In August 1885 he sent the first movement to Elisabeth von Herzogenberg for her opinion. Even after three successful symphonies, he still sought a trusted reader’s judgement.

cues.title: The slow central span
cues.text: The music has withdrawn into the central slow variations. An exposed melodic line now has to sustain the argument that the opening carried in chords. The flute solo belongs to this quieter group, not to a separate slow movement.

cues.title: Major without an ending
cues.text: The central variations turn towards E major. That change softens the harmony without ending the passacaglia: the same underlying design can sustain a major-key episode inside an E minor movement.

cues.title: A lower chorale colour
cues.text: The texture becomes darker and more chordal. The central group includes a trombone chorale: the brass now sustains quiet harmony rather than supplying the opening’s forceful attack.

cues.title: Brahms conducts the premiere
cues.text: Brahms conducted the first orchestral performance in Meiningen on 25 October 1885. The work was well received there. Its severe ending did not prevent an immediate public success, whatever doubts he had expressed privately while finishing it.

cues.title: The full weight returns
cues.text: The orchestra abruptly restores the weight of the opening. E minor reasserts itself after the quiet central group; the returning chordal pattern makes the larger form audible inside the chain of variations.

cues.title: More attacks, same framework
cues.text: The surface grows more active again. Listen for the distinction between quick notes and the slower harmonic pattern beneath them: the variation changes its rhythmic pressure while retaining its inherited proportions.

cues.title: A sudden contraction
cues.text: Listen for the volume to collapse after this fuller passage. Brahms uses a short withdrawal inside the later variations, not another prolonged central slow section; the orchestra soon rebuilds its weight.

cues.title: First heard on two pianos
cues.text: Before the Meiningen premiere, Brahms and Ignaz Brüll played the symphony on two pianos in Vienna. The listeners included Eduard Hanslick, Theodor Billroth and Hans Richter. Its first private audience therefore encountered the argument without the orchestral colours heard here.

cues.title: A late change of texture
cues.text: The sound becomes less brilliant and the repeated attacks give way to a more sustained texture. This late contrast remains inside the variation sequence; the return of quieter music does not undo the earlier orchestral interruption.

cues.title: Not his last music
cues.text: The Fourth remained Brahms’s last symphony, but not his last substantial work. Hearing the clarinettist Richard Mühlfeld in 1891 prompted the Clarinet Trio and Quintet; two clarinet sonatas followed in 1894. His final decade increasingly concentrated its arguments into chamber music.

cues.title: Preparing the final drive
cues.text: The quiet contrast is over. The volume builds towards the coda, where Brahms loosens the strict repetition of the eight-bar units. The form that has governed the movement now has to provide an ending rather than another variation.

cues.title: No room for another retreat
cues.text: The closing passage sustains its force instead of reopening the quiet central space. Short gestures and emphatic chords replace the earlier balance of equally measured variations; the bass keeps the ending directed towards E.

cues.title: E minor to the end
cues.text: The final chords remain in E minor. There is no last-minute major-key conversion: the strong close confirms the tonal condition with which the finale began, then cuts off into a short decay.

composer.name: Modest Mussorgsky
composer.epithet: He made Russian speech, public crowds and the noises of ordinary life determine the shape of opera.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition informally with Mily Balakirev; no conservatory education
Guards officer until 1858; civil servant, including work in the Forestry Department
Balakirev, Borodin, Cui and Rimsky-Korsakov; the critic Vladimir Stasov
Operas, dramatic songs and piano music; many works unfinished or published in other composers’ revisions
composer.background:
Mussorgsky grew up on his family’s estate at Karevo, where his mother taught him the piano and his nurse supplied stories that he later associated with his earliest improvisations. The household belonged to the landowning class. The peasant voices he eventually put into songs and operas came from another social world. Sent to Saint Petersburg for schooling, he studied piano with Anton Gerke and entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852. In 1856 he joined the Preobrazhensky Regiment. His first published piano piece, a polka, belonged to the drawing room.

Meeting Dargomyzhsky and then Balakirev redirected that education. Balakirev taught through playing, criticism and the examination of scores. Mussorgsky left the army in 1858, but composing did not provide a living. The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 disrupted the estate income on which his family depended, and he eventually took civil-service posts. The group later called the Five brought together different professions and musical methods: Borodin was a chemist, Cui a military engineer, Rimsky-Korsakov a naval officer. Their shared opposition to imported academic authority concealed substantial musical disagreements.

intro: A witches’ gathering interrupted by a church bell. This is Rimsky-Korsakov’s 1886 concert version, assembled after Mussorgsky’s death, not the orchestral score Mussorgsky finished in 1867.

cues.title: Motion before melody
cues.text: The opening builds its agitation from rapid string figures and sharply separated orchestral gestures. Listen for the difference between the moving surface and the heavier notes beneath it: the lower instruments do not simply double everything the strings play.

cues.title: An officer leaves service
cues.text: Mussorgsky entered the Preobrazhensky Guards in 1856 and left the army in 1858. He learnt composition informally from Balakirev rather than at a conservatory; his later employment included civil-service work.

cues.title: Smaller, quicker gestures
cues.text: The weight drops away, but the attacks become more frequent. Quietness does not mean rest: short figures keep the pulse active while the orchestra sheds some of its mass.

cues.title: A sudden change of scale
cues.text: Keep the quiet dance in your ear as the volume increases. The change comes through orchestral weight rather than a complete halt and a new beginning.

cues.title: The upper edge sharpens
cues.text: The sound becomes brighter in the coming phrase. Follow the high activity separately from the lower accents: the two layers give the music different kinds of momentum.

cues.title: Another short-lived crest
cues.text: A quick crescendo pushes the orchestra forward, then releases it. Mussorgsky’s material can work in these compact blocks: a repeated figure, an increase in weight, a sudden change of texture.

cues.title: Balakirev rejects the score
cues.text: Mussorgsky finished his original orchestral version in 1867. Balakirev rejected it, and it was not performed in Mussorgsky’s lifetime. The music survived through several further attempts to place the witches’ gathering in a stage work.

cues.title: A different harmonic field
cues.text: The harmony moves away from the opening’s D-centred writing. Listen for a broader line and slower changes of emphasis: a new span is being built rather than another immediate burst.

cues.title: Sustaining the pressure
cues.text: Listen beneath the louder gestures for repeated notes and held support. They allow the upper parts to change shape without making the music feel as though it has started again.

cues.title: The volume breaks upward
cues.text: The phrase reaches a forceful crest, falls back and prepares a still stronger one. Repeated surges, rather than one uninterrupted crescendo, make the gathering increasingly crowded.

cues.title: An editor’s concert piece
cues.text: Rimsky-Korsakov completed this version in 1886, five years after Mussorgsky’s death. He drew on the composer’s later stage versions as well as the earlier material; this is a reconstruction and recomposition, not merely a new orchestration of the 1867 score.

cues.title: Pressure in successive waves
cues.text: The orchestra keeps rebuilding its volume after brief withdrawals. Notice how each new increase also sharpens the upper sound: loudness and brightness reinforce one another without remaining constant.

cues.title: A low starting point
cues.text: The texture suddenly becomes quieter and darker. This is not the ending: the orchestra uses the reduction as the beginning of another climb.

cues.title: Before the interruption
cues.text: Listen for the contrast between this renewed orchestral force and the stillness that follows. The fast section reaches one of its brightest peaks before the whole pattern is broken.

cues.title: The gathering disperses
cues.text: The fast music breaks off. The church bell belongs to the score’s change from the witches’ gathering to daybreak; the orchestral activity gives way to a long, quiet aftermath.

cues.title: An unfinished comic opera
cues.text: Mussorgsky reused the sabbath music in his unfinished opera The Fair at Sorochyntsi, after Gogol. The dream sequence there helped supply the materials from which Rimsky-Korsakov made the familiar concert ending.

cues.title: Listen for the bass
cues.text: The low D gives these quiet phrases a fixed reference point. Attend to how little movement is needed above a sustained foundation; the same orchestra that crowded the fast section can now leave a single line exposed.

cues.title: A minor-key shadow
cues.text: The quiet ending is not harmonically motionless. A darker inflection briefly colours the D-centred music before the major sonority settles again.

cues.title: Repin at the hospital
cues.text: In 1881 Ilya Repin painted Mussorgsky in the Nikolaevsky Military Hospital in Saint Petersburg. The composer died there that March, shortly after his forty-second birthday; the portrait records the hospital gown rather than the uniform of his youth.

cues.title: Resonance without the rush
cues.text: The lower, softer sound carries almost no rapid attacks. Listen to the spaces between changes: the close is sustained by resonance and small shifts of harmony, not by the running figures of the opening.

cues.title: A major-key ending
cues.text: The closing sonority remains centred on D major. The piece that began with restless, conflicting lines ends with the bass and upper harmony agreeing on the same tonic.

composer.name: Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky
composer.epithet: He used the timing of dance and theatre to make a symphony’s return, interruption or collapse physically audible.
facts: Imperial School of Jurisprudence; Saint Petersburg Conservatory, 1862–65, with Anton Rubinstein and Nikolai Zaremba
Nadezhda von Meck supplied an allowance from 1877 to 1890; their correspondence became a major record of his working life
Six numbered symphonies and Manfred; three ballets; operas, concertos, chamber music, piano music and songs
composer.background:
Tchaikovsky was born at Votkinsk, where his father managed an ironworks. Music belonged to the household before it became a profession: his governess Fanny Dürbach remembered the child’s intense responses to it, and he began piano lessons early. His formal training nevertheless pointed towards government service. In 1850 he entered the preparatory class of the Imperial School of Jurisprudence in Saint Petersburg, separated from his family. His mother died of cholera in 1854. After graduating in 1859 he worked in the Ministry of Justice, while concerts, opera and lessons gradually occupied more of his time.

When Anton Rubinstein’s Saint Petersburg Conservatory opened in 1862, Tchaikovsky joined its first generation of students. He studied composition with Rubinstein and theoretical subjects with Nikolai Zaremba, leaving government employment in 1863. The training mattered practically: he could organise large forms, prepare orchestral scores and teach harmony. In 1866 Nikolai Rubinstein recruited him for the new Moscow Conservatory. Tchaikovsky taught there until 1878, wrote criticism and translated pedagogical material. His early reputation grew through this sustained professional work.

movement: Act II, No. 13 · Waltz of the Flowers
forces: Concert band; arrangement by Lawrence Odom
performers: United States Air Force Band, Concert Band
intro: The ballet’s large ensemble waltz, heard in Lawrence Odom’s concert-band arrangement. Listen for the three-beat accompaniment continuing underneath melodies that stretch across several bars.

cues.title: Before the dancers move
cues.text: The introduction holds back the regular waltz accompaniment. This recording uses Lawrence Odom’s concert-band arrangement: follow the melody and bass separately rather than expecting the string colours of Tchaikovsky’s orchestral score.

cues.title: A cadenza delays the dance
cues.text: The opening gives way to an extended cadenza, a passage that loosens the regular pulse. Fast decoration and pauses alternate; the three-beat accompaniment has not yet established its stride.

cues.title: Hoffmann through Dumas
cues.text: The Nutcracker reached Tchaikovsky through Alexandre Dumas’s adaptation of E. T. A. Hoffmann’s story. The ballet’s scenario was prepared by the theatre director Ivan Vsevolozhsky and choreographer Marius Petipa.

cues.title: Three beats underneath
cues.text: The principal waltz establishes D major. Hear the bass mark the beginning of each bar while the accompaniment fills the remaining beats; the melody stretches across those regular units instead of stopping at every bar line.

cues.title: A broader answering phrase
cues.text: The dance grows fuller without losing its three-beat foundation. Listen for the longer melodic arc above the accompaniment: the tune and the bass organise time at different scales.

cues.title: Work interrupted by travel
cues.text: Tchaikovsky began the ballet in 1891, the year he travelled to America for concerts marking the opening of Carnegie Hall. He resumed sustained work after returning to Russia; the orchestration followed in 1892.

cues.title: Expansion, then a smaller sound
cues.text: The phrase swells and then abruptly lightens. The waltz continues through the change; reduced volume makes the next melody feel like a new group of dancers rather than a new piece.

cues.title: The suite came first
cues.text: Tchaikovsky conducted the concert suite in Saint Petersburg on 19 March 1892, nine months before the ballet’s premiere. He placed the Waltz of the Flowers last in the suite; in the theatre further dances still follow it.

cues.title: The minor side of D
cues.text: The middle of the waltz spends time in B minor, D major’s relative minor. The dance metre stays intact, so the change of colour comes from the melody and harmony rather than a different step.

cues.title: The main waltz returns
cues.text: The principal material returns in D major. Repetition gives the movement its balance: the contrasting melodies have occupied the middle, and now the original dance can be heard with more accumulated weight.

cues.title: Preparing the larger finish
cues.text: Listen for the orchestra’s weight increasing before the final run. The melody still keeps its broad shape while the accompaniment prepares a more forceful close.

cues.title: The coda changes direction
cues.text: A darker harmonic turn briefly interrupts the major-key dance. The closing passage uses that detour to make the eventual return to D major more emphatic.

cues.title: More attacks, greater weight
cues.text: The closing figures become more active while the full band reinforces the dance. Listen for the quick movement above the bass: the waltz’s familiar pulse is now carrying a much denser surface.

cues.title: A concert ending
cues.text: The emphatic final chords close the waltz. In the ballet the great pas de deux follows; the concert suite instead makes this D major ending its destination.

work: Symphony No. 6 in B minor “Pathétique”, Op. 74
intro: After the preceding movement’s march, Tchaikovsky writes a slow finale that ends in B minor rather than a victorious major key. Listen for a melody divided between the violin sections, and for the bass taking over as the upper instruments fall silent.

cues.title: One melody, two sections
cues.text: The first and second violins share the opening line, each supplying notes missing from the other part. What sounds like one descending melody is assembled across the orchestra; neither violin section has the complete tune.

cues.title: Written at Klin
cues.text: Tchaikovsky composed the Sixth in February and March 1893 and orchestrated it that summer. His letters describe unusually strong confidence in the work, alongside repeated dissatisfaction with details of the instrumentation.

cues.title: Beginning the lament again
cues.text: After a near-silent pause, the opening kind of phrase returns. Listen to the attack and the withdrawal together: the melody’s downward shape is reinforced by the orchestra repeatedly losing volume.

cues.title: The slow ending was planned
cues.text: In a letter to his nephew Vladimir Davydov on 23 February 1893, Tchaikovsky explained that the finale would be a prolonged Adagio instead of a noisy Allegro. The reversal was part of the design from the beginning.

cues.title: A second kind of line
cues.text: The contrasting Andante grows out of the quiet. Its D major melody has a more continuous gait than the opening lament, but the bass and inner parts keep adding harmonic tension beneath it.

cues.title: Repetition extends the phrase
cues.text: Follow the short melodic shapes as they recur at different pitches. This is a sequence: repetition moves the line onward while delaying its resting point, so a melody that seems simple can support a long crescendo.

cues.title: The nephew in the dedication
cues.text: The symphony is dedicated to Vladimir Davydov. Tchaikovsky told him that it had a private programme which listeners would have to guess; he did not publish an explanatory story to accompany the score.

cues.title: The first large rupture
cues.text: The growth reaches a full-orchestra crest and changes harmonic direction. A few seconds later the volume falls sharply: the expansion does not produce a stable major-key ending.

cues.title: A bewildered first audience
cues.text: Tchaikovsky conducted the premiere in Saint Petersburg on 28 October 1893. Two days later he wrote to his publisher Jurgenson that the symphony had caused bewilderment, while insisting on his own pride in it.

cues.title: The lament comes back
cues.text: The opening material returns after the collapse. The downward melodic gestures resume, but the movement has not yet reached its greatest sustained pressure.

cues.title: Low notes gather weight
cues.text: The quiet phrase begins to build again. Attend to the lower harmony as well as the tune: a crescendo can come from adding support underneath, not merely from forcing the top line higher.

cues.title: A longer span of force
cues.text: This time the increase is sustained. Listen for how long the orchestra keeps the tension active once the louder level has been reached, instead of immediately letting the phrase subside.

cues.title: The last great crest
cues.text: The orchestra remains at nearly full pressure. The line presses towards a dominant harmony, the chord that normally prepares the home key; reaching it postpones the ending rather than completing it.

cues.title: Held harmony, draining sound
cues.text: The harmony holds while the volume drains away. The effect depends on staying with the same sonority: fewer attacks and less brightness replace the earlier surges.

cues.title: Pride, not an explanation
cues.text: In August 1893 Tchaikovsky called the Sixth his most sincere creation in a letter to Davydov. Those letters document his attachment to the symphony; they do not disclose the private programme he said lay behind it.

cues.title: The coda stays minor
cues.text: The music resumes in B minor after the low, quiet transition. There is no conversion to B major: the final span begins by giving the home key a dark, sustained bass foundation.

cues.title: Follow the low pulse
cues.text: Listen below the remaining melody. The low strings’ repeated support matters more as the upper sound diminishes; the ending is made by removing energy and register rather than by adding a final flourish.

cues.title: Below the melody’s range
cues.text: The last B minor sonority sinks into the low strings. Stay with the decay: the quiet bass is the end of the symphony, not an introduction to another movement.

composer.name: Antonín Dvořák
composer.epithet: A theatre violist who made dance accents, remembered songs and classical development work inside the same movement.
facts: Local teachers in Bohemia; Prague Organ School, 1857–59
Violist in Prague’s Provisional Theatre orchestra, 1862–71; organist and private teacher
Prague Conservatory; director of the National Conservatory of Music in New York, 1892–95
Nine symphonies, operas, concertos, chamber music, choral works and songs; B numbers refer to Jarmil Burghauser’s catalogue
composer.background:
Dvořák was born in Nelahozeves, a village north of Prague, where his father kept an inn and worked as a butcher. He learnt violin locally and acquired further musical training at Zlonice before attending the Prague Organ School in 1857–59. He earned his living in ensembles, including the orchestra of Prague’s Provisional Theatre from 1862 to 1871, playing viola under conductors who included Smetana. Opera taught him how a middle part supports singers, how repeated figures sustain a scene and how instrumental colour carries across a crowded theatre.

His early compositions were extensive and often ambitious: chamber music, symphonies and operatic projects accumulated before he had a dependable publisher. Wagner’s influence is audible in the scale and harmonic movement of some of these works. In 1873 he married Anna Čermáková. Teaching and an organist’s post helped support the household while applications for an Austrian state stipend brought his scores to influential readers. The award first received in 1875 brought both honour and money at a point when publication and commissions remained uncertain.

work: Symphony No. 9 in E minor “From the New World”, Op. 95
intro: The cor anglais melody became “Goin’ Home” only after Dvořák’s death. Around that apparently simple song he builds a slow movement with a minor-key middle, a sudden orchestral confrontation and a retreat into chamber music.

cues.title: Chords before the song
cues.text: The wind chords begin in E major, not in the movement’s eventual D♭ major. Their unexpected sequence makes the opening a separate threshold; the melody will arrive only after the harmony has found its new centre.

cues.title: The cor anglais sings
cues.text: The cor anglais carries the main melody over muted strings. It is the lower relative of the oboe, sounding a fifth below its written notes; its opening phrase moves through only a few pitches rather than a full major scale.

cues.title: New York, 1893
cues.text: Dvořák wrote the symphony while directing the National Conservatory of Music in New York. He had arrived in America in 1892 at the invitation of Jeannette Thurber; composing and teaching belonged to the same American appointment.

cues.title: A tune without semitones
cues.text: The opening tune draws on a pentatonic collection: five notes rather than the seven of a major scale. Its first phrases avoid D♭ major’s fourth and seventh degrees, so the melody can sound settled without leaning on the leading note.

cues.title: Song becomes orchestral weight
cues.text: The quiet material expands into a louder statement, then withdraws sharply. Keep the tune in mind through the change of scale: the same movement can treat it as a solo utterance or as an orchestral mass.

cues.title: “Goin’ Home” came later
cues.text: William Arms Fisher, one of Dvořák’s American pupils, added the words “Goin’ Home” in 1922. The melody was written for this symphony; it is not a spiritual that Dvořák borrowed ready-made.

cues.title: Support beneath the melody
cues.text: Listen to the accompaniment during this quieter continuation. Sustained notes can make the harmony change almost without an attack; the melody’s shape remains audible even when the supporting voices do very little.

cues.title: Before the Iowa summer
cues.text: The score was finished in New York on 24 May 1893, before Dvořák’s summer in Spillville, Iowa. His “American” String Quartet and String Quintet came from that later stay among the town’s Czech-speaking community.

cues.title: The minor middle section
cues.text: The middle section changes to C♯ minor. C♯ and D♭ are the same piano key, but changing the surrounding notes alters the harmonic character; quicker figures disturb the opening song’s long breaths.

cues.title: Two rates of movement
cues.text: Through this middle section, separate the moving wind line from the recurring support beneath it. A melody can become more urgent without the bass needing to follow every small note.

cues.title: Longfellow, without a fixed plot
cues.text: Dvořák knew Longfellow’s The Song of Hiawatha before going to America. Scholars connect it with the symphony’s middle movements, but claims that every passage illustrates a particular burial or landscape go beyond the secure documentary evidence.

cues.title: The movement draws inward
cues.text: The sound diminishes and the attacks become sparse. The middle section has not yet finished: this reduction prepares a quicker episode rather than the return of the opening song.

cues.title: Harry Burleigh’s singing
cues.text: The African American singer Harry T. Burleigh introduced Dvořák to spirituals at close quarters in New York. Dvořák advocated learning from their musical character, distinguishing that approach from simply inserting existing tunes into a symphony.

cues.title: The surface starts moving
cues.text: A quicker episode breaks the stillness. The change is in the small notes as well as the volume: repeated activity gathers the orchestra into a continuous build.

cues.title: The symphony breaks in
cues.text: The climax brings material from the first movement into the Largo’s world. Dvořák connects the symphony by recollection: themes heard earlier can interrupt and combine with the music of a later movement.

cues.title: The song returns quietly
cues.text: D♭ major and the opening song return after the orchestral confrontation. The scale is small again; listen for how much more exposed the melody sounds when the preceding mass has disappeared.

cues.title: Do not fill the gaps
cues.text: Let the spaces between the phrases register. Dvořák reduces the accompaniment until changes of register and the continuation of a single line carry the shape; the pauses belong to the music rather than interrupting it.

cues.title: Carnegie Hall, December 1893
cues.text: Anton Seidl conducted the New York Philharmonic in the premiere on 16 December 1893. The Largo’s melody later circulated in vocal and instrumental arrangements, but here it remains part of a symphony whose themes keep returning across movements.

cues.title: The opening chords reconsidered
cues.text: The introductory chord sequence returns near the close. Its slower changes and low register distinguish it from the solo song, bringing back the harmonic threshold through which the movement began.

cues.title: D♭ remains after the song
cues.text: The movement settles on D♭ major at a much lower volume. Listen to the low support and the decay of the final sonority rather than expecting another statement of the tune.

composer.name: Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov
composer.epithet: A naval officer turned teacher who made orchestral register and symmetrical scales the machinery of Russian fairy-tale opera.
facts: Naval College in Saint Petersburg; composition with Mily Balakirev, followed by intensive private study
Saint Petersburg Conservatory from 1871; inspector of naval bands, 1873–84
Married the pianist and composer Nadezhda Purgold in 1872; she assisted with arrangements and editorial work
Fifteen operas, three symphonies, orchestral suites and overtures, songs and teaching books
composer.background:
Rimsky-Korsakov was born in Tikhvin into a family with a tradition of naval service. He entered the Naval College in Saint Petersburg in 1856, while continuing piano lessons and attending opera. His teacher Fyodor Kanille introduced him to Balakirev in 1861. The young officer began a symphony before he had the theoretical equipment expected of a conservatory composition student. A naval voyage on the clipper Almaz took him abroad in 1862–65, interrupting regular contact with the circle while work on the symphony continued. Balakirev conducted the First Symphony in Saint Petersburg in 1865.

His early colleagues included Mussorgsky, Borodin and Cui. With Balakirev they became the group known as the Five, united by friendship and cultural argument despite their differing methods. Rimsky-Korsakov’s orchestral picture Sadko, first written in 1867, already connects a supernatural subject with an unusual pitch organisation. The sea musician’s underwater world encouraged scales and chord relationships outside ordinary major and minor. His experience of ships and oceans gave the subject a biographical setting.
