movement: III. The Young Prince and the Young Princess
performers: San Francisco Symphony Orchestra, Pierre Monteux; Naoum Blinder, violin
intro: A string melody and a lighter dance occupy the third movement of this orchestral suite. The solo violin belongs to the storytelling frame: Rimsky-Korsakov warns against assigning a separate plot incident to every musical detail.

cues.title: A melody in long breaths
cues.text: The violins introduce the broad G major melody. Listen to the tune’s small turns and ornaments against the slower accompaniment: the decoration extends a singing line rather than replacing it with a separate display.

cues.title: A composer in the navy
cues.text: Rimsky-Korsakov sailed aboard the clipper Almaz from 1862 to 1865 while working on his First Symphony. His naval training preceded his career as a conservatory professor; practical knowledge of wind instruments later grew through inspecting naval bands.

cues.title: The line keeps extending
cues.text: The melody moves through another span rather than closing after its first statement. Follow the bass under the sustained upper notes: changes below can redirect the harmony while the tune keeps its vocal shape.

cues.title: Breathing between the phrases
cues.text: Listen for the dip in volume before the next swell. These withdrawals articulate the long melody without needing a heavy accent at every phrase ending.

cues.title: Song yields to dance
cues.text: The large lyrical phrase reaches a crest, then gives way to quicker, lighter activity. Listen for the smaller notes becoming more prominent as the overall volume decreases.

cues.title: Titles, not a screenplay
cues.text: The suite draws on The Thousand and One Nights. In his autobiography Rimsky-Korsakov said the movement titles were only hints for listeners; he did not intend each recurring theme to remain tied to one character or event.

cues.title: Decoration with changing weight
cues.text: The dance alternates stronger gestures with lighter responses. Notice the upper sound continuing to brighten even when the volume briefly drops: colour and loudness are not the same thing.

cues.title: Back towards the opening song
cues.text: The broad lyrical material regains the foreground and returns to G major. The quicker dance has changed the surrounding texture, but the movement’s long melodic span remains recognisable.

cues.title: The professor studies privately
cues.text: Rimsky-Korsakov became a professor at the Saint Petersburg Conservatory in 1871. He later admitted how much theory he still had to learn: systematic study of harmony, counterpoint and fugue accompanied his early years of teaching.

cues.title: The soloist and the frame
cues.text: The solo violin is the suite’s recurring storytelling voice. In this reduced passage, listen for the freer movement of an exposed line rather than the measured weight of the full string section.

cues.title: The orchestra fills out
cues.text: The lyrical sound grows back into an ensemble statement. The melody gains weight from its support; its sustained notes do not have to become fast for the passage to build.

cues.title: San Francisco, March 1942
cues.text: Pierre Monteux recorded this performance with the San Francisco Symphony on 3–4 March 1942 in the War Memorial Opera House. Naoum Blinder plays the solo violin; the surviving transfer comes from the Victor 78-rpm set.

cues.title: The largest final expansion
cues.text: A quiet preparation gives way to the movement’s last large orchestral span. Listen for the sharp increase in weight, then for the sustained line riding above it rather than turning into a march.

cues.title: The melody sheds its weight
cues.text: The full sound withdraws into a quieter close. Follow the familiar melodic outline as its accompaniment becomes less prominent: a return can be made by subtraction as well as by adding instruments.

cues.title: A quiet G major
cues.text: The movement closes quietly in G major. The suite still has its final movement to come: the festival, sea and shipwreck are outside this self-contained lyrical scene.

composer.name: Gabriel Fauré
composer.epithet: A church organist who made the French song and the chamber ensemble laboratories for harmony.
facts: École Niedermeyer, 1854–65; piano with Camille Saint-Saëns
Madeleine: choirmaster 1877–96, organist 1896–1905 · Paris Conservatoire: composition professor 1896–1905, director 1905–20
Mélodies, piano music, chamber music, Requiem, the opera Pénélope
composer.background:
Fauré learned his trade in a school for church musicians. His father was a schoolmaster in the Ariège; at nine, Gabriel was sent to Louis Niedermeyer’s recently founded school in Paris, where plainchant, Renaissance polyphony, organ playing and counterpoint belonged to the ordinary curriculum. The education matters to the harmony. A melody can cadence in minor with an unsharpened seventh degree; a chord can emerge from the independent movement of voices. These possibilities were practical knowledge before they became a recognisable Fauré style.

After Niedermeyer died in 1861, Camille Saint-Saëns took over the piano class and introduced the pupils to Schumann, Liszt and Wagner. Teacher and pupil remained friends for more than sixty years. Fauré’s graduation work, the Cantique de Jean Racine of 1865, already joins the two educations: a flowing keyboard accompaniment beneath a choral texture whose entries are controlled by contrapuntal discipline. Its French text is Racine’s paraphrase of a Latin hymn. The bass supports long phrases that carry the upper voices across the bar-lines.

era.name: The French Line
era.heroCaption: James McNeill Whistler, Nocturne: Blue and Gold — Old Battersea Bridge

performers: Chorale Philippe Caillard; Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo, Louis Frémaux
intro: The prayer for rest begins in F major, with a string melody that moves independently of the voices. Fauré then joins it to the Communion’s prayer for eternal light and recalls the opening of the Requiem itself.

cues.title: Two melodies, not one
cues.text: Before the voices, a moving string line establishes F major. When the tenors take up the prayer, that line does not stop: the accompaniment has a melody of its own.

cues.title: A school for church musicians
cues.text: Fauré entered the École Niedermeyer at nine. Plainchant and counterpoint belonged to his training; Saint-Saëns later taught him piano and introduced him to Schumann, Liszt and Wagner. The church musician and the experimental harmonist had the same education.

cues.title: The petition gains weight
cues.text: The fuller choir makes the plea more insistent. The string motion continues, but the chords beneath the words no longer keep the opening’s F major settled; changes of harmony supply the pressure without a change of basic pulse.

cues.title: The tenor line returns
cues.text: The tenors recover the opening prayer and the volume falls back. Follow the string line underneath: Fauré can restore the same melody without making its accompaniment merely double the singers.

cues.title: From rest to light
cues.text: The text turns to “Lux aeterna”: let eternal light shine upon them. The sopranos’ held note begins a new section; the harmony opens beneath it, replacing the earlier melody-and-accompaniment texture with sustained choral chords.

cues.title: An ordinary Paris funeral
cues.text: Fauré conducted the first version of the Requiem at the Madeleine on 16 January 1888, for the funeral of the architect Joseph Lesoufaché. It had five movements. The Offertoire and Libera me joined it later; the enlarged orchestral version followed in 1900.

cues.title: The choir holds together
cues.text: Listen to the weight of voices moving in chords rather than answering one another in imitation. The sustained choral sound grows stronger across this passage; the changing bass gives those long notes a direction.

cues.title: The whole Requiem remembered
cues.text: The prayer “Requiem aeternam” returns with music from the work’s opening movement. This is a quotation across movements, not another statement of the Agnus Dei tune: Fauré brings the larger work into this movement’s closing pages.

cues.title: One last choral swell
cues.text: The recollection grows into the movement’s strongest swell. Notice how briefly the choir holds that weight before the sound withdraws; the passage does not turn into a separate fast section.

cues.title: The teacher of Ravel
cues.text: In 1896 Fauré became composition professor at the Paris Conservatoire; his pupils included Ravel, Koechlin and Nadia Boulanger. He became its director in 1905, although he had never studied there. Hearing trouble had already begun in 1903.

cues.title: An ending without voices
cues.text: The voices have finished, leaving the orchestra to close the movement. The instrumental melody recalls the opening, but there is no final choral declaration: the last sound belongs to the accompaniment that was never merely an accompaniment.

composer.name: Leoš Janáček
composer.epithet: A Moravian composer who studied the inflections of speech and built operas from short cells, repeated figures and abrupt changes of perspective.
facts: Old Brno monastery choir; Prague Organ School; further study in Leipzig and Vienna
Teacher and choral conductor in Brno; founder and director of the Brno Organ School, 1881–1919
Moravian folk song · Czech speech · Russian literature · Gabriela Preissová, Rudolf Těsnohlídek and Karel Čapek
Nine operas; choral and orchestral works; two string quartets; piano music; folk-song collections
composer.background:
Janáček was born in Hukvaldy in 1854, into a Moravian schoolmaster’s family. At eleven he became a chorister at the Augustinian monastery in Old Brno, where Pavel Křížkovský supplied rigorous musical training. His education continued at the Prague Organ School and, more briefly, in Leipzig and Vienna. He returned to Brno to build his career. Teaching, conducting and organising institutions occupied much of his adult life: he founded the Brno Organ School in 1881 and directed it until 1919. The composer now associated with the modernist opera house spent decades preparing other people’s practical musical education.

He married Zdeňka Schulzová in 1881. Their son Vladimír died in childhood; their daughter Olga died in 1903, aged twenty-one. The marriage endured these losses but was repeatedly strained. Friendship with Dvořák and the repertory of Czech choral societies helped shape the earlier compositions, yet Janáček’s mature manner developed slowly. He was already in his forties when the short motives, irregular phrases and repeated accompaniment figures of his later music began to replace more conventional forms. His position in musical history is therefore misleading if determined only by his birth date, a decade before Strauss.

era.heroCaption: Gustav Klimt, Beethoven Frieze: The Well-Armed Strong One

intro: Janáček wrote this sonata after a worker was killed during demonstrations for a Czech university in Brno. Its second movement builds from a short, returning piano phrase; the interruptions matter as much as the notes.

cues.title: A phrase with gaps
cues.text: Listen for a short melodic shape returning between rests, rather than a tune that unfolds without interruption. On a piano, a held note is already fading; Janáček makes the space after an attack part of the phrase.

cues.title: A worker in Brno
cues.text: The sonata commemorates František Pavlík, a young worker killed during the 1905 demonstrations for a Czech university in Brno. Its title gives a date, 1 October 1905; the two surviving movements are called “Foreboding” and “Death”.

cues.title: After the first outburst
cues.text: The first forceful statement has already collapsed into quiet. Notice how little transition is needed: the piano can move from a full attack to a few detached sounds without an orchestral change of colour.

cues.title: The opening comes back
cues.text: The opening span returns. Listen for the same pattern of quiet phrases, a stronger outburst and withdrawal: repetition gives you a reference against which the later expansion can be measured.

cues.title: A teacher before fame
cues.text: Janáček founded the Brno Organ School in 1881 and directed it until 1919. Teaching, conducting and building musical institutions occupied decades of his life before his operas won international recognition.

cues.title: The decay between attacks
cues.text: In this quiet passage, follow the dying sound after each note as carefully as the next attack. The rests separate statements, but resonance can continue across them; silence on the page is not necessarily silence in the room.

cues.title: Repetition begins to accumulate
cues.text: The repeated material now gathers force instead of withdrawing after a single surge. Listen for an accompaniment figure persisting under changing upper notes: an ostinato is a repeated pattern, not a guarantee of unchanged harmony.

cues.title: A pianist saved it
cues.text: Janáček destroyed the third movement, a funeral march, and later discarded the other two. The pianist who had premiered them kept a copy; she brought it back to his attention in 1924, when he authorised publication.

cues.title: The pressure is sustained
cues.text: The piano remains forceful across successive phrases rather than immediately falling back. Compare this with the brief outbursts near the beginning: the same instrument now has to sustain a much longer span of tension.

cues.title: At the crest
cues.text: The loud passage continues through one more harmonic turn, then begins to recede. Listen for the point where repeated attacks stop adding weight: the return of quieter material is prepared by a loss of force, not a long pause.

cues.title: The opening, made heavier
cues.text: The opening material has returned with more weight than it carried at the start. Listen for the familiar withdrawal after the phrase: recollection preserves its shape, but not its original dynamic scale.

cues.title: Speech written as music
cues.text: Janáček noted the pitches and rhythms of ordinary speech, including the circumstances in which he heard it. His notebooks record an interest in how an utterance changes with its speaker’s situation; his operas likewise build phrases from short, inflected cells.

cues.title: Fewer attacks, more space
cues.text: The final phrases leave more room around each attack. Resist counting only the struck notes: the length of their decay and the wait before the next phrase determine the pace of this ending.

cues.title: The last resonance
cues.text: The closing E♭ minor harmony loses its sound gradually. There is no further attack to restore the earlier momentum; the movement ends with the piano’s resonance, not a final flourish.

composer.name: Edward Elgar
composer.epithet: A Worcester violinist who made orchestral variations into portraits of friends and the concerto into an argument with memory.
facts: Largely self-taught; violin, organ, orchestral playing and his father’s Worcester music shop
Bandmaster, Worcester County Asylum, Powick, 1879–84 · organist, St George’s Catholic Church, 1885–89 · Master of the King’s Musick, 1924–34
Two completed symphonies; violin and cello concertos; choral works; chamber music; five completed Pomp and Circumstance marches
composer.background:
Elgar learned the orchestra from inside it. His father William kept a music shop in Worcester, tuned pianos and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church. Edward read the scores in the shop, played violin in local ensembles, taught several instruments and eventually succeeded his father at the organ. He was born in Lower Broadheath in 1857, a Catholic in a predominantly Anglican musical establishment and a tradesman’s son in a profession increasingly organised around London colleges. He remained sensitive to both distinctions throughout his later success. His practical education taught him how a phrase feels under a bow.

At Powick he wrote quadrilles and polkas for an unusual ensemble, learning to give each instrument useful work. The Three Choirs Festival brought larger repertory within reach: Handel, Mendelssohn and contemporary oratorio, alongside orchestral music from the Continent. Visits to London widened that education. Wagner mattered particularly: the chromatic connection between chords, the orchestral recollection of earlier events and the long postponement of a cadence all entered Elgar’s language. His mature scores acquired part of their English character through their subsequent public use.

era.name: Fin de siècle
era.heroCaption: Gustav Klimt, Beethoven Frieze: The Well-Armed Strong One

work: Variations on an Original Theme “Enigma”, Op. 36
intro: A portrait of August Jaeger, the publisher’s reader who encouraged Elgar when he was close to giving up. Listen for the quiet retreats between its broad orchestral swells.

cues.title: An Adagio in three
cues.text: The quiet string melody moves in three beats to the bar, not the four of the original Enigma theme. Listen for the difference between the steady beat and the longer phrase: the tune does not stop at each bar line.

cues.title: The friend behind Nimrod
cues.text: August Jaeger worked for Elgar’s publisher, Novello, and encouraged him through periods of discouragement. This variation remembers their friendship; the complete set is dedicated “to my friends pictured within”.

cues.title: A public breakthrough
cues.text: Hans Richter conducted the first performance of the Enigma Variations at St James’s Hall, London, on 19 June 1899. Elgar was forty-two; the work established a national reputation after years of teaching and provincial music-making.

cues.title: The strongest swell
cues.text: This is the recording’s strongest swell, though another follows before the end. Listen beneath the melody: moving inner parts keep the harmony changing even while the upper line sustains a note.

cues.title: Scores in the shop
cues.text: Elgar’s father kept a music shop in Worcester and played the organ at St George’s Catholic Church. Elgar learned from its scores and from practical work as a violinist, teacher and organist, rather than a conservatoire composition course.

cues.title: The final withdrawal
cues.text: The orchestra withdraws quickly after the last swell. E♭ major remains, but the volume drains away: Elgar closes the variation by reducing its weight rather than adding another emphatic cadence.

composer.name: Giacomo Puccini
composer.epithet: An opera composer who made a remembered tune, a stage noise or a change of orchestral register determine the timing of a scene.
facts: Lucca; Milan Conservatory, 1880–83, with Antonio Bazzini and Amilcare Ponchielli
Publisher Giulio Ricordi · librettists Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa · later Giuseppe Adami and Renato Simoni
Twelve operas when the three parts of Il trittico are counted separately; songs, sacred and chamber music
composer.background:
Puccini was born into a dynasty of church musicians in Lucca in 1858. His father Michele died when Giacomo was five, and the expectation that the boy would inherit the family profession survived him. Puccini studied locally, played the organ and composed sacred music, including a Mass completed in 1880. Hearing Verdi’s Aida in Pisa in 1876 helped turn his attention towards the theatre. A scholarship enabled him to enter the Milan Conservatory in 1880, where he studied with Antonio Bazzini and Amilcare Ponchielli. His graduation work, the orchestral Capriccio sinfonico, already contains material he would reuse at the beginning of La bohème.

His first opera, Le Villi, failed to win the Sonzogno competition for which it was written, but a performance in Milan in 1884 attracted the publisher Giulio Ricordi. Ricordi supported revisions, further performances and the much less successful Edgar, premiered at La Scala in 1889. The partnership mattered because Puccini composed slowly, demanded repeated alterations to his texts and needed protection against a premature commercial verdict. The theatre was a collective workshop: librettist, publisher, designer and conductor all contributed practical decisions, although Puccini insisted on controlling the length and placement of the decisive moments.

era.name: Fin de siècle
era.heroCaption: Gustav Klimt, Beethoven Frieze: The Well-Armed Strong One

movement: Act I · Sì, mi chiamano Mimì
intro: Mimì introduces herself to Rodolfo: she embroiders flowers, lives alone and waits for spring. Puccini lets ordinary conversation open into a long vocal line, then return to conversation.

cues.title: An answer to Rodolfo
cues.text: Rodolfo has introduced himself as a poet; Mimì answers with her own account of work and solitude. Listen for the alternation of short, speech-like phrases and sustained singing: Puccini makes an aria out of a first conversation.

cues.title: Paris through two librettists
cues.text: Luigi Illica and Giuseppe Giacosa adapted Henry Murger’s stories of Parisian artists for Puccini. The opera puts the lovers’ first meeting in a cold attic; Mimì has come looking for a light for her candle.

cues.title: Speech opens into song
cues.text: The voice expands into the first large swell, then draws back. Notice how a sustained vowel carries more musical weight than a string of quick syllables: Puccini can change the pace of the scene without stopping its conversation.

cues.title: From organ to theatre
cues.text: Puccini came from a family of church musicians in Lucca and worked as an organist. He entered the Milan Conservatory in 1880, studying with Bazzini and Ponchielli, and completed his studies in 1883.

cues.title: Turin, February 1896
cues.text: La bohème first reached the stage at Turin’s Teatro Regio on 1 February 1896. The same team of Puccini, Illica and Giacosa would go on to make Tosca and Madama Butterfly.

cues.title: The broadest vocal span
cues.text: The largest swell grows out of the aria’s quiet middle. Listen to the length of the line rather than individual high notes: the sound builds across several phrases before it recedes.

cues.title: A second rise
cues.text: After the retreat, the voice swells once more. Compare this shorter rise with the preceding long one: the aria is preparing to return to ordinary speech, not to finish with a display cadenza.

cues.title: The conversation remains open
cues.text: The sound dwindles rather than ending with a triumphant high note. Mimì’s account concludes with an apology for disturbing her neighbour; in the opera, this is a pause in the encounter, not the end of the scene.

composer.name: Gustav Mahler
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.

era.heroCaption: Gustav Klimt, Beethoven Frieze: The Well-Armed Strong One

intro: The quiet centre of a loud symphony. After three movements for a full orchestra, Mahler sends home the winds, brass and percussion and writes ten minutes for strings and harp alone.

cues.title: Fourth of five movements
cues.text: The Fifth Symphony runs from a funeral march in C♯ minor to a D major finale. This Adagietto is the hinge before that finale, and the only movement without a single wind instrument.

cues.title: Strings, harp, almost no pulse
cues.text: Soft sustained strings and the harp’s broken chords set up F major. The pulse is so slow that each harmony seems to hang; the first violins’ melody enters above it and moves only when the chord underneath has been fully heard.

cues.title: Maiernigg, 1901
cues.text: Mahler composed the Fifth in the summers of 1901 and 1902 in his composing hut above the Wörthersee in Carinthia, during the years he ran the Vienna Court Opera. He composed only in summer; winters were for the opera house.

cues.title: Leaning notes
cues.text: Listen to how the melody’s important notes arrive: often on a note that clashes with the harmony and then slips by step onto a chord tone. These appoggiaturas, the musical equivalent of a sigh, carry most of the movement’s expression.

cues.title: A letter without words?
cues.text: The conductor Willem Mengelberg wrote in his score that the Adagietto was Mahler’s declaration of love to Alma Schindler, sent to her in manuscript instead of a letter. They met in November 1901 and married in March 1902. The story rests on Mengelberg’s word alone.

cues.title: The first climax
cues.text: The line climbs and the strings thicken. Around 3:00 comes the first big swell, the loudest passage so far, before the music falls back to a whisper.

cues.title: Home again
cues.text: F major returns, quiet and settled. Notice how much of the music’s weight sits in the cellos and basses here: the bass line is a melody in its own right.

cues.title: A darker swell
cues.text: The texture surges again and the harmony turns toward the minor, as if the first section were trying to break out of itself.

cues.title: Fließender: the middle section
cues.text: The marking changes to “more flowing” and the harmony slips into G♭ major, a semitone above F. A shift of a semitone keeps the same room and changes the light.

cues.title: Higher, brighter
cues.text: The violins move up and the sound gets brighter; the middle section builds to its own peak around 5:30 before turning again.

cues.title: The Rückert summer
cues.text: In August 1901, the same summer the Fifth was begun, Mahler set Rückert’s “Ich bin der Welt abhanden gekommen”: “I have become lost to the world.” The song is also in F major and also slow, and its sound world is very close to this movement’s. Of the song he said, “It is myself.”

cues.title: Wandering keys
cues.text: Before coming home the harmony travels through sharper regions. Mahler treats keys as colours to pass through, not as places to stay.

cues.title: The return
cues.text: The opening music comes back in F major, a little fuller than before. The return is the movement’s main event: you hear the same melody again, but now you have been somewhere else.

cues.title: A second life
cues.text: For decades the Adagietto was played on its own as a funeral piece. Leonard Bernstein conducted it at Robert Kennedy’s funeral in St Patrick’s Cathedral in 1968, and Visconti’s film Death in Venice (1971) made it famous far beyond the concert hall.

cues.title: How slow is slow?
cues.text: This performance takes about ten and a half minutes. Mengelberg, who knew Mahler, recorded it in 1926 in about seven; Bruno Walter, Mahler’s assistant, took under eight in 1938. Many modern conductors stretch it past eleven. The marking is only “Sehr langsam”.

cues.title: The final ascent
cues.text: The melody begins its last climb. From about 9:15 comes the loudest passage of the movement, the violins at the top of their line with the full string body behind them.

cues.title: Dissolve
cues.text: The sound thins and the last F major harmony fades into the hall.

cues.title: What comes next
cues.text: The Rondo-Finale begins with a solo horn and later turns this movement’s melody into something quick and light-footed. In the symphony, the love song becomes material for a comedy.

movement: IV. Urlicht — Sehr feierlich, aber schlicht
performers: Barbara Schubert, the DuPage Symphony Orchestra
intro: After three orchestral movements, a single alto gives the Second Symphony its first words. A poem from Des Knaben Wunderhorn becomes a five-minute declaration of faith, with a brass chorale rather than an operatic accompaniment.

cues.title: A single human voice
cues.text: This is the first sung movement of the Second Symphony. The alto’s opening phrase is separated from the brass response; Mahler asks for “very solemn, but simple”, not an operatic scene.

cues.title: A hymn without words
cues.text: The brass answers with a chorale: a melody harmonised in measured blocks, like a hymn. Its fuller sound contrasts with the solitary opening voice; the orchestral reply takes longer than the phrase it answers.

cues.title: A poem from 1808
cues.text: Urlicht appears in the second volume of Des Knaben Wunderhorn, published in Heidelberg in 1808 by Achim von Arnim and Clemens Brentano. Mahler takes the words from this collection of German folk poetry, but the melody and its orchestral setting are his own.

cues.title: Summer at Steinbach
cues.text: An early orchestral manuscript is dated 19 July 1893 at Steinbach am Attersee. Mahler was then chief conductor at Hamburg’s Stadttheater, a post he held from 1891 to 1897; the lake was his summer workplace.

cues.title: Listen beneath the voice
cues.text: The melody moves in long spans over a slowly changing accompaniment. Listen past the held vocal notes to the chords underneath: the song’s sense of motion often comes from harmony rather than a busy surface.

cues.title: The angel on the road
cues.text: The broad opening gives way to quicker movement. The poem turns from a statement about human suffering to a small narrative: a traveller, a road and an angel blocking the way.

cues.title: Refusing the angel
cues.text: The poem’s speaker refuses to be turned away from heaven: “Ich bin von Gott und will wieder zu Gott!” — “I am from God and want to return to God.” This is the traveller’s reply to the angel, not a prayer asking permission.

cues.title: A sustained crest
cues.text: The line swells towards the loudest crest of this performance, around 3:50. A sustained vocal phrase, rather than a quicker beat, produces the pressure; the sound then withdraws sharply.

cues.title: One more broad phrase
cues.text: The closing phrase makes another broad swell, then draws back. Its long notes leave space to hear the harmony change underneath; the volume falls well before the final chord.

cues.title: Settling on D♭
cues.text: The D♭ major close fades without a final accent. In the complete symphony, this little song stands immediately before the immense choral finale: one person’s confidence comes before the chorus’s answer.

composer.name: Gustav Mahler
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.

intro: Mahler begins with sleigh bells and a G major violin tune, then builds a sonata movement from material that first sounds almost domestic. Listen for how the same themes change character when played against one another.

cues.title: Bells before the tune
cues.text: Flutes and sleigh bells precede the violin melody. The bells are not a festive extra added to an already complete tune: their short figure is part of the movement’s material and will interrupt it again.

cues.title: The opera director
cues.text: Mahler was director of the Vienna Court Opera from 1897 to 1907. This symphony was written during his summer breaks in 1899 and 1900; the rest of his year belonged chiefly to rehearsals and performances.

cues.title: A first expansion
cues.text: The opening music grows louder as the harmony moves towards D major, G’s dominant. Listen for the change that follows: the short, articulated figures give way to a longer singing phrase.

cues.title: A longer singing line
cues.text: The second theme belongs chiefly to the cellos, and Mahler marks it “broadly sung”. Listen to its long notes rather than expecting the opening tune’s clipped rhythm: the contrast is in the length and shape of the phrases as well as their key.

cues.title: An abrupt withdrawal
cues.text: The singing line stops dominating, and the orchestra suddenly becomes much quieter. Small, articulated figures take over; Mahler changes the scale of the music without ending the movement or beginning a new one.

cues.title: The ending came first
cues.text: The Fourth grows out of Das himmlische Leben, a Wunderhorn song Mahler composed in 1892. He first considered it for the Third Symphony, then made it the Fourth’s finale and wrote three orchestral movements to lead towards it.

cues.title: Still in the exposition
cues.text: G major and the opening material have already come back, but this is not yet the recapitulation. Mahler includes a return within his exposition, the section that introduces the themes; the long development still lies ahead.

cues.title: A room above the lake
cues.text: The first sketches were made during Mahler’s 1899 holiday at Aussee. He finished the work the following summer at Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, where a separate composing hut allowed him to work away from the household.

cues.title: The development starts working
cues.text: Fragments of the earlier themes become material for the development, the section that changes their keys and combines them. The opening’s bell figure is part of this process; its return no longer guarantees G major.

cues.title: The flutes offer another tune
cues.text: A new major-key melody appears in the flutes. Its repeated notes and dotted rhythms are relatives of the opening theme, not a digression; Mahler will also draw on this material in the symphony’s sung finale.

cues.title: Several lines at once
cues.text: The tune breaks into a busier exchange among instrumental parts. Follow one line across the changes of colour: a phrase can continue in one section of the orchestra while another cuts across it.

cues.title: No explanatory programme
cues.text: For the Fourth, Mahler withheld the kind of narrative programme he had supplied for earlier symphonies. The sung text of the finale remained, but listeners were not given a story to assign to every event in the orchestral movements.

cues.title: Fragments under pressure
cues.text: Short figures overlap instead of taking orderly turns. Listen for the difference between a chord, whose notes are heard together as one harmony, and counterpoint, in which each instrumental part keeps its own melodic direction.

cues.title: Towards the central collision
cues.text: The same orchestra that began with a few bell strokes now drives several lines together at full weight. The next half-minute reaches the movement’s loudest sustained passage; notice how quickly the texture empties afterwards.

cues.title: Signals after the outburst
cues.text: After the central outburst, military-style calls replace the crowded texture. Listen for the repeated-note signals in the brass: isolated gestures, not another long singing theme.

cues.title: The opening comes back
cues.text: G major and the opening material return. This is the recapitulation: the themes heard before the development are heard again, but their reappearance follows the central orchestral crisis, not a repeat sign.

cues.title: The return grows louder
cues.text: The returning music swells to almost the weight of the central climax. A recapitulation need not be a quieter repeat: Mahler lets the old material build new pressure before the broad second theme is heard again.

cues.title: The second theme comes home
cues.text: The broad second theme is now heard in the orbit of G major rather than its earlier D major. Sonata form brings material that belonged to a different key into the tonic, the home key; the melody can stay recognisable while its harmonic setting changes.

cues.title: Another sudden thinning
cues.text: The fuller singing line gives way to a much thinner, more articulated texture. Quiet does not mean static here: the notes become shorter and more numerous as the volume falls.

cues.title: Twice in one evening
cues.text: On 23 October 1904, Mahler conducted the Fourth twice at the same Concertgebouw concert in Amsterdam, with an interval between performances. Mengelberg proposed the repetition and prepared the orchestra; Mahler conducted both readings.

cues.title: The closing pages
cues.text: The closing stretch is not a long victory march. Mahler alternates fuller statements with small withdrawals, keeping the ending unsettled even while G major reasserts itself.

cues.title: Munich, November 1901
cues.text: Mahler conducted the premiere in Munich on 25 November 1901. The audience heard four movements rather than the Second’s five or the Third’s six, yet this more compact symphony still met with boos.

cues.title: Almost a false ending
cues.text: The sound shrinks towards one of the movement’s quietest points. Keep listening beyond this withdrawal: the first movement does not end by fading away, although Mahler lets it approach silence before the final burst.

cues.title: A compact last word
cues.text: The orchestra suddenly recovers its full sound and finishes in G major. Mahler gives the movement a short, emphatic ending, not the long fade of the Adagietto.

composer.name: Claude Debussy
composer.epithet: He made a chord’s spacing, a scale’s missing notes and an instrument’s register determine the course of a piece.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1872; piano with Antoine Marmontel, composition with Ernest Guiraud
Prix de Rome 1884 · Paris Exposition 1889 · Pelléas et Mélisande 1902
One completed opera, orchestral triptychs, piano collections, songs, a quartet and three late sonatas
French Symbolist poetry · Russian music · Javanese gamelan · eighteenth-century French keyboard music
composer.background:
Debussy was born above his parents’ china shop in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, outside Paris. Neither parent was a professional musician. His father’s involvement in the Paris Commune brought imprisonment in 1871; through a connection made during that imprisonment, the boy came to the piano teacher Antoinette Mauté, Verlaine’s mother-in-law. He entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1872, aged ten. Antoine Marmontel trained him as a pianist; Ernest Guiraud later taught him composition. His resistance to harmonic rules developed inside this education: he could play, analyse and compete successfully in the system he came to distrust.

From 1880 he spent summers working for Nadezhda von Meck, Tchaikovsky’s patron, playing chamber music and teaching her children. Travel with her household took him to Italy and Russia. In Paris he accompanied the soprano Marie Vasnier, with whom he had an affair, and wrote songs for her flexible high voice. In their accompaniments, the piano’s register, resonance and passing harmonic changes can supply a second interpretation of the words. The early songs also show how thoroughly he knew the French vocal tradition he would alter.

movement: I. De l’aube à midi sur la mer
forces: Concert band; transcription by Lawrence Odom
performers: United States Air Force Band, Concert Band
intro: From dawn to noon: the first of Debussy’s three symphonic sketches, heard here in Lawrence Odom’s concert-band transcription. Follow the changes of pulse and register as short figures accumulate into the closing chorale.

cues.title: A bass before a tune
cues.text: The opening stays low and very quiet, centred on B. Short figures gradually become distinct above the sustained foundation. This is Lawrence Odom’s concert-band transcription: the original orchestral string parts have been redistributed, so do not listen for a violin section.

cues.title: The sailor who became a pianist
cues.text: Debussy knew the sea through childhood visits to Cannes. His father had considered a seafaring career for him; piano lessons took him instead to the Paris Conservatoire at ten. He began La Mer in 1903 and completed it in 1905.

cues.title: Listen below the fragments
cues.text: Keep one ear on the sustained lower notes while following the shorter gestures above them. Debussy separates the speeds of the layers: the accompaniment need not change with every turn of the melody. The slow introduction gathers momentum through their overlap.

cues.title: Dawn acquires a pulse
cues.text: The introduction gives way to the main movement and a clearer D♭ major region. The melodic ideas remain short. Rather than announcing a long tune and repeating it, Debussy changes their rhythm, register and surroundings as the movement proceeds.

cues.title: Hokusai on the cover
cues.text: Debussy chose an adaptation of Hokusai’s Great Wave off Kanagawa for the cover of the first edition in 1905. The subtitle is “three symphonic sketches”. The printed image belongs to the work’s own publication history, not a later record designer’s association.

cues.title: Two against three
cues.text: Throughout this movement, groups of two and three repeatedly share the same stretch of time. Listen for a quick figure that does not divide the beat in the same way as its neighbour. That friction keeps the surface active without requiring a faster underlying pulse.

cues.title: Java heard in Paris
cues.text: At the Paris Exposition of 1889 Debussy heard a Javanese gamelan. Its layered percussion gave him a practical encounter with a musical tradition outside his Conservatoire education. The piano piece Pagodes, written in 1903, makes that encounter explicit through repeated patterns and gong-like bass notes.

cues.title: Activity is not volume
cues.text: The short figures become more closely packed, yet this is still relatively quiet music. Follow the attacks rather than the loudness: an increase in activity can change the texture before the ensemble makes a substantial crescendo.

cues.title: A crest, then withdrawal
cues.text: This swell does not lead straight to the ending. Over the next half-minute the sound steadily retreats, leaving space for another large span. Hear that withdrawal as a structural break, not simply the ensemble playing the same material more softly.

cues.title: After the long withdrawal
cues.text: A fresh melodic span begins after the near-disappearance. The bass and harmony move into a new region, while the phrase has room to extend. The movement’s shape depends on these restarts as much as on its crescendos.

cues.title: More weight, more brightness
cues.text: The ensemble becomes more forceful and the upper part of the sound more prominent. Notice that the quieter beginning of this span remains close behind us: Debussy makes a large change of scale within a single continuous phrase.

cues.title: The footing changes again
cues.text: The swell falls away, and the harmony changes before another broad tune has settled. Follow the bass through this passage. A held upper note can sound different when the lower parts move, even without a conspicuous new melody.

cues.title: The first audience
cues.text: Camille Chevillard conducted the Lamoureux Orchestra in the premiere on 15 October 1905. Its reception was mixed. Debussy himself conducted La Mer in Paris in January 1908; those performances helped turn the work into a public success.

cues.title: A household changes
cues.text: While composing La Mer, Debussy left Lilly Texier for Emma Bardac. Their daughter Claude-Emma, called Chouchou, was born in October 1905, shortly after the premiere. He later dedicated the piano suite Children’s Corner to her.

cues.title: The closing ascent
cues.text: The long quiet passage gives way to a broader phrase and the final ascent. The contrast comes before maximum volume: the music first changes its weight and pace, then gathers the full ensemble behind the close.

cues.title: Noon in the brass
cues.text: The closing chorale gives the brass broad chords rather than fleeting fragments. The quick internal movement and the slower chord changes now occupy different layers of the same climax. This is the first movement’s noon, not the end of the three-part work.

cues.title: The chord and its aftermath
cues.text: The last chord leaves a short resonance after the players stop. The next movement of La Mer is Jeux de vagues, “Play of the waves”: a separate movement that exchanges this broad ending for much more changeable motion.

intro: A submerged cathedral takes shape through piano resonance: bare intervals grow into broad chords, then recede. Marcelle Meyer’s 1956 recording makes the distance between the quiet opening and the full keyboard part of the form.

cues.title: Fifths before full chords
cues.text: The piano begins with open fifths: G and D, without the third that would identify a major or minor chord. These bare intervals move upwards together. The gaps between attacks leave the instrument’s resonance audible.

cues.title: The drowned city of Ys
cues.text: The title refers to the Breton legend of Ys, a city swallowed by the sea. In the story associated with this prelude, a cathedral rises from the water and its bells, chants and organ can be heard. Debussy supplies those suggestions with a piano alone.

cues.title: Emerging from the mist
cues.text: The bass settles on B and the movement becomes more continuous. Debussy’s instruction in this part of the score is “Peu à peu sortant de la brume”: gradually emerging from the mist. The change is made through register, rhythm and increasing weight, not a new instrument.

cues.title: A melody made of chords
cues.text: Follow the top of each chord while also hearing the notes underneath move with it. This parallel motion lets a melodic line acquire thickness without becoming a tune over an independent accompaniment. The spacing of the chord is part of the sound you recognise.

cues.title: An organ without pipes
cues.text: The broad chords suggest an organ, but the piano cannot sustain them indefinitely. Listen to each attack and the decay that follows it. Debussy asks for “Sonore sans dureté” — sonorous without harshness — rather than a percussive hammering of the tune.

cues.title: Trained inside the rules
cues.text: Debussy entered the Paris Conservatoire at ten, studied piano with Marmontel and composition with Guiraud, and won the Prix de Rome in 1884. His later treatment of chords came from a musician who had mastered the institution’s harmonic exercises, not avoided them.

cues.title: A second ascent
cues.text: After the quiet withdrawal, the sound gathers weight again. This rise is shorter than the first great expansion; listen for the approach to the peak and the rapid retreat afterwards, rather than expecting a literal repeat of the earlier passage.

cues.title: The same phrase, farther away
cues.text: The broad melody returns at a reduced volume and in a lower register. Debussy labels this return an echo of the phrase heard earlier. The accompanying motion continues underneath, so the recollection has a different texture from the first declaration.

cues.title: The title comes afterwards
cues.text: Debussy published the first book of twelve Préludes in 1910 and the second in 1913. On the printed page each title appears after its piece, in parentheses. The pianist encounters the notes before the composer names the image.

cues.title: Let the resonance finish
cues.text: The final chord leaves C, G and the added D in the resonance. That extra note does not have to resolve into a plain triad. Let the fading sound finish the phrase; the last attack is not the end of what the piano contributes.

composer.name: Richard Strauss
composer.epithet: An orchestral storyteller who took opera to the harmonic edge in Salome and Elektra, then made conversation and recollection its central events.
facts: Munich; composition with Friedrich Wilhelm Meyer; practical conducting apprenticeship with Hans von Bülow at Meiningen
Meiningen · Munich · Weimar · Berlin Court Opera, 1898–1918 · Vienna State Opera, co-director 1919–24
Hugo von Hofmannsthal: six operas, from Elektra to Arabella
Tone poems, fifteen operas, concertos, chamber works and more than two hundred songs
composer.background:
Richard Strauss grew up hearing the horn at close quarters. His father Franz was principal horn of the Munich Court Orchestra, an exacting player who performed Wagner while disliking his music. The household’s approved models were Mozart, Haydn and Beethoven; Richard’s early chamber works, concertos and symphonies begin within that inheritance. His mother Josepha belonged to the Pschorr brewing family. Born in Munich in 1864, he studied privately, receiving composition lessons from Friedrich Wilhelm Meyer and learning what an orchestra could execute through his father’s colleagues. His two horn concertos, separated by nearly sixty years, preserve that early instrumental familiarity.

Hans von Bülow brought him to Meiningen in 1885, first as an assistant and then as his successor. Rehearsing an orchestra trained by Bülow supplied a practical education in balance, articulation and the management of complex scores. Another Meiningen musician, Alexander Ritter, urged him towards Liszt’s symphonic poems and Wagner’s music dramas. Strauss had already begun reconsidering his father’s prejudices; Ritter helped give the change a compositional direction. The orchestra could sustain an argument shaped by a character or a literary situation.

intro: A recurring pair of themes gives Strauss’s prankster an identity through disguises, interruptions and a final trial. This complete concert-band performance transfers the orchestral story to winds and percussion.

cues.title: A story in rondo form
cues.text: Strauss puts “in rondo form” in the title: recurring themes identify Till as the episodes change around him. The opening is a quiet prologue; listen for the contrast between this broad manner and the shorter, more pointed figures that follow.

cues.title: Accents against the metre
cues.text: The phrases become more active. Listen for a winding tune whose accents resist the regular two-beat sway of 6/8: in the orchestral score, Strauss first gives this signature to a horn, then gives Till a second, clipped clarinet motif.

cues.title: A horn player’s son
cues.text: Strauss’s father Franz played horn in the Munich Court Orchestra. He admired Mozart, Haydn and Beethoven and disliked Wagner, though he played in Wagner premieres. Richard grew up with that combination of instrumental expertise and musical argument.

cues.title: A sudden retreat
cues.text: A loud burst gives way to a much quieter texture. These sudden changes of scale do structural work: the same band can sound like a crowd in one phrase and a few conspirators in the next.

cues.title: The printed trickster
cues.text: The Eulenspiegel stories survive in printed accounts from the early sixteenth century, although their hero supposedly lived in the fourteenth. They repeatedly set a literal-minded rogue against tradesmen, clerics and scholars; Strauss selects episodes rather than following one continuous book.

cues.title: Quiet becomes commotion
cues.text: The restrained passage breaks into a bright, forceful attack. Listen to the speed of the change: Strauss does not need a long crescendo to turn a quiet episode into public commotion.

cues.title: A smoother surface
cues.text: The surface smooths out: sharply separated attacks give way to sustained phrases, and the sound darkens. In the story, Till can adopt respectable manners; musically, a change of articulation lets him do it without acquiring a wholly new identity.

cues.title: Learning from Bülow
cues.text: Hans von Bülow brought the young Strauss to Meiningen in 1885. Rehearsing its orchestra gave him practical experience of balance and articulation; Alexander Ritter, another musician there, encouraged his interest in Liszt’s tone poems and Wagner’s dramas.

cues.title: Harmony changes the setting
cues.text: Listen for the harmonic distance travelled by these quiet phrases. The music moves through several tonal regions before its next sustained increase in volume; a new episode can be prepared by harmony rather than a percussion signal.

cues.title: A more lyrical episode
cues.text: A sustained, lyrical manner takes over. Keep the short identifying motifs in mind through the longer phrases: a rondo’s episodes can differ in pace and register without losing contact with their recurring material.

cues.title: The attacks crowd closer
cues.text: The activity increases and the band grows louder. Compare the short, closely spaced attacks with the sustained writing of the previous minute: a change in the number of events can sharpen a build-up before the main peak arrives.

cues.title: Pauline and the theatre
cues.text: Strauss married the soprano Pauline de Ahna in September 1894, during the period of this tone poem. She had sung in his first opera, Guntram; the four songs of Op. 27 were his wedding gift to her.

cues.title: Follow the separate strands
cues.text: Listen past the uppermost line. Strauss uses counterpoint — independently moving parts sounding together — to make an argument out of several voices, rather than simply adding accompaniment beneath a tune.

cues.title: A bright edge, then quiet
cues.text: The sound acquires a sharply brighter edge before falling back. Listen for the contrast between a densely occupied register and the thinner passage that follows; loudness alone does not account for the change.

cues.title: Activity almost stops
cues.text: The busy surface gives way to held sound. Follow the harmony through this suspension: the reduction in attacks makes changes underneath more exposed than they were in the preceding commotion.

cues.title: Cologne, November 1895
cues.text: Strauss completed Till Eulenspiegel in May 1895; its premiere followed in Cologne that November. He initially resisted supplying a detailed programme, then sanctioned an account based on notes he had written into his score.

cues.title: Familiar energy returns
cues.text: The quiet suspension ends and the quick-moving manner returns. Listen for recognisable fragments inside the renewed activity: Strauss can recall earlier music while making its surroundings more crowded.

cues.title: Figures across broader accents
cues.text: The sound becomes louder and brighter. Listen for quick figures cutting across broader accents rather than treating the band as one enormous melody; different rates of movement can remain audible within the same full texture.

cues.title: The composer on the podium
cues.text: Strauss returned to Munich as a conductor in 1894 and moved to Berlin in 1898. The tone poems were written alongside an opera-house career: rehearsing other composers’ scores remained part of his daily work.

cues.title: Packed attacks
cues.text: The quick figures are now packed close together, followed by another large swell. Compare this density with the long held sounds around nine minutes: the number of attacks has become one of the main ways Strauss controls the scale.

cues.title: The comedy is interrupted
cues.text: Rapid figures give way to heavier, more sustained statements. In Strauss’s story, the prankster now faces judgement: short replies confront an authority that will not be laughed away.

cues.title: Unequal replies
cues.text: Loud blocks alternate with exposed, quieter responses. Listen to their unequal weight: a short answering gesture can remain recognisable while losing any power to redirect the larger phrase.

cues.title: Towards silence
cues.text: The sound recedes in stages until almost nothing remains. The story reaches Till’s execution; Strauss separates the end of the character’s life from the end of the piece by leaving this near-silent interval before the narration resumes.

cues.title: The narrator returns
cues.text: The gentle opening manner returns in F major. This is an epilogue, not another escapade: the story’s frame reappears after the action has stopped.

cues.title: Strauss changes the ending
cues.text: The execution is Strauss’s departure from the traditional stories, in which Till repeatedly escapes. The tone poem is not a literal illustration of a fixed tale: the composer alters the narrative to give his musical ending its conditions.

cues.title: One last interruption
cues.text: A final loud interruption cuts through the quiet epilogue. Strauss gives the ending the abruptness of another prank, then stops; the soft narration does not get the last word.

composer.name: Jean Sibelius
composer.born: 8 December 1865, Hämeenlinna, Grand Duchy of Finland
composer.epithet: A symphonist who let small figures gather into themes and movements change shape while their underlying pulse continued.
facts: Helsinki with Martin Wegelius, 1885–89 · Berlin with Albert Becker · Vienna with Robert Fuchs and Karl Goldmark
Ainola, designed by Lars Sonck near Lake Tuusula; the family moved there in 1904
Swedish at home; Finnish education and Finnish texts in Kullervo and Luonnotar
Seven numbered symphonies; violin concerto; tone poems, incidental music, songs and chamber works
composer.background:
Sibelius was born in 1865 in Hämeenlinna, when Finland was an autonomous grand duchy within the Russian Empire. His family spoke Swedish, but he attended a Finnish-language school and encountered the Kalevala, Elias Lönnrot’s compilation of traditional epic poetry, in Finnish. The later national figure grew up between these cultures. His father, a doctor, died in 1868. Violin playing became the young Sibelius’s principal musical ambition, and family chamber music gave him an early practical knowledge of strings. He adopted the French form Jean from the visiting cards of a deceased uncle, replacing the familiar Janne professionally.

He entered the Helsinki Music Institute in 1885 after briefly beginning law studies. Martin Wegelius taught him composition; Ferruccio Busoni, then teaching piano in Helsinki, became a friend. Further study with Albert Becker in Berlin and Robert Fuchs and Karl Goldmark in Vienna extended his knowledge of Continental music. His hope of becoming a professional violin virtuoso did not survive an unsuccessful Vienna audition. The instrument nevertheless remained central to his melodic imagination: sustained notes against tremolando strings, rapid changes of register and the tension of a long line across the bow recur throughout the orchestral works.

intro: A dying woman dreams that she is dancing: this waltz began as theatre music, not a ballroom miniature. Judith Bokor’s 1925 recording gives the orchestral melody to cello with piano accompaniment.

cues.title: A dance in three
cues.text: Listen for the three-beat accompaniment under the cello’s longer notes. A waltz supplies a regular step, but the melody can stretch across it; this arrangement makes the difference between the two parts particularly exposed.

cues.title: The partner is Death
cues.text: Sibelius wrote the music in 1903 for Kuolema, a play by his brother-in-law Arvid Järnefelt. In the scene behind this waltz, an old woman dreams of a ball; her dancing partner is Death.

cues.title: More weight in the line
cues.text: The cello line gains weight after the opening’s restrained phrases. Keep the accompaniment in your ear: the dance pulse and the melodic swell are separate things, so a louder phrase need not mean a faster step.

cues.title: A home outside Helsinki
cues.text: Sibelius and his family moved to Ainola in September 1904, the year the concert version of this waltz appeared. Lars Sonck designed the house near Lake Tuusula; its name refers to Sibelius’s wife, Aino.

cues.title: The dance draws back
cues.text: The volume drops sharply, breaking the preceding build-up. Listen to how the waltz persists at a reduced scale: a quieter return can keep a dance recognisable without preserving its earlier momentum.

cues.title: From stage to concert
cues.text: Sibelius conducted the concert premiere in Helsinki on 25 April 1904. The separate publication turned one number from a play into an independent concert piece; its original title had been Valse lente, “Slow waltz”.

cues.title: The late climax
cues.text: The strongest passage arrives in the last quarter of the performance. The melodic line carries more weight than at the opening; listen for the way this extended swell delays the eventual retreat into quiet.

cues.title: Leaving the dance
cues.text: The melody and accompaniment withdraw, leaving the final chords exposed. The dance does not end in a ballroom flourish: Sibelius’s postlude is quiet, and the last sound is allowed to die away.

composer.name: Erik Satie
composer.epithet: A cabaret pianist who separated repetition from development, and musical seriousness from ceremonial behaviour.
facts: Paris Conservatoire; later counterpoint with Albert Roussel at the Schola Cantorum
Suzanne Valadon · Jean Cocteau · Pablo Picasso · Francis Picabia · René Clair
Piano pieces, songs, ballets, Socrate, music intended to accompany ordinary activity
composer.background:
Satie was born in the Norman port of Honfleur to a French father and a Scottish mother. After his mother died in 1872, he lived with his paternal grandparents and received lessons from a local organist. He later joined his father in Paris and entered the Conservatoire in 1879. His periods of study ended without the normal professional qualifications. His mature music would expose elementary actions — a bass note, a repeated chord, a scale fragment.

By the late 1880s he was working in Montmartre, including at the Chat Noir cabaret. The three Sarabandes of 1887 and Gymnopédies of 1888 came from this period. The latter use a slow triple metre, low bass notes and chords on the second beat. Major sevenths remain part of the sonority instead of being immediately corrected into consonances. Their regular accompaniment continues beneath a melody whose phrase-endings often avoid the sort of cadence that would make the next phrase feel inevitable.

era.name: The French Line
era.heroCaption: James McNeill Whistler, Nocturne: Blue and Gold — Old Battersea Bridge

intro: A bass note on beat one, a chord on beat two, and a melody that crosses the repeated pattern. Satie’s first Gymnopédie lets unresolved sevenths remain in the harmony instead of demanding their immediate resolution.

cues.title: Bass, chord, empty beat
cues.text: The left hand places a bass on the first beat and a chord on the second, leaving the third beat without a new accompaniment attack. G major seventh alternates with D major seventh. The melody crosses this regular pattern rather than supplying a note for every beat.

cues.title: Montmartre, not the Conservatoire
cues.text: Satie wrote the three Gymnopédies in 1888, during his early years in Montmartre’s cabaret world. He had left the Paris Conservatoire without completing its training. Piano work at venues including the Chat Noir paid for a life outside the official institutions.

cues.title: A swell without acceleration
cues.text: The line gains weight, but the bass-and-chord pattern keeps the same measured pace. Listen for the distinction between a louder phrase and a faster one: Satie can intensify this small texture without filling the space between its beats.

cues.title: Almost the same again
cues.text: The quiet opening pattern returns. Satie repeats a large span rather than breaking the tune into fragments for development. Keep the first ending in mind: the second traversal will eventually change its destination.

cues.title: Debussy changes the medium
cues.text: Debussy later orchestrated the first and third Gymnopédies, reversing their order in his pair. He left the second alone. The familiar piano piece therefore also belongs to an orchestral history, although this recording preserves Satie’s original single instrument.

cues.title: Back to counterpoint at thirty-nine
cues.text: In 1905 Satie entered the Schola Cantorum and studied counterpoint with Albert Roussel. He was thirty-nine and already the composer of these pieces. The later fugues and canons came from sustained technical study, not just the eccentric persona attached to his name.

cues.title: A different final third
cues.text: The second half does not end exactly like the first. F♮ takes the place of the opening’s F♯ in the final D minor harmony. The last chord decays instead of being followed by another turn of the bass pattern.

composer.name: Alexander Scriabin
composer.epithet: A pianist who replaced the need for a resolving tonic with recurring harmonic fields, accelerating figures and carefully organised light.
facts: Moscow Conservatory, 1888–92; piano with Vasily Safonov, composition studies with Taneyev and Arensky
Piano at the Moscow Conservatory from 1898; left regular teaching in 1903
Mitrofan Belyayev; later Serge Koussevitzky, who conducted the premiere of Prometheus
Ten numbered piano sonatas, preludes and études; three numbered symphonies, a piano concerto and two large orchestral poems
composer.background:
Scriabin was born in Moscow into a family whose musical and military occupations coexisted. His mother, Lyubov, a trained pianist, died while he was an infant; his father’s diplomatic career left much of his upbringing to female relatives. He attended a cadet school while pursuing music, then entered the Moscow Conservatory in 1888. Rachmaninoff was a fellow student. Scriabin studied piano with Vasily Safonov and theoretical subjects with Sergei Taneyev and Anton Arensky, graduating as a pianist in 1892 with the full composition course unfinished. His earliest published music identifies the piano as both instrument and compositional laboratory.

Chopin supplied recognisable genres: prelude, étude, mazurka, nocturne and impromptu. Scriabin’s Twenty-four Preludes, Op. 11, traverse all major and minor keys in the order familiar from Chopin’s Op. 28. The influence extends to melody floating over an independently patterned accompaniment and to chromatic notes that delay a cadence. An injury to his right hand during his student years made the distribution of work between the hands a practical concern. The Prelude and Nocturne for the left hand, Op. 9, create melody, bass and harmonic filling within the reach of one hand.

era.name: Fin de siècle
era.heroCaption: Gustav Klimt, Beethoven Frieze: The Well-Armed Strong One

work: Étude in D♯ minor, Op. 8 No. 12
intro: A short étude that asks for weight as well as speed: the right-hand melody is projected in octaves over widely spaced left-hand figures. Listen for the quieter middle and the heavier return of the opening.

cues.title: Octaves over a wide bass
cues.text: The right hand projects the melody in octaves while the left covers wide distances beneath it. Listen for the singing top line rather than treating every note in the accompaniment as equally important.

cues.title: A Moscow-trained pianist
cues.text: Scriabin graduated from the Moscow Conservatory as a pianist in 1892. Rachmaninoff was a fellow student; Scriabin’s first published works likewise centred on the piano.

cues.title: A quieter middle
cues.text: The volume drops and the harmony moves towards F♯ major. The hands still have plenty to do, but the melody no longer presses forward with the opening’s weight.

cues.title: Belyayev backs the composer
cues.text: The publisher and patron Mitrofan Belyayev began supporting Scriabin in 1894. He published the twelve études of Op. 8 in 1895, helping turn a young pianist’s manuscripts into a public catalogue.

cues.title: The opening returns heavier
cues.text: The D♯ minor material returns with greater force. The accompaniment becomes denser beneath the octave melody; the reprise increases the physical demands instead of merely repeating the opening.

cues.title: Students at the White House
cues.text: Awadagin Pratt gave this performance at the White House Classical Music Student Workshop Concert on 4 November 2009. The recording comes from the White House’s video of the event.

cues.title: The attacks spread out
cues.text: The closing gestures become more widely spaced. After the dense accompaniment, the piano’s struck sound is allowed to decay instead of being immediately renewed by another running figure.

composer.name: Sergei Rachmaninoff
composer.epithet: A composer-pianist who built long melodies over tolling basses, and carried Russian chant into the concertos and dances of his American exile.
facts: Moscow Conservatory: piano with Nikolai Zverev and Alexander Siloti; counterpoint with Sergei Taneyev, composition with Anton Arensky
Mamontov’s Moscow Private Russian Opera, 1897–98 · Bolshoi Theatre, 1904–06
Ivanovka near Tambov · Dresden · New York · Villa Senar, Lake Lucerne · Beverly Hills
Four piano concertos, three symphonies, three completed operas, choral music, songs and piano works

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Interview with Leonard Liebling, The Musical Courier, 1939

composer.background:
Rachmaninoff learnt the sound of Russian worship before he learnt orchestration. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where unaccompanied voices and bells occupied different parts of the ceremony: chant inside the church, metal sounding above and outside it. His music repeatedly brings the two together. A melody moves in narrow steps while bass notes toll beneath it; a chord is struck again before its previous resonance has died. The C♯ minor Prelude, the Second Piano Concerto and The Bells make this audible without requiring an actual church bell. The All-Night Vigil removes the instruments altogether, leaving a choir to produce both the sustained line and the accumulating weight of the harmony.

Born into a landowning family in 1873, he spent his early childhood at Oneg, near Novgorod. His father’s financial failures brought the sale of the estates and a move to St Petersburg. Rachmaninoff entered its Conservatory in 1883, but his general schoolwork deteriorated; his parents separated, and his sister Sofia died of diphtheria. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a transfer to Moscow and the supervision of Nikolai Zverev. The move exchanged a disorganised household for one in which practice, meals and attendance at concerts were regulated by a piano teacher.

performers: Sviatoslav Richter, Warsaw National Philharmonic Orchestra, Stanisław Wisłocki
intro: The piano begins alone with tolling chords, then gives the first melody to the orchestra. Listen for the changing division of labour: the soloist supplies accompaniment, sings, and turns the same material into a march.

cues.title: Not yet C minor
cues.text: Repeated piano chords answer a low F. Although the concerto is in C minor, these opening harmonies circle F minor; each toll grows louder before the orchestra arrives.

cues.title: The orchestra takes the melody
cues.text: The orchestra takes the first melody in C minor while the piano supplies running broken chords. Keep the two layers separate: the tune advances mainly by steps; the keyboard fills the space between them.

cues.title: After the First Symphony
cues.text: The failure of Rachmaninoff’s First Symphony in 1897 damaged his confidence for roughly three years. He composed little, but did not stop working: conducting and teaching continued through the period that preceded this concerto.

cues.title: Melody versus activity
cues.text: Throughout this opening section, distinguish the bass, the running figures and the slower melodic line. Rachmaninoff can give the most notes to a player who is not carrying the tune; the piano is often the accompaniment rather than the speaker.

cues.title: The doctor in the dedication
cues.text: From January to April 1900 Rachmaninoff consulted Nikolai Dahl, a physician who used hypnosis and repeated encouragement. Dahl was also an amateur musician. The concerto’s dedication names him, not a pianist or patron.

cues.title: The piano becomes the singer
cues.text: The second subject belongs first to the piano, in E♭ major, the relative major of C minor. Instead of decorating someone else’s melody, the soloist shapes a sustained line above its own accompaniment.

cues.title: The phrase expands
cues.text: The sound grows fuller and louder without leaving the second subject’s tonal region. Follow the long melodic notes through the piano’s smaller figures: a phrase can broaden even while the number of attacks increases.

cues.title: The development begins quietly
cues.text: The settled E♭ major span gives way to quieter music. In the development, fragments of the two subjects travel between keys instead of returning as complete tunes; recognition depends on rhythm and contour as much as on the original harmony.

cues.title: Moscow, November 1901
cues.text: Rachmaninoff played the complete concerto’s premiere in Moscow on 9 November 1901, with Alexander Siloti conducting. Siloti was his cousin and former piano teacher. The first movement was finished last, after the other two had already been performed.

cues.title: Held sound, moving sound
cues.text: This relatively sustained passage is a pause before another increase in activity. Listen for the piano’s attacks to tighten into a more insistent pattern over the next few phrases.

cues.title: Harmony without a resting place
cues.text: The middle of the movement passes through several key regions in quick succession. The bass keeps relocating beneath fragments of themes already introduced; the rising pressure comes from harmonic motion as well as increasing volume.

cues.title: The return, made martial
cues.text: At the central peak, the piano’s chordal attacks compete with the orchestra rather than decorate it. The first subject returns against a march-like piano part: the same melody has acquired a different accompaniment.

cues.title: The peak falls away
cues.text: The full sound begins to recede. Notice how quickly Rachmaninoff reduces the pressure after sustaining the climax: the melody continues, but the accompaniment no longer has to strike with the same weight.

cues.title: A pianist in the opera pit
cues.text: During the 1897–98 season Rachmaninoff conducted at Savva Mamontov’s Moscow Private Russian Opera and worked with the bass Feodor Chaliapin. In 1898 he conducted Chaliapin as the Mayor in Rimsky-Korsakov’s May Night: his experience of melody included accompanying a singer from the pit.

cues.title: The second subject changes hands
cues.text: The second subject is recast as a horn solo, with the piano no longer its singer. The quieter, sustained texture makes a melodic return sound different without needing a new tune.

cues.title: A concerto in the cinema
cues.text: David Lean’s Brief Encounter used the Second Concerto in 1945. Its railway-station meetings and restrained conversations gave the music another setting: Celia Johnson and Trevor Howard play two married people whose affair cannot become a shared life.

cues.title: A brief opening into major
cues.text: A short major-key colouring interrupts the return towards C minor. Listen for E♭ to reassert the minor mode: the concerto’s first movement does not adopt the major-key ending that Rachmaninoff reserves for the finale.

cues.title: The ending holds back
cues.text: The closing section draws on the first subject, still quietly. Rachmaninoff delays the final acceleration: a coda can spend time reducing the music before it makes its last, concentrated burst.

cues.title: The last acceleration
cues.text: The attacks become more frequent and the volume rises sharply. The final chords close in C minor; the earlier major-key glimpse has not changed the destination.
