intro: A slow movement with a fast centre. The piano’s circling accompaniment passes beneath a melody first shared by flute and clarinet; later the soloist breaks out into a cadenza.

cues.title: A bridge between keys
cues.text: Muted strings begin in the C minor left by the first movement, then move towards E major. Rachmaninoff writes the connection into the music: the slow movement’s key is reached, not simply announced.

cues.title: The piano makes a pulse
cues.text: The piano’s broken chords establish a repeating motion beneath the melody. Listen for the two different rates: the accompaniment keeps turning while the tune takes much longer to complete a phrase.

cues.title: A melody shared by winds
cues.text: The opening tune begins with flute and continues through an extended clarinet solo. Follow the line across the change of instrument rather than treating each timbre as a new theme; the piano remains underneath it.

cues.title: Heard before the first movement
cues.text: This Adagio and the finale were first performed in Moscow on 15 December 1900, almost eleven months before the complete concerto. Rachmaninoff played and Siloti conducted at a benefit for the Ladies’ Charity Prison Committee.

cues.title: A pianist’s sustained note
cues.text: A piano note starts to fade as soon as it is struck; wind and string players can continue feeding a note with breath or bow. Listen for how the moving accompaniment supports long melodic notes without requiring every instrument to sustain sound in the same way.

cues.title: The phrase leans away
cues.text: The harmony begins to pull away from the opening’s E-major centre. The melodic pace remains broad, but the bass and inner notes change its direction; a slow tune need not sit on a static chord.

cues.title: A marriage in 1902
cues.text: The year after the complete concerto’s premiere, Rachmaninoff married Natalia Satina, his first cousin. Their daughters Irina and Tatiana were born in 1903 and 1907. The Satins’ estate at Ivanovka became his summer base for composition.

cues.title: The middle begins to move
cues.text: The accompaniment becomes more active and the harmony moves into minor-key territory. This is the movement’s contrasting middle, not another quiet repetition of the opening song; its eventual destination is a piano cadenza.

cues.title: The sound gains weight
cues.text: The middle section grows substantially louder. Listen to the difference between speed and weight: more forceful chords can intensify a passage without every layer moving faster.

cues.title: Two pianos that same year
cues.text: Rachmaninoff completed his Second Suite for two pianos in April 1901, during the same recovery of confidence that produced the concerto. He and Siloti gave its premiere that November: the concerto’s conductor was also a partner at the keyboard.

cues.title: Another climb
cues.text: The central section resumes its climb after a quieter interval. Successive phrases increase the volume towards another peak rather than prolonging the evenly paced song with which the movement began.

cues.title: Not the final peak
cues.text: The swell falls back, but the middle section is not finished. Listen for a second accumulation of force: the next large arrival exceeds the one that has just passed.

cues.title: Cadenza territory
cues.text: The soloist’s central display breaks the regular accompaniment pattern. Listen for the alternation of rapid figures, broader chords and pauses: a cadenza can change the perceived pulse without a new theme.

cues.title: A run into silence
cues.text: The rapid piano figures break off into a near-silence. Let the gap register before the next phrase: it separates the solo display from the slow music’s return more decisively than a simple reduction in tempo would.

cues.title: The song returns quietly
cues.text: The opening material returns in E major after the cadenza’s final gestures. The melody is recognisable, but its surroundings are quieter; returning home is not the same event as arriving there for the first time.

cues.title: The borrowed verse
cues.text: Eric Carmen used this movement’s melody for the verse of “All by Myself” in 1975. The familiar title belongs to the chorus, not to the borrowed passage; the concerto supplies the tune that begins the song’s account of loneliness.

cues.title: Below the returning melody
cues.text: During the return, listen below the melody: the piano’s arpeggios keep the harmony moving even when the orchestral phrase holds a note. Slow melodic rhythm and continuous smaller notes occupy different layers.

cues.title: The final broad swell
cues.text: The returning song reaches its last broad swell in E major. This is not a reprise of the cadenza’s rapid display: the increase in volume comes within the restored slow-moving texture.

cues.title: Closing in E major
cues.text: The texture subsides and the final harmonies are spaced more widely. E major remains in place while the sound decays; the movement ends quietly rather than answering its central climax with another one.

work: Prelude in C♯ minor, Op. 3 No. 2
intro: Rachmaninoff plays the Prelude he wrote at nineteen, recorded for Edison in 1919. Three low notes generate a slow opening, an agitated middle and a return written across four staves.

cues.title: Three notes, then an answer
cues.text: The low A–G♯–C♯ figure supplies the Prelude’s opening signal. Quiet chords answer it; the distinction is between a few strongly projected notes and the softer voices around them, not between two separate themes.

cues.title: Nineteen and newly qualified
cues.text: Rachmaninoff wrote the Prelude in 1892, the year he graduated in composition from the Moscow Conservatory. It became the second of five Morceaux de fantaisie, Op. 3, dedicated to his teacher Anton Arensky.

cues.title: Inside the chords
cues.text: Listen inside the quiet texture rather than following only the highest notes. A chord contains several moving voices; Rachmaninoff’s piano writing depends on their unequal weight, with a melodic note made distinct from the harmony that surrounds it.

cues.title: Siloti takes it abroad
cues.text: Alexander Siloti played the Prelude on his 1898 tour of Europe and America. Its popularity soon overshadowed Rachmaninoff’s other music; audiences would demand it as an encore long after he had written much larger works.

cues.title: The middle gathers force
cues.text: The agitated middle now accumulates louder, more frequent attacks. Hear the melodic notes through the triplet movement: the rapid figures lead towards the return of the opening material rather than supplying an unrelated episode.

cues.title: The opening, enlarged
cues.text: The opening material returns in broad, heavily weighted chords. Rachmaninoff spreads the notation across four staves, two for each hand: the extra space separates registers and voices, not extra players.

cues.title: The composer at the keyboard
cues.text: This is Rachmaninoff himself, recorded for Edison in 1919 and issued in December 1920. The transfer comes from Edison Diamond Disc 82187-R; the Commons copy was cleaned and restored by Adam Cuerden.

cues.title: After the weight
cues.text: The closing chords are widely spaced and very soft. C♯ minor remains while the piano’s resonance fades; the loud return does not get the last word.

composer.name: Charles Ives
composer.epithet: A church organist and insurance executive who made hymns, marching bands and incompatible tempos coexist inside concert music.
facts: With his father George Ives in Danbury; composition with Horatio Parker at Yale, 1894–98
Church organist until 1902; New York insurance business, ultimately Ives & Myrick
The Concord Sonata and Essays Before a Sonata at his own expense; 114 Songs, 1922
American hymn tunes · marches · ragtime · Beethoven · Emerson and Thoreau
composer.background:
Charles Ives grew up in Danbury, Connecticut, where his father George directed bands, played the cornet and taught music. George had served as a Union bandmaster during the American Civil War. The son’s later recollections describe experiments with bands playing different tunes, quarter-tone instruments and singing in one key against an accompaniment in another. These accounts are filtered through a son’s memory of his father, but the musical questions they pose recur in the scores: how far apart can independent parts move before they stop making a perceptible whole?

Ives was also trained in conventional musicianship. He became a paid church organist as a teenager and wrote the organ Variations on America in 1891. At Yale, from 1894 to 1898, Horatio Parker taught him counterpoint, orchestration and large-scale form. His First Symphony belongs to that apprenticeship, with audible debts to European symphonic writing. George died in 1894, shortly after Charles entered Yale. The practical musical culture of Danbury subsequently became both a source of material and a standard against which Ives judged the professional concert world.

era.name: Modernism
era.heroCaption: Wassily Kandinsky, Impression III (Concert)

intro: Ives imagines music-making in the Alcott family’s house in Concord. Hymn-like chords and the rhythm of Beethoven’s Fifth share a piano whose hands do not always agree about the key.

cues.title: A hymn at home
cues.text: The piano begins with quiet, widely spaced chords and a melody shaped like a hymn. This is the sonata’s recurring “human faith” melody, heard here much more plainly than in the crowded first two movements.

cues.title: Three members of one family
cues.text: Ives’s accompanying essay names Bronson Alcott, the philosopher; Louisa May, the novelist; and Elizabeth, the family pianist who became Beth in Little Women. His portrait includes domestic piano-playing as well as the Transcendentalists’ arguments.

cues.title: The chords harden
cues.text: The quiet opening breaks into louder, more densely struck writing. Listen for the short-short-short-long rhythm of Beethoven’s Fifth: Ives folds it into his own melody rather than quoting a whole passage of the symphony.

cues.title: A rhythm survives the collision
cues.text: The first big climax gathers around C minor. The repeated-note rhythm remains recognisable even when the chords crowd it with conflicting notes; follow that rhythm through the thicker piano sound.

cues.title: Music after the office
cues.text: Ives studied composition with Horatio Parker at Yale, then entered the New York insurance business in 1898. He remained a church organist until 1902; later, his successful agency with Julian Myrick paid for composing, copying and publishing music outside the concert profession.

cues.title: The parlour episode
cues.text: The middle episode borrows the manner of nineteenth-century parlour music: a singable tune with an accompaniment, rather than the previous collisions of heavy chords. B♭ major now holds for long stretches.

cues.title: Printed for strangers
cues.text: Ives paid to print the sonata in 1920 and mailed copies to two hundred people in January 1921. Individual movements reached audiences first; John Kirkpatrick gave the complete public premiere at New York’s Town Hall on 20 January 1939.

cues.title: Pressure returns
cues.text: The tune grows louder and the accompaniment fills in. A more chromatic transition follows: the earlier B♭ harmony no longer holds the phrases in place, and the piano presses towards another broad statement of the theme.

cues.title: The theme assembled
cues.text: The “human faith” melody arrives in C major, in broad chords. In the complete sonata, material scattered through “Emerson” and “Hawthorne” now joins into a continuous tune; the Beethoven rhythm belongs inside that tune.

cues.title: One last resonance
cues.text: The harmony briefly looks back towards B♭ before the final C major chord. Listen to how long the piano’s resonance remains after the last attack: the ending includes the decay of the instrument, not just the written notes.

composer.name: Arnold Schoenberg
composer.epithet: A Viennese teacher who took motivic development beyond the key signature, then made twelve notes carry the work of a tonal system.
facts: Largely self-taught; counterpoint lessons with Alexander Zemlinsky; close study of Bach, Beethoven, Brahms and Wagner
Berg and Webern from 1904 · Prussian Academy of Arts, Berlin, 1926–33 · University of California, Los Angeles, 1936–44
Developing variation · free atonality · twelve-tone composition · Sprechstimme
Painter; author of Harmonielehre (1911); founder of the Society for Private Musical Performances
composer.background:
Arnold Schoenberg was born in Vienna’s Leopoldstadt, the son of a Jewish shopkeeper, and learned the violin as a child. When his father died in 1889, the family’s finances made extended formal study impossible. He worked in a bank from 1891 to 1895, played chamber music with friends and learned composition by examining scores. Alexander Zemlinsky, whom he met through the amateur orchestra Polyhymnia, gave him counterpoint lessons. Schoenberg’s later teaching grew from this close reading: he explained, with unusual insistence, what each note in Bach, Mozart, Beethoven and Brahms was doing.

In the 1890s the apparent opposition between Brahms and Wagner organised Viennese musical argument. Schoenberg took techniques from both. From Brahms came the continuous alteration of a small motif, later described as developing variation; from Wagner came chromatic harmony whose resolution could be postponed across an entire scene. Verklärte Nacht, written in 1899 for string sextet, applies these procedures to Richard Dehmel’s poem about a woman confessing to her lover that she carries another man’s child. The opening D minor eventually transforms into D major, supplying the work’s large-scale harmonic argument.

intro: “I feel air from another planet”: Stefan George’s words accompany Schoenberg’s departure from a governing key. Four strings and a soprano carry the finale; the twelve-tone method is still more than a decade away.

cues.title: Strings without a tonic
cues.text: The quartet begins alone at the edge of audibility. Its chromatic lines avoid the bass-and-cadence pattern that would establish a home key; the soprano is absent from this instrumental introduction.

cues.title: Bank clerk and musician
cues.text: Schoenberg worked in a Vienna bank from 1891 to 1895, playing chamber music and studying scores outside working hours. Alexander Zemlinsky became his counterpoint teacher; most of his musical education took place outside a conservatoire.

cues.title: Air from another planet
cues.text: The soprano’s opening sentence is “Ich fühle Luft von anderem Planeten” — “I feel air from another planet.” Listen to the voice as another melodic part among the strings: this is sustained singing, not the speech-song Schoenberg later uses in Pierrot lunaire.

cues.title: George’s seventh ring
cues.text: Both poems in the quartet come from Stefan George’s Der siebente Ring, published in 1907. “Litanei”, the preceding movement, is a prayer; “Entrückung” describes release from earthly sensations. The soprano enters the quartet only in these last two movements.

cues.title: The texture brightens
cues.text: The sound brightens and the phrases become more active. Follow the string lines as independent melodies rather than treating all four players as a single accompaniment beneath the singer.

cues.title: Gmunden, summer 1908
cues.text: Schoenberg worked on the quartet at Gmunden on the Traunsee during the summer of 1908. His wife Mathilde’s affair with the painter Richard Gerstl belongs to the same year, but his earlier scores had already begun loosening the ties to a home key.

cues.title: Follow the moving parts
cues.text: Instead of waiting for a familiar chord progression, follow a short melodic shape as its rhythm or register changes. Schoenberg calls this kind of continuous reshaping “developing variation”; a related gesture can connect phrases that share no settled key.

cues.title: A sudden crest
cues.text: A quieter stretch leads to a brief, forceful swell around four and a half minutes. The crest lasts only a few seconds before the ensemble withdraws again; the movement’s shape depends on these changes of pressure as much as on its harmonies.

cues.title: An audience interrupts
cues.text: The Rosé Quartet and soprano Marie Gutheil-Schoder gave the Vienna premiere in December 1908. Writing about it in 1936–37, Schoenberg recalled laughter beginning in the second movement and continuing through much of the two George settings.

cues.title: More attacks, more pressure
cues.text: Shorter, more frequent attacks push the texture forward. The passage becomes louder as well as more active, then rapidly subsides: listen for the difference between the surge itself and the space it leaves behind.

cues.title: A quiet restart
cues.text: A near-whisper gives way to fresh, closely spaced figures. Soft playing does not stop the counterpoint: new attacks accumulate before the volume has fully recovered.

cues.title: Teaching the older grammar
cues.text: Alban Berg and Anton Webern became Schoenberg’s pupils in 1904. His Harmonielehre, published in 1911, teaches tonal harmony: he continued explaining how traditional chords work while his own new compositions dispensed with a governing key.

cues.title: The largest swell
cues.text: The movement reaches its strongest surge. Do not take the first crest for an ending: a sharp drop is followed by another forceful wave before the music finally settles into its long closing paragraph.

cues.title: Four strings again
cues.text: The voice has finished, and the quartet carries the coda alone. The texture becomes sustained rather than sharply articulated; the final paragraph has time to reconsider the work’s F♯ tonal centre.

cues.title: Silence in the hall
cues.text: Schoenberg’s account of the premiere singles out this coda. After the audience had interrupted even the singer, he remembered the final string-only passage being heard without audible disturbance. This is his retrospective testimony, written nearly thirty years after the concert.

cues.title: A recognisable destination
cues.text: The closing paragraph draws towards F♯ major. The quartet’s first movement began in F♯ minor: a recognisable destination survives even though much of this finale has avoided conventional routes between keys.

cues.title: The final harmony fades
cues.text: The last F♯ major harmony is allowed to fade. It closes this quartet without turning the preceding chromatic lines into an ordinary progression of keys.

composer.epithet: An engineer of instrumental colour who made a piano imitate water, an orchestra imitate a machine, and old dances carry the names of the dead.

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: Ravel, as remembered by his friend M. D. Calvocoressi

composer.background:
Ravel was born in Ciboure, across the harbour from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, to Marie Delouart, a Basque woman who had lived in Madrid, and Pierre-Joseph Ravel, a Swiss-born engineer. The family moved to Paris when Maurice was three months old. His father encouraged music as well as an interest in machinery; his mother’s songs gave him an early acquaintance with Spanish idioms. Basque ancestry and Spanish musical theatre remained distinct resources: the uneven pulse of the Piano Trio differs from the habanera of the Rapsodie espagnole. He returned to the Basque coast for holidays and composition, but received his musical education in Paris.

He entered the Conservatoire in 1889, initially as a pianist, and studied with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot. Failure to win the required prizes cost him his place in 1895. Readmitted in 1897 to Fauré’s composition class, he also learnt counterpoint from André Gedalge. Fauré encouraged the individual ear without relaxing the demands of construction; Gedalge supplied the discipline behind the fugues and independent inner parts. Ravel did not become a virtuoso pianist. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, introduced much of the difficult piano music, including Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit.

intro: Two melodies and a two-bar drum rhythm survive an almost continuous crescendo. Ravel makes the changing instruments do the work that changing themes and keys usually do.

sections.label: The rhythm and the first soloists

cues.title: Two tunes, one crescendo
cues.text: The snare drum establishes a two-bar rhythm in three beats. Above it, Ravel repeats two melodies, usually twice each before changing to the other; the principal development is the growing orchestra.

cues.title: The flute alone
cues.text: A flute gives the first melody over the drum and plucked strings. Its notes belong to C major; the bass keeps returning to C and G rather than following the tune through a succession of new harmonies.

cues.title: The clarinet repeats it
cues.text: The clarinet takes the same melody. Compare its sustained reed tone with the flute’s breathier attack: the tune has not developed, but its delivery has changed.

cues.title: A replacement for Albéniz
cues.text: Ida Rubinstein commissioned a ballet from Ravel in 1928. He initially planned to orchestrate music from Albéniz’s Iberia; difficulties over the orchestration rights led him instead to write a new piece.

cues.title: Bassoon, high in its range
cues.text: The bassoon introduces the second melody, playing well above the register usually associated with the instrument. This tune ranges farther than the first and brings flattened notes against the unchanged bass.

cues.title: The small clarinet
cues.text: The E♭ clarinet repeats the bassoon’s melody. This smaller member of the clarinet family gives the same line a more penetrating upper register; the snare pattern continues underneath.

cues.title: Ciboure and Paris
cues.text: Ravel was born in Ciboure in 1875 to a Basque mother and a Swiss-born engineer father. The family moved to Paris when he was three months old; his musical education was Parisian, while Spanish dance remained a recurring subject.

cues.title: The oboe d’amore
cues.text: The first melody returns on the oboe d’amore, pitched between the oboe and cor anglais. Ravel has not transposed the tune: a new instrument supplies the contrast that a new key might otherwise provide.

cues.title: Trumpet inside the flute
cues.text: A muted trumpet and a flute share the melody, the flute an octave above. Listen for the combined tone rather than two competing solos: the instruments agree on the line but contribute different attacks and overtones.

cues.title: A dance on a table
cues.text: At the Paris Opéra premiere on 22 November 1928, Rubinstein danced in Bronislava Nijinska’s choreography. The scenario placed her on a table in a Spanish tavern; Alexandre Benois supplied the designs.

cues.title: The tenor saxophone
cues.text: The second melody passes to the tenor saxophone. Its single reed gives the long notes a different edge from the bassoon’s earlier statement; the accompaniment is accumulating without abandoning its repeated pattern.

cues.title: A higher saxophone
cues.text: The saxophone colour moves higher for the repeated melody. Follow the long line over the short drum strokes: the melody crosses the bar lines while the accompaniment keeps counting in three.

cues.title: An invented composite tone
cues.text: Horn, celesta and two piccolos combine on the first melody. The celesta adds high octaves; the piccolos reinforce other upper pitches. Ravel constructs a composite tone by making separate instruments behave like components of one sound.

cues.title: The house at Montfort
cues.text: Ravel settled at Le Belvédère in Montfort-l’Amaury in 1921. The small house still preserves his piano and collections, including coffee cups with holes: objects whose appearances conceal deliberate tricks.

cues.title: A choir of reeds
cues.text: Oboe, oboe d’amore, cor anglais and clarinets take over the first melody. The solo succession is becoming a succession of mixtures; several wind players now shape the tune together.

cues.title: The exposed trombone
cues.text: A solo trombone takes the second melody high in its range. The line’s wide descent is now a brass solo rather than a woodwind one, with the drum still refusing to change its rhythm.

cues.title: The winds answer together
cues.text: A larger woodwind combination repeats the second melody. The change from one exposed trombone to several winds widens the sound without providing another tune.

cues.title: The violins take the tune
cues.text: The first violins join the melodic foreground with the winds. Until this stage, the strings have principally served the accompaniment; bowed string tone now becomes part of the tune’s increasing weight.

cues.title: More strings, wider spacing
cues.text: The second violins join the first in the melody’s next statement. Doubling the line across registers increases its breadth; repetition is now also a test of how much sound the same notes can carry.

cues.title: Factories rather than taverns
cues.text: In a 1932 interview with the London Evening Standard, Ravel connected Boléro with his fascination for factory machinery. He said he wanted a vast factory in the background of a staging, rather than treating the tavern as the only possible setting.

cues.title: Find the original bass
cues.text: Through the thicker strings and winds, try to keep hold of the repeated bass and snare rhythm. The foreground keeps acquiring players, but those simple underlying patterns are what make each addition measurable.

cues.title: A sharper orchestral edge
cues.text: Another increase in weight and upper-register sound brings the second melody closer to the final orchestral statements. The phrases still descend to their familiar endings; the crescendo does not rewrite them.

cues.title: The first tune’s last round
cues.text: The first melody makes its final complete statement. Compare this massed sound with the solitary flute at the beginning: orchestration has supplied nearly all the large-scale change.

cues.title: One more second melody
cues.text: The second melody returns at almost the full weight of the orchestra. Keep listening beneath it: the decisive change will be in the harmonic foundation, after so many repetitions over C and G.

cues.title: The sudden E major
cues.text: The harmony finally moves to E major, a major third above C. After nearly thirteen minutes of a fixed tonal centre, eight bars in another key carry the force of a much larger disruption.

cues.title: The final rupture
cues.text: C returns amid trombone slides and percussion. The orchestra takes up the rhythm that the snare has maintained from the opening; the last dissonance falls onto C major, and the sound cuts off rather than fading through a diminuendo.

intro: Before the solo horn of the orchestral version, there was a piano melody held above evenly spaced chords. Thérèse Dussaut plays the 1899 original: an imagined court dance, not the funeral of a particular princess.

cues.title: A line above the chords
cues.text: The piano gives the melody the top of the texture, above evenly spaced chords. Listen for the first long note: it is held across the middle of the bar, so the tune does not simply march in step with its accompaniment.

cues.title: A student of Fauré
cues.text: Ravel wrote the Pavane in 1899, two years after entering Fauré’s composition class at the Paris Conservatoire. Fauré also introduced him to the salon of the Princesse de Polignac, who became the work’s dedicatee.

cues.title: Let the phrase release
cues.text: In this first contrasting episode, a brief swell gives way to a much quieter phrase. Listen to the piano’s decay between attacks: Dussaut can reduce the weight of a chord without letting the dance’s underlying pulse disappear.

cues.title: The refrain comes back
cues.text: The opening melody returns. This is a rondo principle on a small scale: the familiar tune separates contrasting episodes, giving the ear a fixed point without requiring every passage to sound alike.

cues.title: An imagined Spanish court
cues.text: The title does not commemorate a particular dead princess. Ravel described a dance that such a princess might have performed at the Spanish court in earlier centuries; the pavane supplies a historical dance type, not a funeral programme.

cues.title: The contrasting central episode
cues.text: After a pause, a new episode opens a different harmonic region. The movement is still measured, but the phrases now build to stronger peaks than those of the opening refrain.

cues.title: Another rise and retreat
cues.text: The episode repeats its pattern of expansion and release. Keep the upper melody in focus as the chords grow heavier beneath it; the louder writing still needs a distinct singing line.

cues.title: The final return
cues.text: The opening tune returns after a nearly silent pause. Its familiarity restores the refrain’s proportions after the broader episode; this last appearance carries the piece to its close.

cues.title: From piano to orchestra
cues.text: Ricardo Viñes gave the piano premiere on 5 April 1902 at the Société nationale de musique. Ravel orchestrated the piece in 1910, giving its opening melody to a solo horn; this recording preserves the earlier keyboard version.

cues.title: The final G major
cues.text: The last G major chord is allowed to ring. With no new notes to sustain the line, the piano’s natural decay becomes the ending.

intro: Four string players begin by putting their bows aside. The scherzo sets plucked attacks against sustained lines, with a slower middle section interrupting the friction between groups of two and three.

cues.title: Four plucked instruments
cues.text: All four players begin pizzicato: plucking the strings rather than bowing them. The short attacks expose the rhythmic disagreement inside the bar, where groups of three quavers compete with groups of two.

cues.title: Bows change the attack
cues.text: The bowed writing allows the line to continue between attacks instead of dying away after each pluck. Listen for the contrast between a singing phrase and the clipped rhythm: Ravel makes changes of playing technique part of the form.

cues.title: Dedicated to his teacher
cues.text: Ravel completed the quartet in 1903 and dedicated it to Gabriel Fauré. He had entered Fauré’s composition class in 1897 and continued attending as an auditor after losing his formal place at the Conservatoire.

cues.title: A muted middle section
cues.text: The busy scherzo gives way to a slow middle section, with mutes on the strings. Sustained lines replace the opening’s exposed pattern of attacks; the change in colour is as important as the change of pace.

cues.title: Paris, March 1904
cues.text: The Heymann Quartet gave the first performance on 5 March 1904 at a Société nationale de musique concert in Paris. This remained Ravel’s only string quartet, although he later returned to strings alone in the Sonata for Violin and Cello.

cues.title: Long notes, moving harmony
cues.text: In this middle section, changes of harmony do not require the crisp collective attacks of the opening. Follow the sustained parts separately: a line can continue while another player changes the chord around it.

cues.title: Motion begins to gather
cues.text: Shorter gestures begin to restore the scherzo’s activity. The return is prepared through changing articulation and more frequent attacks before the opening music regains its full force.

cues.title: Debussy’s earlier quartet
cues.text: Debussy’s quartet of 1893 also places a pizzicato scherzo second in a four-movement design. Ravel likewise carries related themes between movements; the shared framework was one reason early critics compared the two works.

cues.title: The plucked pulse rebuilds
cues.text: The quick, short attacks return quietly before the opening material recovers its strength. Listen to their spacing rather than their volume: rhythmic activity can increase while the players still hold the sound back.

cues.title: The scherzo restored
cues.text: The opening material is back in a shortened return. Plucked attacks again alternate with bowed melody; the quartet does not need extra instruments to make two sharply different kinds of sound.

cues.title: Short strokes to finish
cues.text: The longer bowed phrases give way to shorter attacks. Listen to the spaces between the last notes: their separate strokes, followed by the strings’ decay, close the movement.

composer.name: Béla Bartók
composer.born: 25 March 1881, Nagyszentmiklós, Hungary (now Sânnicolau Mare, Romania)
composer.epithet: A pianist and fieldworker who turned the modes, rhythms and performance habits of peasant music into new kinds of quartet and orchestral argument.
facts: Budapest Academy of Music, 1899–1903: piano with István Thomán, composition with Hans Koessler
Piano professor, Budapest Academy, 1907–34 · Hungarian Academy of Sciences folk-music project, 1934–40 · Columbia University research in American exile
Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian villages · Biskra, Algeria, 1913 · Turkey, 1936
Six string quartets · three piano concertos · two violin concertos · three stage works · folk-music collections and pedagogical music
composer.background:
Bartók was born in Nagyszentmiklós, a town in the Hungarian half of Austria-Hungary which became part of Romania after the First World War. His father, who directed an agricultural school, died in 1888; his mother, Paula Voit, supported Béla and his sister by teaching. After several moves the family settled in Pozsony, now Bratislava. The changing names on this map matter: the Hungarian, Slovak and Romanian communities he later recorded occupied overlapping musical territories. His professional education began within the German-speaking conservatoire tradition.

At the Budapest Academy from 1899 to 1903, he studied piano with István Thomán, a pupil of Liszt, and composition with Hans Koessler. Hearing Richard Strauss’s Also sprach Zarathustra in 1902 helped release him from student exercises. Kossuth, composed in 1903, made the Hungarian revolutionary leader the subject of a large orchestral narrative and caricatured Haydn’s imperial anthem as the Austrian enemy. This early nationalist programme preceded the comparative research that would complicate his understanding of national music.

intro: The fast movement of Bartók’s Second Quartet sets repeated notes against shifting accents. Its narrow melodic figures owe something to the Arab music he recorded in Algeria, rather than to a Hungarian dance tune.

cues.title: A pitch that stays put
cues.text: After a short opening gesture, the second violin repeats D in octaves while the other instruments move around it. The accompaniment behaves like a drone with a pulse: its pitch stays fixed, but its repeated attacks keep the dance moving.

cues.title: An anchor, not a key
cues.text: A repeated pitch does not necessarily establish a major or minor key. Listen to D as an anchor against changing notes around it; the dissonances come from the moving parts, not from a new bass chord on every beat.

cues.title: Algeria, 1913
cues.text: Bartók travelled to Biskra and nearby settlements in Algeria in June 1913 to record Arab music. The narrow melodies and repeated rhythmic figures of this movement absorb aspects of that music; the quartet is not an arrangement of a collected Hungarian tune.

cues.title: The repeated attacks return
cues.text: The rapid reiterations return after a less densely articulated passage. Four bowed instruments can behave like a percussion ensemble without losing their separate pitches: listen for the repeated notes against the more mobile lines.

cues.title: The dance breaks apart
cues.text: The continuous drive gives way to quieter, separated gestures. This movement works like a loose rondo: the insistent dance can return between episodes whose thinner textures interrupt its momentum.

cues.title: A recording and a notebook
cues.text: Bartók began collecting with a phonograph in 1906, but kept writing melodies down in the field as well. A wax cylinder preserved one performance; the notebook let him compare verses and correct a singer’s accidental slip rather than treating the recording as definitive.

cues.title: Almost below the surface
cues.text: The quartet sinks to one of the movement’s quietest passages. Short figures and gaps replace the earlier stream of repeated attacks; listen for the individual parts rather than trying to maintain the opening’s pounding pulse.

cues.title: A quartet during the war
cues.text: Bartók completed the work in 1917 and dedicated it to the Waldbauer–Kerpely Quartet, which gave the Budapest premiere on 3 March 1918. This fast movement is enclosed by a Moderato and a slow finale: the whole quartet does not end with the dance.

cues.title: A sharper edge
cues.text: Listen for the increasingly bright edge to the string sound as this passage continues. Longer-held notes can intensify the texture without increasing the number of attacks; the next return of the repeated figures will change that balance again.

cues.title: The drive comes back
cues.text: The repeated-note drive returns at full force. Hear the change in articulation as well as volume: the sustained sounds of the previous passage give way to tightly packed attacks.

cues.title: Pressure, then withdrawal
cues.text: A forceful crest gives way to a long drop in volume. The quieter ending that follows is not a slow movement: Bartók is preparing to combine extreme speed with restrained sound.

cues.title: Prestissimo under the breath
cues.text: The closing rush is marked Prestissimo, but also pianissimo and muted. A mute damps a string instrument’s bridge, changing its colour as well as its volume; the rapid notes need not sound like another loud climax.

cues.title: The final burst
cues.text: The quiet coda turns sharply louder for its last gestures. The cutoff comes quickly after this final burst; within the complete quartet, a slow Lento follows rather than another fast conclusion.

composer.name: Igor Stravinsky
composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: A composer of ballets who made the placement of an accent as consequential as a change of harmony.
facts: Russia · Switzerland 1914–20 · France 1920–39 · United States from 1939
Sergei Diaghilev · Vaslav Nijinsky · C. F. Ramuz · George Balanchine · W. H. Auden
Ballets, operas, symphonies, sacred choral music and chamber works; three successive approaches to tonality
composer.background:
Igor Stravinsky grew up in a St Petersburg household in which opera was a profession: his father, Fyodor, was a bass at the Mariinsky Theatre. Born at the family’s summer residence in Oranienbaum in 1882, Igor began piano lessons at ten but entered St Petersburg University to study law. Through a fellow student, Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, he met Vladimir’s father, whose private teaching became more important than a conservatory course. Regular lessons between 1905 and 1908 covered orchestration as practical work: distributing a passage among instruments, then comparing the result with the teacher’s solution. The Symphony in E♭, Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks belong to this apprenticeship, with traces of Tchaikovsky, Alexander Glazunov and the Russian fairy-tale orchestra.

In 1906 he married his cousin Catherine Nossenko; their four children were born between 1907 and 1914. Sergei Diaghilev heard the young composer’s orchestral music in 1909 and first employed him to orchestrate Chopin for Les Sylphides. A larger commission followed: The Firebird, with choreography by Michel Fokine. Its premiere at the Paris Opéra on 25 June 1910, with Tamara Karsavina in the title role, made Stravinsky’s reputation outside Russia. The distinction between human and supernatural characters is audible in the harmony: folk-like diatonic tunes for Ivan and the princesses, chromatic and symmetrical scales for the Firebird and Kashchei. The closing horn melody expands into an orchestral procession without abandoning its short repeating phrases.

intro: The Firebird forces the sorcerer Kashchei and his creatures to dance until they collapse. This is Thomas Knox’s wind-band arrangement: brass, woodwind and percussion carry the ballet’s displaced accents without an orchestral string section.
license: Public domain in the US (US Marine Band recording; composition published 1910)

cues.title: Kashchei’s enforced dance
cues.text: This is not a dance the sorcerer chooses: the Firebird compels him and his followers to move. The opening’s separated gestures gather into more continuous motion; in this band arrangement, wind attacks carry the rhythmic edges normally shared with orchestral strings.

cues.title: From law to orchestration
cues.text: Stravinsky entered St Petersburg University to study law in 1901. His decisive musical training came privately from Rimsky-Korsakov, whose regular lessons in 1905–08 included the practical work of orchestration; he did not follow a conservatoire course.

cues.title: Accents across the pulse
cues.text: Follow the underlying pulse separately from the accented notes. The short figures become more crowded and the sound brighter, but a sudden reduction in volume is approaching; the dance advances through contrasts rather than one continuous crescendo.

cues.title: Paris, June 1910
cues.text: The Firebird opened at the Paris Opéra on 25 June 1910 for Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes. Michel Fokine choreographed it and Tamara Karsavina danced the title role. Stravinsky had turned twenty-eight only eight days before the premiere.

cues.title: A longer line
cues.text: The sharply articulated gestures give way to more sustained writing. Listen for a longer melodic span across the pulse: the number of separate attacks drops, even as the band begins to increase its weight again.

cues.title: Low and suddenly quiet
cues.text: The sound abruptly drops into a darker, quieter register. Repeated figures gather again from this reduced texture, becoming more active before the brighter upper sound returns.

cues.title: Two more ballets
cues.text: Diaghilev followed The Firebird with commissions for Petrushka, first performed in 1911, and The Rite of Spring in 1913. Within four Paris seasons, Stravinsky moved from this Russian fairy tale to a puppet’s tragedy and an invented pagan sacrifice.

cues.title: The closing surge
cues.text: The band builds to another forceful peak, then pulls back. Keep listening through that retreat: the strongest sustained sound is still to come, rather than at the first crest of the closing passage.

cues.title: The final sound holds
cues.text: The last sonority is held rather than driven forward by repeated attacks. Its sustained weight makes the ending different from the clipped figures that began the dance; the remaining sound is allowed to die away.

composer.background:
Prokofiev grew up on the Sontsovka estate in Ukraine, where his father managed the agricultural business and his mother played Beethoven and Chopin at the piano. He remembered hearing sonatas from another room after being put to bed. The keyboard was therefore familiar before the concert hall: his mother wrote down his first pieces, and a visit to Moscow opera performances in 1900 prompted the nine-year-old to compose The Giant for performance at home. Sergei Taneyev subsequently recommended professional instruction. Reinhold Glière spent the summers of 1902 and 1903 at Sontsovka, teaching composition and helping the boy turn his accumulating pieces into larger forms.

He entered the St Petersburg Conservatory at thirteen, bringing manuscripts of his compositions. Rimsky-Korsakov taught orchestration, Anatoly Lyadov harmony and counterpoint, Nikolai Tcherepnin conducting, and Anna Esipova piano. Tcherepnin’s attention to Haydn and Mozart mattered as much as the harmonic experiments Prokofiev pursued outside class. Nikolai Myaskovsky, an older fellow student, became a lifelong correspondent and a critic whose objections he took seriously. Their correspondence continued to test decisions about form and orchestration long after the Conservatory.

intro: Two hands share a stream of repeated notes; chromatic lines and displaced accents keep changing what those notes mean. Martha Argerich plays the Toccata Prokofiev wrote while he was still a St Petersburg Conservatory student.

cues.title: One note, two hands
cues.text: The hands share repeated Ds before chromatic neighbours begin crowding the note. Listen for the difference between the steady semiquavers and the accents laid across them: the pulse stays regular while the weight keeps moving.

cues.title: A classmate’s fingers
cues.text: Prokofiev dedicated the Toccata to Nikolay Shtember, his fellow pupil in Anna Esipova’s piano class at the St Petersburg Conservatory. Written in spring 1912, it tested Shtember’s technique and the composer’s own.

cues.title: Seventy-five roubles
cues.text: Koussevitzky’s publishing firm rejected the Toccata. Jurgenson offered fifty roubles; Prokofiev negotiated seventy-five, then complained about the delayed proofs. The first edition finally appeared in July 1913.

cues.title: The mechanism thins
cues.text: The volume falls sharply and D becomes a fixed point again. Prokofiev does not insert a slow melody here: he reduces the weight of the repeated-note writing, letting the same basic mechanism work more quietly.

cues.title: More weight, less stability
cues.text: The quieter stretch gives way to a much heavier passage. Chromatic movement takes the harmony away from the repeated D of the opening; follow the changing bass beneath the attacks rather than trying to turn every accent into a new beat.

cues.title: A restrained American debut
cues.text: At his American debut in the Brooklyn Museum on 29 October 1918, Prokofiev played the Toccata before a reception for an exhibition of Boris Anisfeld’s work. According to his diary, he softened its impact for the audience, even leaving notes out.

cues.title: D takes the weight
cues.text: D settles into the bass again, now under much louder playing than at the opening. The returning pitch gives the ear a reference point even while the upper notes continue to collide with it.

cues.title: The attacks almost stop
cues.text: The sound drains away and the repeated attacks become widely spaced. This interruption matters because nearly everything before it has depended on maintaining the stream of semiquavers.

cues.title: A last concentrated burst
cues.text: After that break, rapid attacks return at full weight. Listen through the final blow to its decay: the piece stops the repeated-note pattern rather than fading it into the distance.

movement: Complete · Allegro ma non troppo — Scherzo — Andante — Vivace
intro: Written in 1912, the Second Sonata puts long melodies, a short scherzo and a tarantella finale into four movements. Listen for the accompaniment: changing the notes beneath a melody often changes its character more drastically than changing the melody itself.

cues.title: Two against three
cues.text: The opening melody moves in pairs while the accompaniment divides the beat into three. Listen to the hands separately: the melodic line and the triplets beneath it organise the same pulse differently.

cues.title: Before the Conservatory
cues.text: Prokofiev’s mother was his first piano teacher. Private study with Reinhold Glière preceded his admission to the St Petersburg Conservatory at thirteen; there, Rimsky-Korsakov taught him orchestration and Lyadov taught harmony and counterpoint.

cues.title: A longer melodic breath
cues.text: In this more restrained passage, follow the tune across the accompaniment’s smaller gestures. The first movement sets a singing second idea against its sharply articulated material; the contrast is between ways of phrasing, not simply loud and soft.

cues.title: Moscow, February 1914
cues.text: Jurgenson published the sonata in 1913, before its first public performance. Prokofiev introduced it himself on 5 February 1914 in the Small Hall of the Moscow Conservatory.

cues.title: The development begins
cues.text: A quiet close gives way to renewed activity. This is the development: material already heard is taken apart and put into different combinations, rather than simply repeated in its original order.

cues.title: Short figures gain weight
cues.text: The middle of the movement grows heavier through repeated short gestures. Listen for the distinction between a fragment that keeps coming back and a melody that carries on to its next phrase: the development works largely with the former.

cues.title: His own examination piece
cues.text: For the Conservatory’s 1914 piano competition, Prokofiev played his First Piano Concerto rather than a concerto by an established composer. He won the Anton Rubinstein Prize for piano playing; the work he submitted was his own.

cues.title: Return with altered balance
cues.text: Earlier material returns, but Prokofiev does not preserve the first hearing’s balance. Listen for familiar figures with changed accompaniment and register: a return in sonata form need not be a replay.

cues.title: Diaghilev’s rejected ballet
cues.text: In London in 1914, Prokofiev met Sergei Diaghilev. The ballet commission that followed, Ala and Lolli, was rejected; its music survived in the Scythian Suite. The pianist was already seeking work in the theatre.

cues.title: Growing out of a sonatina
cues.text: The first movement grew from an earlier sonatina. Prokofiev added a scherzo drawn from a piece written for Lyadov’s composition class, then two new movements. Reworking earlier material was part of the sonata’s construction from the beginning.

cues.title: A compact closing surge
cues.text: After the softened phrases, the piano gathers weight for a compact close. Notice how quickly the surge gives way to a pause: the first movement does not run straight into the scherzo.

cues.title: The scherzo takes over
cues.text: The second movement replaces the first movement’s long argument with short, sharply accented figures. A recurring accompaniment keeps the motion going while the hands throw brief gestures across it.

cues.title: Less weight, clipped gestures
cues.text: The volume drops abruptly in the scherzo’s middle section. The gestures remain short, but their spacing and emphasis change; listen for articulation, the length of each note, rather than only for a new tune.

cues.title: A heavier scherzo close
cues.text: The short figures gather weight again. Their repeated attacks now produce a louder closing stretch, with much less room between gestures than the slow movement will allow.

cues.title: The Andante opens
cues.text: The slow movement begins with a rocking accompaniment beneath a gradually unfolding melody. After the scherzo’s short attacks, the pianist has to sustain a line across the decay of individual piano notes.

cues.title: The dedication came later
cues.text: The published sonata is dedicated to Maximilian Schmidthof, Prokofiev’s fellow student and close friend, who died by suicide in 1913. The music had been completed in 1912, before his death; the dedication is not a programme for its four movements.

cues.title: A slow phrase expands
cues.text: The line grows louder without acquiring the scherzo’s density of attacks. Prokofiev builds this swell by increasing the weight of a slow phrase rather than replacing it with a fast one.

cues.title: More than two voices
cues.text: In the Andante’s more layered writing, separate the upper melody from the moving inner notes and the bass. The middle voice has its own chromatic line; it is not simply filling in chords beneath the tune.

cues.title: Three works from 1912
cues.text: The Second Sonata belongs to the same year as the Toccata, Op. 11, and the completion of the First Piano Concerto. The repeated-note study, the concerto and this four-movement work test different uses of the same instrument.

cues.title: The slow movement’s weight
cues.text: The strongest sustained sonority in this recording arrives inside the slow movement, not the finale. The long phrase reaches its peak through heavier playing while retaining the Andante’s measured pace.

cues.title: Lyricism was there already
cues.text: Prokofiev later complained that critics had overlooked the lyrical element in his early music. In his 1941 autobiography he ranked it above the toccata-like writing for which he was already famous.

cues.title: A tarantella finale
cues.text: The finale sets off as a tarantella, a quick dance in compound time: each main beat divides into three. Its running accompaniment restores continuous motion after the Andante’s pauses.

cues.title: Eastward out of Russia
cues.text: In 1918 Prokofiev left Russia by travelling east through Siberia and Japan to the United States. His subsequent career took him between America and Europe before he settled with his family in Moscow in 1936.

cues.title: Listen for the interruption
cues.text: The rushing finale is about to pull back sharply. Listen through the quieter gap rather than treating it as an ending: Prokofiev interrupts the running texture and then sets the music moving again.

cues.title: The attacks crowd together
cues.text: The quieter restart gives way to more closely packed attacks. Keep track of the lower part as the upper figures become busier: the accompaniment helps distinguish the phrase from the rapid notes on its surface.

cues.title: An archival performance
cues.text: The Commons file credits E.M. Zinger and dates this performance to 8 October 1962. Its stated source is the archive of the Glinka Novosibirsk Conservatory, rather than a commercial record label.

cues.title: Melody within the pattern
cues.text: As the figures become busier again, listen for the notes that stand out above the pattern. Rapid piano writing can carry a melodic outline inside its passagework; not every struck note needs equal emphasis.

cues.title: Weight to the end
cues.text: The closing passage keeps its weight rather than gradually diminishing. Listen through the last attacks to the final sound’s decay: there is no extended quiet coda after the finale’s argument.
